items.title: Cataloguing what it binds
items.text:
The plane brings nineteen document specs your application never writes — sessions, credentials, grants, tenant bindings. If you declare a spec inventory, merge them in rather than listing them by hand, so an identity release cannot leave your catalogue behind:

specs = SpecRegistry().register(order_spec).merge(forze_identity.spec_contributions())

Wiring only part of the plane? Name the parts you wire. spec_contributions() catalogues all three planes, and the inventory check refuses a spec catalogued but never bound, so an authn-only application has to narrow it:

forze_identity.spec_contributions(planes=["authn"])

Narrow only for a plane you genuinely do not wire — the check is worth keeping strict, and it still fires from the bound side if you narrow too far. One caveat that is easy to miss, and it is the default: authn's principal-eligibility gate reads the authz policy-principal document unless you opt out, so planes=["authn"] belongs with eligibility="allow_all" on the authn module — the declared opt-out for a deployment with no authz plane. Leave the gate on its default and authn binds an authz document, which the inventory check will tell you about.

Identity settles who the caller is; scoping which data they may reach is Multi-tenancy.

items.title: Multi-tenancy
items.text:
When one deployment serves many customers, three questions that sound alike are actually distinct — and Forze keeps them apart:

  • Who is calling — the authenticated principal (AuthnIdentity).
  • Which tenant the request belongs to — TenantIdentity.
  • How that tenant's data stays isolated from everyone else's.

Keeping these separate is what lets the same handler serve every tenant without a line of tenant-handling code in it.

items.title: Binding the tenant to a request
items.text:
At the boundary — HTTP middleware, typically — a request is authenticated, its tenant resolved, and both bound to the execution context:

  1. Authenticate into an AuthnIdentity (plus an optional hint, such as a JWT tid claim).
  2. Resolve the TenantIdentity. A resolver validates any hints against the principal's actual memberships — it is authoritative, so a hint can never grant access the principal doesn't have. With no hint, a principal with no membership, or with several, gets no tenant, and tenant-scoped work refuses it.
  3. Bind both with ctx.inv_ctx.bind(...), so every adapter can call ctx.inv_ctx.get_tenant() on its own.

From there, adapters read the tenant themselves. A handler never threads a tenant_id through its arguments — it just asks for the orders port and gets this tenant's orders.

Don't authenticate against tenant-scoped data

Credential checks run before the tenant is resolved. If an authentication route reads a tenant-scoped store, bootstrap can deadlock. Keep the document routes used during authentication tenant-unaware.

items.title: Where to draw the boundary
items.text:
Isolation is layered — you choose where one tenant's data ends and the next's begins. The same TenantIdentity can decide a marker on each row, the namespace it lives in, or the whole connection. Forze names these three tiers, weakest to strongest, and every integration reports which one its wiring actually reaches:

Tier What tenants share Reached by tagged one container — every record carries its tenant, a filter a forgotten predicate can leak past tenant_aware=True (a SQL tenant_id column, a graph property, a Redis key prefix, an object-store path prefix) namespace a separate container each on one instance — a name boundary a query can't cross a per-tenant resolver on every relation a route names (a Postgres schema, a Mongo collection, a dataset, a bucket, an index, a Redis or queue namespace) dedicated nothing — a separate instance per tenant a routed client resolving per-tenant credentials

The names are deliberately storage-agnostic — they classify by the isolation you get, not the switch you flip. The jump that matters is tagged → namespace: a tagged marker is a filter a forgotten predicate can leak past (a SQL tenant_id column, a graph property — table partitioning included, since pruning still relies on the marker), whereas a namespace is a separate container — a name-resolution boundary a query cannot cross.

So tenant_aware=True reaches tagged on every backend. On a key/path store the marker is a prefix (tenant:{id}:… on Redis, a path prefix on object storage, a prefixed queue name). A per-tenant resolver, and routed clients, reach namespace and dedicated the same way everywhere. Wiring rates the switch, not what it builds: a Redis per-tenant namespace rates namespace though its keys share one keyspace, and a tenant_aware queue rates tagged though each tenant gets a queue of its own.

items.title: The tenant marker (tagged)
items.text: The lightest cut: one connection, one shared container, a tenant marker. tenant_aware=True makes the adapter filter every read and stamp every write with the bound tenant — a tenant_id column on Postgres or Mongo, a property on a graph node, a key or path prefix on Redis or object storage. Correctness rests on the marker: a forgotten predicate leaks. Combining it with a stronger cut is redundant — acceptable as defense-in-depth, and startup warns when it spots the overlap.

items.title: Per-tenant containers (namespace)
items.text:
A container per tenant — a name boundary a query can't cross. Point a route's relation — or its named resource, a bucket / dataset / index / namespace — at a resolver instead of a static value, evaluated per request against the bound tenant:

PostgresDocumentConfig(
    read=lambda tid: (f"tenant_{tid.hex[:8]}", "orders"),
    write=lambda tid: (f"tenant_{tid.hex[:8]}", "orders"),
    bookkeeping_strategy="application",
)

Every relation the route names needs a resolver: one static relation holds every tenant's rows, so the route keeps the tier its tenant_aware flag gives. It counts even when the spec doesn't use it, such as a history table with history off. The tenancy matrix lists the routes that work differently.

Because the name is only known per request, startup schema validation (which needs fixed names) skips these routes.

items.title: Routed clients (dedicated)
items.text:
A routed client resolves credentials per TenantIdentity and pools connections by fingerprint, so tenants that share an endpoint reuse pools. You swap it in at wiring time — RoutedPostgresClient for PostgresClient — and the specs and handlers don't change. For backend calls the routed facade doesn't wrap, client_scope() yields the current tenant's pooled inner client.

Credential rotation. The fingerprint is a rebuild trigger: when a tenant's stored credentials change, the pooled client is evicted and rebuilt — wire your secret store's rotation signal to evict_tenant(), or set fingerprint_ttl to poll. That model fits credentials that change rarely. A provider that mints short-lived tokens is different: fingerprint only the stable identity (endpoint, account, key id) and have the client fetch the current token through a callback per connection or request — feeding the token into the fingerprint would read every mint as a rotation and tear down a healthy pool.

Eviction affects work in flight on the old client too: unguarded (the default) it is disposed immediately, failing whatever is mid-call; guarded=True drains it only after in-flight operations finish. Long-lived streams re-acquire the pooled client per poll (the routed SQS consume does), so a rotation moves the consumer onto fresh credentials at the next poll instead of tearing it down.

Postgres routed clients

Set introspector_cache_partition_key on the deps module so the schema catalog cache partitions by tenant — required when the client is routed.

items.title: Which integration reaches which tier
items.text:
Each integration derives the tier its wiring reaches, and the backend sets the ceiling — an in-process store can't route a per-tenant connection. Three shapes cover it:

  • A column store (Postgres / Mongo / Firestore documents, most analytics) spans the whole ladder: tagged (column) → namespace (schema/collection resolver) → dedicated (routed client).
  • A key/path store (Redis, S3/GCS, queues) spans the same ladder: tagged (a tenant key or path prefix) → namespace (a per-tenant namespace or bucket resolver) → dedicated (routed client).
  • An in-process backend caps low: DuckDB analytics at tagged, the mock at namespace, with no routed-client equivalent.

The exhaustive per-port breakdown — every integration, its mechanism, and its ceiling — is the tenancy matrix.

Isolating messaging you consume

A store you query under the bound tenant scopes itself. A stream or queue you drain in the background does not: the consumer runs with no ambient tenant, so isolating it means binding the tenant on the read side — a sharded gateway/relay for realtime, or a per-tenant worker for a queue. The outbox stays tenant-global by default (rows carry their tenant for routing, not isolation; the relay binds each row's tenant as it forwards). The per-resource read-side rules are in the tenancy matrix.

items.title: Declaring a minimum
items.text:
Deriving a tier is descriptive. You can also make it prescriptive: set required_tenant_isolation on any deps module and wiring refuses to assemble anything weaker — a fail-closed floor checked once, at startup, never per request.

PostgresDepsModule(
    client=RoutedPostgresClient(...),
    required_tenant_isolation="dedicated",  # nothing short of a per-tenant connection
)

Each module derives the tier it actually reaches from the config it already carries — a routed client → dedicated, a per-tenant resolver on every relation a route names → namespace (the tenancy matrix lists the exceptions), tenant_aware → tagged — and raises a clear configuration error when that's below the floor. A floor a backend can never reach (dedicated on in-process DuckDB, or on single-client Neo4j) fails as a capability mismatch rather than a silent misconfiguration, because each integration's ceiling is known. Leave it unset (the default) and nothing is enforced.

Where the floor earns its keep

Untrusted or self-scoping query paths — a raw SQL hatch, an analytics query trusted to filter itself — are only as safe as the store underneath them. Declaring required_tenant_isolation="dedicated" refuses to wire them anywhere a shared store could leak.

A route that executes statement text the framework didn't build carries a second, undeclarable floor from its StatementOrigin — see Tenancy matrix → statement origin.

items.title: Provisioning per-tenant infrastructure
items.text:
The stronger tiers assume the per-tenant container already exists — a schema, a dataset, a bucket. Onboarding a tenant should create it; offboarding should tear it down. TenantProvisionerPort is that seam, wired through the tenancy module:

from forze.application.integrations.storage import ObjectStorageTenantProvisioner
from forze_identity.tenancy.execution import TenancyDepsModule

TenancyDepsModule(
    tenant_management={"main"},
    tenant_provisioner=ObjectStorageTenantProvisioner(
        client=s3_client,
        bucket=lambda tid: f"tenant-{tid}",
    ),
)

TenantManagementPort.provision_tenant(...) records the tenant first, then runs the provisioner — a failure leaves the record for an idempotent retry — and deprovision_tenant(...) runs the inverse. Provisioners are idempotent and receive the onboarded TenantIdentity explicitly: it is generally not the ambient bound tenant, since an admin onboards tenant X without acting as X. Compose one per integration with CompositeTenantProvisioner, wrap a callable with FunctionTenantProvisioner, or ship nothing (NoopTenantProvisioner, the default) and provision out of band. Forze includes ObjectStorageTenantProvisioner (ensures a bucket) and, from forze_postgres, PostgresSchemaTenantProvisioner (CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS) — teardown is opt-in wherever it would destroy data.

A tenant-routed client resolves its backend from the ambient tenant, so the database provisioners (Postgres, MongoDB) refuse one: pass the unrouted admin client for the deployment the tenants live on. ObjectStorageTenantProvisioner accepts a routed S3 or GCS client and names the onboarded tenant to it, so the bucket is created on that tenant's own backend with its credentials — which must already resolve when provision_tenant runs.

MongoDB has no schema to create — a database exists once something is written to it — so MongoDatabaseTenantProvisioner (forze_mongo) writes a marker document into the tenant's own database instead. The write proves at onboarding that the connection can reach the tenant's container, and the marker records who is in that container, so an offboarding that drops the database can refuse when the name resolves somewhere another tenant lives — and it holds a lock kept outside that database while it decides, so an onboarding cannot land in the gap between the check and the drop.

Isolating tenants by data boundary pairs naturally with isolating them by key — sealing each tenant's data under its own keys is Encryption.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
Every integration is an optional package — forze[postgres], forze[redis], and so on — that implements Forze contracts for one backend. They share a common shape: a client and ports in kernel/, concrete adapters/, and execution/ deps + lifecycle modules you wire exactly as shown in Wiring. Your handlers never import them; they resolve ports from the context.

Per-backend pages cover the specifics — configuration, schema expectations, and caveats. The authoritative, always-current set is the [project.optional-dependencies] extras in pyproject.toml; each forze[<name>] maps to the <name> extra.

items.title: Available integrations
items.text:
Area Extras Data postgres · mongo · firestore · neo4j · redis · s3 · gcs · meilisearch · bigquery · clickhouse · duckdb Messaging kafka · rabbitmq · sqs Workflows temporal · inngest Inbound fastapi · socketio · mcp Identity authn · oidc Secrets & keys vault · kms-aws · kms-gcp · kms-yc Outbound http · inference-http · inference-sagemaker

Each row maps to a forze[<extra>] package; their precise contract coverage is on each integration's page. Two key backends need no extra at all: the self-hosted local KMS and the in-memory mock.

The remaining extras are not backend integrations: dst and cli are tooling (deterministic simulation testing and the forze command-line tool, whose ops group runs your operations from a terminal or a Job), mock-server serves the in-memory mock over HTTP, sandbox-container is the container tier of the sandbox execution plane, observability adds the OTLP exporter for telemetry, and zstd adds the zstd codec for portable archives.

Install one or several at once — uv add 'forze[fastapi,postgres,redis]'.

items.title: Connection settings
items.text:
Every integration ships a <Backend>Settings model holding the endpoint, the credentials and the client knobs a deployment sets — the thing an application would otherwise declare for itself, once per backend, and get subtly wrong. They are plain pydantic BaseModels, so you mount them on your own settings root and the environment fills them in:

from forze_postgres import PostgresSettings
from forze_rabbitmq import RabbitMQSettings
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_nested_delimiter="__")

    postgres: PostgresSettings = PostgresSettings()
    rabbitmq: RabbitMQSettings = RabbitMQSettings()

POSTGRES__HOST, RABBITMQ__VHOST and the rest then populate them. The prefix, the delimiter and the extra-key policy stay yours — Forze ships no BaseSettings root, because those are deployment decisions.

Each model exposes what its wiring takes:

It gives you Where it goes .dsn / .uri / .url / .address / .servers the lifecycle step's connection argument .config the same step's config=, as the backend's own config object .require_host() / .require_endpoint() / .require_project_id() wherever the wiring wants a plain str 
lifecycle = LifecyclePlan.from_modules(
    postgres_lifecycle_step(dsn=settings.postgres.dsn, config=settings.postgres.config),
)

Three rules hold across all of them:

  • A missing endpoint is refused by name, when it is read rather than when the model is built — so Settings() still constructs with an empty environment, and a boot without POSTGRES__HOST fails saying so instead of dialling localhost.
  • Unset knobs are dropped, not forwarded as None. The defaults live in the backend's own config object, never in a second copy on the settings model.
  • Secrets are SecretStr and the assembled URL is one too wherever it carries a credential, so neither reaches a log by accident. The assembled value is a plain property rather than a serialized field: model_dump() on a settings root works even where a mounted backend was never configured, and no DSN lands in a dump.
  • ssl=True verifies the server certificate — sslmode=verify-full, neo4j+s://, rediss://, https://. A deployment that wants weaker TLS leaves the flag off and configures the backend's own environment variables.

The URL-building models share forze.base.settings.EndpointSettings for the parts that are URL grammar rather than backend knowledge — bracketing a bare IPv6 host, joining the port. The scheme and the query parameters stay in each package, because that is the part that actually differs.

forze.base.settings.RuntimeSettings is the same idea for the process itself: the argument lists of bootstrap_logging and bootstrap_telemetry. See Grafana stack.

Two packages ship no settings model, for the same reason both times: they are inbound, so there is no connection to configure. fastapi and mcp serve requests; where they bind is the deployment's uvicorn or transport concern, not the integration's.

Everything else has one, including the ones that are barely a connection at all: duckdb is in-process, so DuckDbSettings carries the database path and the two resource limits that decide whether a query is slow or the container is killed; SocketIOSettings carries the Redis backplane — the URL, the channel, and whether this process publishes without subscribing (build the URL from a RedisSettings.dsn, since integration packages do not import each other); GcpKmsSettings is one emulator endpoint and one timeout, because Google's credentials come from the ambient environment.

items.title: Authentication
items.text: forze[authn] is the built-in authentication stack — the forze_identity.authn plane. It implements the verify-then-resolve seam from Identity & access: password (Argon2), bearer-token (Forze JWT), and API-key verifiers, paired with resolvers that map a VerifiedAssertion to a UUID principal.

items.title: Install
items.text:
uv add 'forze[authn]'

It's document-backed — the account, session, and identity-mapping stores are ordinary document specs you wire to a database.

items.title: Wire it
items.text:
AuthnDepsModule registers a first-party stack per route. authn enables the credential families a route accepts; kernel carries the signing/secret config:

from forze.application.execution import DepsRegistry
from forze_identity.authn import AuthnDepsModule, AuthnKernelConfig

deps = DepsRegistry.from_modules(
    AuthnDepsModule(
        kernel=AuthnKernelConfig(...),
        authn={"api": frozenset({"token", "api_key"})},
    ),
)

A route's AuthnSpec selects verifiers and a resolver by profile name; override the defaults via token_verifiers, resolvers, etc. Each override must name a route in authn, and a verifier override a method that route enables; any other is refused when the module is built. A token_verifiers override also needs a resolvers override on its route: the default resolver would take an external token's subject as an internal principal id.

By default every wired route checks the authenticating principal against an active policy_principal document — the posture for deployments running the authz plane. A token-only service with no authz plane opts out explicitly:

AuthnDepsModule(..., eligibility="allow_all")

That is a declared decision, never a silent fallback (an unknown value is refused at wiring): with it, deactivating a principal no longer blocks token issuance, so revocation rests entirely on credential lifecycle — session revoke and API-key revoke.

items.title: What it provides
items.text: Capability Default implementation Dep key Orchestrator AuthnOrchestrator AuthnDepKey Token verifier ForzeJwtTokenVerifier TokenVerifierDepKey Password verifier Argon2PasswordVerifier PasswordVerifierDepKey API-key verifier HmacApiKeyVerifier ApiKeyVerifierDepKey Principal resolver JwtNativeUuidResolver PrincipalResolverDepKey

items.title: Check sessions and API keys from Redis
items.text:
By default every token verification reads its session row, and every API-key verification its key row. With revocation_states on the kernel, a token carries its session's family (fam) and the principal's epoch (pep), and the verifier checks them against states cached in Redis, reading Postgres only for what Redis misses. With key_mac too, every live cached state is signed, and API keys are checked the same way, from a state cached under the key's digest. The eligibility read stays for both, except that a token's is skipped when the authz kernel carries the same configuration (below).

from datetime import timedelta

from forze.application.contracts.authn import RevocationStatesDepKey
from forze.application.contracts.resilience import PortPolicy
from forze_identity.authn import AuthnKernelConfig, RevocationStates, StateMacKeys
from forze_postgres import PostgresPrincipalEpochConfig
from forze_redis import RedisRevocationStatesConfig

kernel = AuthnKernelConfig(
    access_token_secret=secret,
    refresh_token_pepper=pepper,
    api_key_pepper=api_key_pepper,
    revocation_states=RevocationStates(
        route="authn-revocations",
        ttl=timedelta(minutes=5),
        key_mac=StateMacKeys(active=mac_key),  # optional: signed states, API keys too
    ),
)
states = {"authn-revocations": RedisRevocationStatesConfig(namespace="authn-revocations")}
epochs = PostgresPrincipalEpochConfig(relation=("public", "authn_principal_epochs"))
breaker = PortPolicy(
    key=RevocationStatesDepKey,
    policy="authn-revocations",
    methods=("read", "read_api_key"),
)

Wire states as RedisDepsModule(revocation_states=...), epochs as PostgresDepsModule(principal_epochs=...), on the database that holds the sessions, and breaker in ResilienceDepsModule(port_policies=...) under a policy with a circuit breaker, so a Redis outage stops costing every verification its timeout (50 ms by default). Bind it to the reads only: an open breaker on the writes would fail every attempt of a revocation's write-through at once. The states route is resolved by RevocationStatesSpec under RevocationStatesDepKey, and the epochs under PrincipalEpochDepKey. Create the epochs table yourself and never delete its rows:

CREATE TABLE authn_principal_epochs (
    principal_id uuid   PRIMARY KEY,
    epoch        bigint NOT NULL
);
  • Without key_mac, Redis is trusted for sessions. The session states and epochs then carry no MAC, so whoever can write the states' namespace can restore a live state or an older epoch, and a revoked token is admitted until its own exp. Let nothing but the identity plane write that namespace. With key_mac, each epoch and live family or session state carries a MAC and a not-after, as an API key's state does (below): one forged, copied from another principal or session, or cached before key_mac was set is read from Postgres, and one replayed over a newer state stops verifying ttl after it was cached. Its MAC covers the states route, the principal and the state key, not the namespace, so give every deployment its own key_mac.
  • Transactions are required. With the fast path on, issuing and revoking sessions refuse to run outside a transaction (authn_revocation_requires_transaction), so keep tx_route set on both registries. They refuse the same way, before writing, in a transaction that does not hold every store they write (the epochs, and for a deactivation or a password change the credentials and sessions too): a store on another database would commit on its own. The Postgres stores report it; one that cannot is not checked. Issue and logout serialize on the epoch's row on Postgres only, with the revocation at read committed (the default); a revocation at repeatable read or serializable is refused (authn_epoch_isolation). On Postgres, a raise of the epoch (a logout everywhere, a password change or reset) first locks the policy principal's row, as an issue does before it holds the epoch, so a deactivation of that row later in the same transaction, through SQL or its document port, waits for a concurrent login instead of deadlocking with it. The authn deactivation takes the credentials first and ends with revoke_tokens itself, so do not call revoke_tokens before it. Revoking an API key needs no transaction: its state is written once the key's row has committed, whichever way it runs.
  • session_binding. "session" (the default) refuses a token once a refresh replaced its session, as without the fast path; "family" admits it until its own exp while the family is live. A logout, a family revocation and refresh-token reuse refuse it either way.
  • Minting re-reads the credential. A session, an API key, a password account or an invite issued in a request that authenticated with an access token re-reads that token's session and epoch from Postgres first, whoever it is issued for, so a token admitted inside the window mints nothing that outlives it. The same mints in a request that authenticated with an API key (with key_mac set) re-read the key's row the same way (api_key_revoked). A session is issued only inside a transaction (above), where the re-read takes locks; above read committed, a revocation committed since the transaction's snapshot fails it with a serialization error. An API key, a password account or an invite can be minted outside one, tx_route=None included: the re-read then takes no lock but reads the latest commit, and a revocation committing after it is ordered after the mint, which it leaves in place, as it would a locked mint it waited for. Revoking a credential never revokes what was minted from it before. A WebSocket or Socket.IO connection carries what its handshake (or its last reauth) verified to each command, so a command that mints re-reads that credential the same way: once a revocation ends it, or a refresh elsewhere rotates the token's session (under "session" binding), the socket's mints are refused until it reauths.
  • Redis down. A Redis error or timeout makes the same checks from Postgres, so an outage never admits a credential the fast path would refuse. Tokens issued before the fast path carry no fam or pep, and keep the session-row check until they expire.

items.title: API keys
items.text:
A key's cached state is the only proof the key exists: a hit reads no row, and the verifier takes the principal, the delegation actor and the expiry from the state. So everything able to write the states' Redis namespace is kept from minting a key:

  • Each live state carries a MAC under key_mac, over the states route, the state's full Redis key (its namespace included), the key's digest and every field. A state forged without the key, copied onto another key's digest, or copied in from another namespace fails it and is read from Postgres. revoked carries none: forging it can refuse a key, never admit one.
  • Each live state carries a not-after, the earlier of the key's own expiry and ttl after the lookup read Redis's clock. It is checked against Redis's clock from the same read, so a live state replayed over revoked, with no expiry of its own, stops verifying no later than any other state would. A state the application's clock puts more than ttl past its not-after is a miss too, so a Redis server that lies about its clock cannot stretch it further. The key's expiry is still checked on the application's clock.
  • A state that fails either check stays a miss until it expires or is deleted: a lookup never overwrites a state, so a tampered key costs one row read per verification, never an admission. Keys nobody issued are never cached.

Give every deployment its own key_mac. The MAC binds a state to its route and namespace, so deployments that share one Redis are kept apart; but two deployments with the same namespace name and the same key_mac, a staging copy of production or customers served from one secrets bundle, accept each other's states, and a state copied from one admits its key in the other without a row read. Never reuse another secret as key_mac either: the kernel refuses one equal to any of its peppers, its token secret or an HS256 signer's secret (authn_state_mac_key_reused). It cannot see a key held by an asymmetric or KMS-backed signer; what makes any reuse harmless is that each MAC key is used only through a key derived from it.

A states store of your own needs ApiKeyStatesPort as well as RevocationStatesPort for API keys: with key_mac set, the build refuses one without it (authn_api_key_states_unsupported). The Redis and mock stores implement both.

StateMacKeys takes keys of at least 32 bytes. To rotate one, make the new key active and move the old one to previous, on every process that verifies or revokes; after ttl, when every state signed under the old key has expired, drop it. A state signed under a key no longer configured is read from Postgres, so dropping it early costs reads, not admissions. A key carries no tenant, cached or not, and a deactivated principal's keys are still refused, by the eligibility read or, where it is skipped, by the epoch the deactivation raised, except within the replay window under The window.

items.title: The window
items.text:
A revocation writes its states to Redis once it commits: revoked for each family, session or API key it ended, or the raised epoch for a logout, a password change or reset, or a deactivation. A revoked credential stays admitted for at most ttl after that commit, on Redis's clock, and only when one of these leaves a stale state in place:

  • The write-through never lands.
  • Every one of write_attempts failed. It is logged at error level and counted; revoking an API key again writes its state again.
  • The process died between the commit and the write. Nothing logs it.
  • The process that revoked was not configured, for example during a rolling deploy, from another service, or without key_mac for an API key. Nothing logs it.
  • The credential was revoked around the authn adapters, through its document port. Nothing logs it.
  • Redis lost the revocation's key while an earlier lookup was still writing: an eviction, a flush, a restart, or a failover that dropped an acknowledged write. Nothing logs these.
  • Whoever can write Redis replayed a state cached before the revocation. With key_mac, it verifies until its not-after, ttl after it was cached. Nothing logs it. Without key_mac, nothing bounds a replay but the token's own exp, as said above.

An access token is also bounded by its own exp; an API key may have no expiry, so its window is ttl alone. Configure every process that verifies or revokes, and give the states a Redis namespace nothing else flushes or evicts.

Redis's clock. Every expiry and every not-after is set on Redis's clock, from TIME in the script that reads or writes the state or relative to it with PX, so the bound has no skew term against the application's clock. It does lean on the Redis primary's clock: a failover to a replica whose clock lags lengthens every state by the lag, and moving the primary's clock back does the same. Keep its clock synchronized, and let only operators change it. The application's clock caps an API-key state at ttl past its not-after, so with the application two ttl or more ahead of Redis every key state is refused as soon as it is written, and every key verification reads its row; each such refusal is counted as clock_skew.

items.title: Metrics
items.text:
instrument_revocation_states({"default": kernel.revocation_states}) exports five counters, labelled by credential (session or api_key):

Counter Counts forze.authn.revocation_states.hits verifications answered from Redis alone, refusals included forze.authn.revocation_states.misses verifications that read Postgres for a state Redis lacked or could not trust forze.authn.revocation_states.fallbacks verifications whose Redis read failed, timed out or met an open breaker forze.authn.revocation_states.write_failures revocations whose write-through failed every attempt forze.authn.revocation_states.clock_skew API-key states refused because the application's clock is two ttl or more ahead of Redis's

Alert on any write_failures: each is a revoked credential admitted for up to ttl. A rising fallbacks rate is Redis being down for verifications, a steady clock_skew is a clock to fix, and misses against hits is what the cache saves. The metrics reference lists them with the rest.

items.title: Skip the eligibility read
items.text:
Every verification also reads the policy principal, to refuse a deactivated one. Pass the same RevocationStates to the authz kernel, and a token the fast path admitted on its principal's current epoch skips that read too, as does an API key whose cached state recorded that epoch:

from forze_identity.authz import AuthzDepsModule, AuthzKernelConfig

states_config = RevocationStates(
    route="authn-revocations",
    ttl=timedelta(minutes=5),
    key_mac=StateMacKeys(active=mac_key),
)
authn_kernel = AuthnKernelConfig(..., revocation_states=states_config)
authz_kernel = AuthzKernelConfig(revocation_states=states_config)

With it, every write that may deactivate a policy principal raises the principal's epoch in its transaction and writes it through to Redis after commit, whichever path writes it: the authz registry's deactivate_principal, the authn deactivation, or your own update, bulk patch, upsert or delete of the policy_principal_spec document through its document port. A token issued before is then refused by its epoch, so the eligibility read has nothing left to catch.

  • Signed epochs only. The skip trusts the cached epoch, so the authz kernel refuses revocation_states without key_mac (authn_eligibility_skip_requires_key_mac), and a PolicyPrincipalEpochHook registered by hand without it leaves every verification reading. Unsigned, an older epoch restored in Redis would admit a deactivated principal's tokens until their exp.
  • What still reads. Only the check right after the verification, in the same request, about the token's own subject, is skipped. Issuing a session (login, refresh, tenant switch) reads under the principal's row lock, and a delegated actor is always read, even when it is the subject. Tokens issued before the fast path and passwords read as before.
  • API keys. A key's state written on a miss records the principal's epoch, read before the principal is found active; a later verification whose state carries the principal's current cached epoch skips the read, and reads neither the key's row nor the principal. The miss itself reads, and so does a key whose principal's epoch has moved since, whose principal was inactive when its state was written, or whose state an earlier release wrote. During a rolling deploy, a process of an earlier release reads such a state as a miss, from the key's row, until it expires.
  • Inside a transaction, a key always reads. The transaction may have raised the epoch itself, which reaches the cache only after commit.
  • A missing cached epoch. The verification compares the database's epoch instead and writes it back: as sound, since a deactivation raises the epoch in its own transaction, and one read where the eligibility check would make one. If that read fails, it reads eligibility.
  • Two Redis reads. A key's state and its principal's epoch sit on different Redis Cluster slots, so a warm verification reads them one after the other, each bounded by timeout: twice timeout at worst before it falls back to the eligibility read.
  • The same rules as revocations. Such a write refuses to run outside a transaction, or in one that holds neither its own write nor the epoch's (a scope on another route or another database), before it writes (authn_revocation_requires_transaction); it refuses above read committed too (authn_epoch_isolation). A deactivation whose write-through never lands is enforced within ttl. For a logout and a deactivation in one transaction, see Transactions are required (above).
  • Configure every process that writes policy principals. A process without the authz configuration raises no epoch, and a token it should have ended is admitted until its own exp, an API key until its cached state expires (ttl); so is one deactivated by a write around the document port (SQL, or another spec over the same table), or one deactivated before you turned this on through a path that raised no epoch (the authz registry alone). Logins and refreshes still read eligibility, so none of these can be extended. Keep the policy principals on the database whose transaction holds the epochs, so a deactivation and its raise commit together.
  • Postgres only. The skip needs the policy principal on Postgres, where an issue's locking read excludes a concurrent deactivation, and the principal epochs there too, so a raise is held to the deactivation's transaction; elsewhere, the mock included, every verification reads. Without the authz configuration every verification reads, as before. With a different one, building the eligibility gate (on the first authentication or issue) is refused (authn_revocation_states_mismatch).

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• Document-backed: wire the account / session / identity-mapping specs to a document store (Postgres, Mongo, …). kernel is required only when a route mints first-party tokens.
  • Transactions: the kit's login, refresh, logout, password change and reset, and deactivation run their writes in a transaction on build_authn_registry(..., tx_route=...), and the tenant switch on build_tenancy_registry(..., tx_route=...); both default to "default". Register a transaction manager on each route you use, for the database holding the session and principal documents, e.g. PostgresDepsModule(..., tx={"default"}). A deactivation then commits whole. On Postgres an issue also reads the principal with a row lock that lasts until its session commits, so a concurrent deactivation either revokes the new session or refuses the issue; Mongo's locking read takes no lock, so there the race remains. A password change, a reset and a deactivation likewise read the password account with a row lock on Postgres, right before they write it, and hash before they take it: of a change or reset and a deactivation, the second waits, so the deactivation closes the changed account, or the change or reset reads it closed and is refused. The lock goes to the write table of the password-account route when it differs from read, and otherwise to read, which must then accept FOR UPDATE: a table or a single-table view does, a view that joins or groups does not, as on a read-only route over such a view. Without the lock (outside a transaction, or on Mongo) a deactivation whose close of the password account or of an API key a concurrent write made stale reads it again and closes it, a few times at most; a conflict the backend itself reports still fails the transaction. tx_route=None runs the writes without a transaction and gives up these guarantees. Refresh refuses to run inside a transaction the caller already opened: a reused refresh token's family is revoked in a transaction of its own, which an enclosing one would roll back.
  • Overlapping refreshes: presenting a rotated refresh token again is reuse, and its whole family is revoked. Tabs sharing one refresh cookie hit that on a benign race. AuthnKernelConfig(refresh_token=RefreshTokenConfig(reuse_grace=timedelta(seconds=10))) refuses a token rotated within the grace, while its successor is unused, with the authentication error refresh_superseded and revokes nothing. A refresh that loses the rotation to a concurrent one gets the same error where the store detects the stale write itself, as Postgres does; a backend that aborts the transaction on the conflict, as Mongo does, still answers with the conflict. Either way the client refreshes again with the token it now holds. A stolen token replayed within the grace mints nothing, and its holder learns only that it was just rotated, but it raises REFRESH_SUPERSEDED, not the REFRESH_REUSE_DETECTED theft signal, so keep the grace to seconds. It must be shorter than the refresh lifetime; the default 0 keeps strict reuse detection.
  • Issued API keys: issue_api_key returns an IssuedApiKey; its raw key, shown only at issuance, is issued.secret. It stays out of repr() and str(), so logging the result does not log the key.
  • Browser clients: the generated login/refresh/logout routes can carry their tokens in HttpOnly cookies instead of response bodies — see cookie mode. Logout revokes the sessions from the access cookie's identity or, without one, the refresh cookie (the logout_by_refresh_token operation, through TokenLifecyclePort.revoke_tokens_by_refresh_token). The access cookie expires first, so the refresh cookie's path must cover the logout route; runtime_lifespan refuses to start otherwise.
  • Authorization is a sibling plane — forze_identity.authz (AuthzDepsModule).
  • The conceptual model (verify → resolve, resolver flavors) is in Identity & access; this page is the wiring.
  • For external IdPs, pair this with the OIDC verifier.

items.title: BigQuery
items.text: forze[bigquery] implements the analytics contracts on Google BigQuery — named, parameterized SQL against pre-provisioned tables, plus optional append. This is warehouse reads, not OLTP document storage.

items.title: Install
items.text:
uv add 'forze[bigquery]'

Needs Google BigQuery (or the goccy/bigquery-emulator via BIGQUERY_EMULATOR_HOST).

items.title: The client
items.text:
from forze_bigquery import BigQueryClient

bq = BigQueryClient()

RoutedBigQueryClient resolves a per-tenant project/credentials.

items.title: Settings
items.text: BigQuerySettings holds the project, the optional service-account file and maximum_bytes_billed, the ceiling that stops a runaway query costing money — see connection settings.

items.title: Wire it
items.text:
Each analytics route maps query_keys to SQL, keyed by AnalyticsSpec.name:

from forze.application.execution import DepsRegistry, LifecyclePlan
from forze_bigquery import BigQueryAnalyticsConfig, BigQueryClient, BigQueryDepsModule, BigQueryQueryConfig, bigquery_lifecycle_step

events = BigQueryAnalyticsConfig(
    dataset="analytics",
    queries={"daily": BigQueryQueryConfig(sql="SELECT day, value FROM analytics.metrics WHERE day = @day")},
)

deps = DepsRegistry.from_modules(BigQueryDepsModule(client=bq, analytics={"events": events}))
lifecycle = LifecyclePlan.from_steps(bigquery_lifecycle_step(project_id="my-project"))

items.title: What it provides
items.text: Contract Keyed by Analytics query (run / run_page / run_cursor / run_chunked) AnalyticsSpec.name Analytics ingest (append) AnalyticsSpec.name (ingest_relation)

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• Tables are pre-provisioned; queries are named Standard SQL with @param placeholders bound from each query's params model. Forze does not rewrite read SQL — qualify tables yourself.
  • Ingest targets a relation (dataset, table), static or a per-tenant resolver.
  • Out of scope: load jobs, MERGE, and DDL — manage those externally.

items.title: ClickHouse
items.text: forze[clickhouse] implements the analytics contracts on ClickHouse — named, parameterized SQL against pre-provisioned tables, plus optional append. Like BigQuery, this is warehouse reads, not document storage.

items.title: Install
items.text:
uv add 'forze[clickhouse]'

Needs a ClickHouse server.

items.title: The client
items.text:
from forze_clickhouse import ClickHouseClient

ch = ClickHouseClient()

RoutedClickHouseClient resolves per-tenant host/database/credentials.

items.title: Settings
items.text: ClickHouseSettings is the mountable form of ClickHouseConfig: the same host, port, credentials and database, as a pydantic model your settings root can carry. With secure set and no port given it resolves 8443 rather than ClickHouseConfig's 8123, which is the plaintext listener. See connection settings.

items.title: Wire it
items.text:
Each analytics route maps query_keys to SQL, keyed by AnalyticsSpec.name:

from forze.application.execution import DepsRegistry, LifecyclePlan
from forze_clickhouse import (
    ClickHouseAnalyticsConfig,
    ClickHouseClient,
    ClickHouseConfig,
    ClickHouseDepsModule,
    ClickHouseQueryConfig,
    clickhouse_lifecycle_step,
)

events = ClickHouseAnalyticsConfig(
    database="analytics",
    queries={"daily": ClickHouseQueryConfig(sql="SELECT day, value FROM analytics.metrics WHERE day = {day:Date}")},
)

deps = DepsRegistry.from_modules(ClickHouseDepsModule(client=ch, analytics={"events": events}))
lifecycle = LifecyclePlan.from_steps(
    clickhouse_lifecycle_step(connection=ClickHouseConfig(host="localhost", port=8123)),
)

items.title: What it provides
items.text: Contract Keyed by Analytics query (run / run_page / run_cursor / run_chunked) AnalyticsSpec.name Analytics ingest (append) AnalyticsSpec.name (ingest_relation)

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• Tables are pre-provisioned; queries are named SQL with server-side {field:Type} params bound from the params model. Read SQL isn't rewritten.
  • The lifecycle step takes connection=ClickHouseConfig(...) (host, port, credentials, database).
  • For stable deep pagination, set cursor_column on the query config (keyset) instead of offset cursors.

items.title: DuckDB
items.text:
forze[duckdb] implements the analytics query contract with an embedded DuckDB engine. Where ClickHouse and BigQuery are standing warehouses, DuckDB is compute without a server: point it at Parquet, CSV, Iceberg or Delta files on S3/GCS (or local disk) and it runs the scan in-process. It suits heavy analytics that don't need ultra-low-latency serving — and, being Docker-free, it doubles as an analytics backend in tests.

It is query-only (no ingest, no table management): named, parameterized queries returning typed rows, exactly like the other analytics adapters. With a per-tenant routed client it also serves trusted dynamic reads over an Iceberg lake.

items.title: Install
items.text:
uv add 'forze[duckdb]'

No server to run — DuckDB is a library. Reading object storage pulls the httpfs extension (and iceberg / delta for those formats) on first use.

The extra installs DuckDB 1.5 or 2 (duckdb>=1.5.6,<3). Both clients run on both majors with the same code. The repository's lock tests on 2.0.0, and CI runs the DuckDB suites on 1.5.6 as well. Where the per-tenant lake client behaves differently on the two, the section on it says so.

items.title: The client
items.text:
from forze_duckdb import DuckDbClient

duck = DuckDbClient()

The engine is synchronous and in-process; the client runs each query on a dedicated bounded executor (DuckDB releases the GIL, so the event loop stays responsive) with its own cursor, and honors per-query timeouts via interrupt.

items.title: The lake source
items.text:
Sources are declared as typed descriptors that compile to scan expressions and auto-load the extensions they need — no hand-written SQL strings:

from forze_duckdb import ParquetSource, IcebergSource, DeltaSource

events = ParquetSource("s3://bucket/events/*.parquet")   # also CsvSource, JsonSource

Object-storage credentials render to DuckDB secrets, resolved at startup from the wired secrets backend via a secret_ref (or supplied inline for local runs):

from forze.application.contracts.secrets import SecretRef
from forze_duckdb import S3Credentials

creds = S3Credentials(name="lake", secret_ref=SecretRef(path="lake/s3"))

items.title: Settings
items.text: DuckDbSettings carries the database path and the resource limits — memory_limit in particular, since DuckDB otherwise sizes itself from the host's memory rather than the cgroup's, which is how a query gets the container OOM-killed. Extensions, object stores and named sources stay wiring arguments. See connection settings.

items.title: Wire it
items.text:
Each analytics route maps query_keys to DuckDB SQL (referencing a registered source view or an inline read_parquet(...)), keyed by AnalyticsSpec.name. The lifecycle step opens the connection, loads extensions, registers credentials and source views:

from forze.application.execution import DepsRegistry, LifecyclePlan
from forze_duckdb import (
    DuckDbAnalyticsConfig,
    DuckDbClient,
    DuckDbDepsModule,
    DuckDbQueryConfig,
    ParquetSource,
    S3Credentials,
    duckdb_lifecycle_step,
)
from forze.application.contracts.secrets import SecretRef

duck = DuckDbClient()

events = DuckDbAnalyticsConfig(
    queries={"by_day": DuckDbQueryConfig(
        sql="SELECT day, sum(total) AS total FROM events WHERE day >= $since GROUP BY day",
    )},
)

deps = DepsRegistry.from_modules(DuckDbDepsModule(client=duck, analytics={"events": events}))
lifecycle = LifecyclePlan.from_steps(
    duckdb_lifecycle_step(
        object_stores=(S3Credentials(name="lake", secret_ref=SecretRef(path="lake/s3")),),
        sources={"events": ParquetSource("s3://bucket/events/*.parquet")},
    ),
)

For a runnable, Docker-free walkthrough, see the analytics recipe.

items.title: Per-tenant lake reads (dedicated)
items.text:
One DuckDbClient is one engine for every tenant: whatever credentials it holds, every statement can use. RoutedDuckDbClient instead builds an unnamed :memory: instance per tenant, attached to that tenant's own warehouse in an Iceberg REST catalog (Lakekeeper) with the tenant's own OAuth2 principal. The instance holds that principal's client secret for its whole life, and the S3 credentials the catalog vends for a statement until the statement ends. Neither reaches another tenant's data. That is the dedicated tier, and it is what lets a dynamic-read route run compiled statements here:

from datetime import timedelta

from forze.application.contracts.secrets import SecretRef
from forze.application.execution import DepsRegistry, LifecyclePlan
from forze.application.execution.lifecycle.builtin import routed_client_lifecycle_step
from forze_duckdb import (
    DuckDbDepsModule,
    DuckDbDynamicReadConfig,
    LakeTenantCatalog,
    RoutedDuckDbClient,
)

lake = RoutedDuckDbClient(
    secrets=secrets,                       # SecretsPort; holds LakeCatalogCredentials
    secret_ref_for_tenant=lambda t: SecretRef(path=f"tenants/{t}/lake"),
    tenant_provider=current_tenant,
    catalog_for_tenant=lambda t: LakeTenantCatalog(
        uri="https://lakekeeper:8181/catalog",
        warehouse=f"wh-{t}",
        oauth2_server_uri="https://idp/realms/lake/protocol/openid-connect/token",
        oauth2_scope="lakekeeper",
        storage_prefix=f"s3://lake/{t}/",
    ),
    extension_directory="/opt/duckdb/extensions",   # httpfs, iceberg, avro: in the image
    ca_cert_file="/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt",   # HTTPS on DuckDB 2 reads it
)

widgets = DuckDbDynamicReadConfig(
    provenance="trusted",                  # the only tier admitted
    namespace="gold",                      # USE lake.gold before every statement
    statement_timeout=timedelta(seconds=5),
)

deps = DepsRegistry.from_modules(DuckDbDepsModule(client=lake, dynamic_reads={"widgets": widgets}))
lifecycle = LifecyclePlan.from_steps(routed_client_lifecycle_step("duckdb_lake", client=lake))

The secret holds LakeCatalogCredentials: client_id and client_secret, never a static token, because a token is never refreshed. An empty client_id is refused on first use, since the iceberg build for DuckDB 1.5 never refreshes a token issued for one.

Each instance is built by one fixed sequence and serves nothing until it has read the result back:

connect(":memory:", persistent secrets off, extension autoload/autoinstall off,
        temp_directory '', extension_directory)
LOAD httpfs; LOAD iceberg                       -- never INSTALL; iceberg also loads avro
SET GLOBAL enable_global_s3_configuration=false; s3 keys cleared
SET GLOBAL ca_cert_file                         -- if configured
SET GLOBAL allowed_directories=[storage_prefix, catalog uri/]
SET GLOBAL allowed_paths=[token endpoint, ca_cert_file]
SET GLOBAL enable_external_access=false
CREATE SECRET (TYPE iceberg, client credentials, scope)
ATTACH warehouse AS lake (vended_credentials, READ_ONLY)
SET GLOBAL http_timeout; HTTP metadata and external file caches off
SET GLOBAL lock_configuration=true
attest                                          -- settings, secrets, databases, refusals

The allowlist is the one bound inside the engine on what can be opened, local or remote. Anything outside it is refused before any request: another tenant's prefix, a local path, any other URL. It names the catalog and the IdP because DuckDB 2 checks the iceberg extension's own requests against it. Analytics SQL on the instance can therefore also send GETs into the catalog's tree, which every tenant shares, and to the token endpoint. They carry no token, and the catalog and the IdP refuse them. The allowlist matches a path by its spelling: it resolves no .., and it does not re-check where a redirect leads. No filesystem is disabled: DuckDB 2 reaches neither the catalog with HTTPFileSystem off nor its CA bundle with LocalFileSystem off. For HTTPS to the catalog, the IdP or the store, set ca_cert_file to a PEM bundle: DuckDB 2 reads it through the allowlist, and without it the session does not build. Any statement on the instance can read that file. The same sequence runs on DuckDB 1.5.

What keeps credentials in is not the allowlist but their being unreadable: duckdb_secrets() stays redacted, the s3_* options are cleared, no secret persists, and the lock keeps it so. The attestation reads each of these back, and checks by effect that a local path, an unlisted URL, the token endpoint with a path or query added, a sibling of the prefix or the catalog tree, a file beside the CA bundle, and a write to lake are all refused.

A session that does not attest raises duckdb_session_attestation_failed, and one whose sequence fails (an extension missing from the image, a principal the catalog refuses) raises duckdb_session_setup_failed. Both are configuration errors, and the instance is closed. A setup error carries the engine's message with the tenant's client secret and DuckDB's quote of the statement removed, and does not chain the engine's error. Each statement then runs on a fresh cursor: USE lake.<namespace>, DuckDB's own parser checks that the text is exactly one SELECT, the classified statement runs unmodified, and a result with two columns of the same name is refused. A dynamic read may read only tables it names (dynamic_read_statement_invalid otherwise):

  • no table function but range, generate_series and unnest. The others take a path, a URL, a table name or SQL text (read_parquet, iceberg_scan, query, query_table), and PRAGMA is refused on 1.5 as on 2;
  • no path or URL as a table name, so nothing a statement writes reaches the allowlist's spelling match. Parsing binds nothing, so any name holding /, : or . counts as one: a table whose own name has a dot cannot be read dynamically;
  • no table named through a catalog the instance has not attached, or nested deeper than catalog.schema.table: DuckDB 2 would read it as a nested namespace and resolve only its last level, a table the statement did not name.

After every read, dynamic or analytics, the per-table S3 secrets the catalog vended for it are dropped. On DuckDB 1.5 a kept secret outranks the next statement's fresh one, so once it expired every later read of that table would fail. DuckDB 2 discards it when the statement ends, and the drop finds nothing. If a drop fails, the read's own rows or error still come back, and the instance is retired: it refuses further statements (duckdb_instance_retired), and the next call builds a fresh one.

What the route promises, and who keeps each promise:

Property Kept by Read-only the catalog's select-only grant and the store; the READ_ONLY attach and parser classification are belts One statement DuckDB's parser, before anything runs Timeout the client interrupts the cursor, also when the caller is cancelled. A CPU-bound statement stops at once. A catalog or store request that hangs is not cut short: the caller still gets dynamic_read_timeout on time, but the worker holds its slot until the request ends. On DuckDB 2 that is http_timeout × (1 + http_retries, default 3); on 1.5 about 120 s, whatever http_timeout says Row cap the shell fetches cap + 1 rows from a streaming result and refuses the overflow Container the tenant's instance, principal and vended credentials (dedicated) Untrusted statements refused at wiring (duckdb_dynamic_read_untrusted_refused); a provenance other than "trusted" or "untrusted" is duckdb_dynamic_read_provenance_invalid

Wiring refuses a dynamic route on a plain DuckDbClient (its origin floor is namespace), and an http_timeout above the smallest route timeout. Named analytics routes work on the routed client too and derive dedicated; their SQL names tables as lake.<namespace>.<table>. A nested namespace is written dotted, namespace="gold.sub". DuckDB lists it as one schema, so SQL names its tables bare or as lake."gold.sub".<table>.

Operating it:

  • Size max_concurrent_queries_total for hung requests. It bounds statements across all tenants (default 8), and peak memory is about that many times engine.memory_limit. A tenant whose catalog or store stops answering holds a slot per stuck request: http_timeout × (1 + http_retries) on DuckDB 2, about 120 s on 1.5. Waiting for a slot counts against a statement's timeout.
  • Call evict_tenant after a grant is restored or a namespace is created. An instance that once found a namespace missing keeps it missing for its life. Rotate credentials or remap a tenant's catalog the same way, or set fingerprint_ttl. An evicted instance closes in the background, and close() waits for those teardowns.
  • A revocation lands at the next statement, or after the authorizer's check cache expires: OpenFGA caches checks for 10 s when its cache is on.
  • The deployment owns the outer controls. The worker must hold no ambient cloud credentials, write nowhere it should not, and egress only to the catalog, the IdP and the store. An s3:// path inside the tenant's prefix with no vended secret behind it goes, unsigned, to the public AWS endpoint. The engine follows a redirect from any of the three without re-checking it, and the store, not the allowlist, refuses a .. key outside the vended credential's table.
  • Keep sts-token-validity-seconds well above the longest statement. The engine does not re-vend a credential that expires mid-statement: the statement fails with an HTTP 400 from the store. A statement that starts after expiry loads the table again and gets a fresh credential.

items.title: What it provides
items.text: Contract Keyed by Analytics query (run / run_page / run_cursor / run_chunked) AnalyticsSpec.name Dynamic read (run / select), on RoutedDuckDbClient only DynamicReadSpec.name

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• Query-only. Writing/maintaining tables (Iceberg/Delta compaction, ingest) is an ETL/ops concern, not a domain port — keep it out of the adapter.
  • Source styles compose. Register named views (sources=) and reference them in SQL, or inline read_parquet('s3://…') in a query — both work.
  • Iceberg/Delta: point IcebergSource at the table's current *.metadata.json (the table-directory form needs a version-hint.text many writers omit); for in-place tables read with allow_moved_paths=False.
  • Concurrency: each query gets its own cursor, so parallel reads don't serialize. Cap parallelism with DuckDbConfig(max_concurrent_queries=...).
  • Cursor pagination is offset-based; a full terminal page reports has_more until the next (short) page confirms the end.

items.title: FastAPI
items.text: forze[fastapi] connects an ExecutionRuntime to a FastAPI app: it runs the runtime from the app's lifespan, binds per-request context (and identity) via middleware, and maps CoreExceptions to HTTP responses. Routes are ordinary FastAPI handlers that resolve the context and run operations — written by hand, or generated from an operation registry.

items.title: Install
items.text:
uv add 'forze[fastapi]'

No external service — FastAPI is in-process.

items.title: Run the runtime from lifespan
items.text:
The runtime's lifecycle opens and closes every backing client (Postgres, Redis, …). runtime_lifespan holds runtime.scope() open for the app's lifetime — context created and startup run on app startup, shutdown run (and the context reset) on app shutdown, even if the app's lifetime ends with an error:

from fastapi import FastAPI
from forze.application.execution import build_runtime
from forze_fastapi import runtime_lifespan

runtime = build_runtime(...)  # deps modules + lifecycle modules/steps

app = FastAPI(title="Orders API", lifespan=runtime_lifespan(runtime))

build_runtime assembles the runtime in one call — it builds and freezes the deps registry and the lifecycle plan and returns the ExecutionRuntime.

items.title: Build the runtime at startup
items.text:
Pass build instead of a runtime, and the lifespan builds it at startup and drops it at shutdown. Use it when an app factory must import without the environment its runtime needs, such as secrets to validate or clients to connect. Use it too when every worker process needs its own runtime. The routes are wired before that runtime exists, so wire them to the lifespan, which hands them the runtime once it is built:

from fastapi import APIRouter, FastAPI
from forze.application.execution import build_runtime
from forze_fastapi import runtime_lifespan
from forze_fastapi.middlewares import InvocationMetadataMiddleware
from forze_fastapi.routes import attach_readiness_route


def create_app() -> FastAPI:
    lifespan = runtime_lifespan(build=lambda: build_runtime(...))
    app = FastAPI(title="Orders API", lifespan=lifespan)
    app.add_middleware(InvocationMetadataMiddleware, ctx_dep=lifespan.get_context)

    router = APIRouter()
    attach_readiness_route(router, lifespan.runtime)
    app.include_router(router)

    return app

lifespan.get_context is the ctx_dep for middlewares and generated routes, and lifespan.runtime is the runtime provider that attach_readiness_route takes. A build that raises fails the startup, so the server never serves. The lifespan holds one runtime at a time. Entered again while it runs, it refuses with configuration rather than build a second one. Entered after its runtime was torn down, it builds a new one.

items.title: Run a mounted app's lifespan
items.text:
Starlette never runs the lifespan of a mounted app. When a mounted app needs its own lifespan, such as the session manager of an MCP HTTP app, pass the app in nested. Its lifespan is entered with that app, as Starlette enters a top-level app's, so whatever it sets on app.state is what the app's routes read from request.app.state:

from fastapi import FastAPI
from forze.application.execution import build_runtime
from forze_fastapi import runtime_lifespan
from forze_mcp import build_mcp_server


def create_app() -> FastAPI:
    # Built before the lifespan exists, so the factory looks it up on each call.
    server = build_mcp_server(registry, lambda: lifespan.get_context(), name="orders")
    mcp_app = server.http_app(path="/")

    lifespan = runtime_lifespan(build=lambda: build_runtime(...), nested=(mcp_app,))
    app = FastAPI(title="Orders API", lifespan=lifespan)
    app.mount("/mcp", mcp_app)

    return app

The startup checks run first, then the runtime is built and its scope opens. The nested lifespans are entered in order inside the scope, so they can use the runtime. On shutdown the runtime drains first, with its drain_budget. Then the nested lifespans exit in reverse, and then the runtime tears down. So the drain phases always run while the mounted apps are up. With a drain_budget on the lifespan, a SIGTERM drains while the app still serves, and the shutdown finds the drain done. A lifetime that ends in an error or a cancellation skips the drain ahead of the exits, and the teardown drains after them.

An entry in nested can also be a lifespan callable, which takes an app and returns an async context manager, as Starlette's lifespan= does. It is called with the outer app.

If a nested lifespan raises on entry, the startup fails, and the lifespans already entered and the scope exit. If one raises on exit, the others still exit, the runtime still tears down, and the error is raised. State a nested lifespan yields is merged, a later key over an earlier one, and reaches request.state in every app.

items.title: Bind request context
items.text:
Two ASGI middlewares attach the per-request context, both given a factory that returns the current ExecutionContext — runtime.get_context is that factory (lifespan.get_context when the lifespan builds the runtime):

from forze_fastapi.middlewares import (
    InvocationMetadataMiddleware,
    SecurityContextMiddleware,
)

app.add_middleware(InvocationMetadataMiddleware, ctx_dep=runtime.get_context)
app.add_middleware(SecurityContextMiddleware, ctx_dep=runtime.get_context)

InvocationMetadataMiddleware binds correlation/execution metadata and the Idempotency-Key header; SecurityContextMiddleware binds the authenticated identity and tenant.

Outside a short list of exact paths, a request whose credential fails to verify is refused before routing, and so is one that no ingress authenticates at all (AuthnRequirement(required=True), the default; a CORS preflight passes, for a CORS layer to answer). That list is the handful of paths that exist because the caller has no working credential — login, refresh, password reset, cookie-mode logout, and any public page such as FastAPI's /docs and /openapi.json. Name them exactly, as mounted:

app.add_middleware(
    SecurityContextMiddleware,
    ctx_dep=runtime.get_context,
    anonymous_paths={"/auth/login", "/auth/refresh", "/docs", "/openapi.json"},
)

On those paths a missing credential, or an authentication-kind failure — an expired or invalid credential, ambiguous credentials, a tenant mismatch — binds no identity instead of 401ing, so the route authenticates from its body or serves anonymously. A valid credential still binds normally, and every other failure kind still returns the error response: a secrets-store outage is a server fault, not a missing credential. This matters most in cookie mode, where a stale access cookie rides every request including the one that would replace it. Paths are exact, never prefixes.

On an application mounted under a prefix, with the middleware added to the mounted application, an entry may be the full path or the path relative to the mount:

api = FastAPI()
api.add_middleware(
    SecurityContextMiddleware,
    ctx_dep=runtime.get_context,
    anonymous_paths={"/auth/login", "/auth/refresh"},  # relative to the mount
)
app.mount("/v1", api)  # /v1/auth/login is anonymous; "/v1/auth/login" works too

A server root_path counts as a mount the same way. An entry whose leading path segments are the mount prefix (/v1 or /v1/... under /v1, not /v1x) is only ever read as a full path, so no entry names two routes. A middleware added to the parent application sees no mount: list full paths there. bypass_paths and allowed_websocket_paths, below, read their entries the same way.

The relative reading trusts the ASGI root_path, so it must come from server configuration: a Mount, or the server's --root-path. Never derive it from a request header. A middleware that sets it from X-Forwarded-Prefix lets the client choose the prefix, and a relative entry would then admit paths the startup checks never verified. The startup checks see only the app's own root_path and its mounts. A root path the server sets (--root-path, typically behind a proxy that strips the prefix) is invisible to them: under one, list entries relative to it, which match with or without it.

Probe paths want the opposite treatment. Both middlewares resolve the execution context on every HTTP request, so in front of /livez they answer 500 while the runtime scope is not yet open — precisely the window a liveness probe exists to observe. Name the paths neither middleware should run for at all:

from forze.base.logging import DEFAULT_HEALTH_PATHS

app.add_middleware(
    InvocationMetadataMiddleware,
    ctx_dep=runtime.get_context,
    bypass_paths=DEFAULT_HEALTH_PATHS,
)

A bypassed path serves with no identity, no tenant and no invocation envelope bound, and no error shaping — list probe and scrape paths, never anything that reads or writes tenant data. anonymous_paths is the softer tool: it still runs the middleware, and still binds a valid credential. Paths are exact here too, so a route under a bypassed path stays governed — and they include every router prefix, since middleware runs before routing: list /api/livez, not /livez, for a router included under /api. On an application mounted under a prefix, an entry may be the full path or the path relative to the mount, as for anonymous_paths.

check_bypass_paths fails the boot on the three ways that goes wrong: a bypassed path serving a generated operation route (it would read and write tenant data with nothing bound), the two middlewares carrying different sets (the one still resolving the context fails the request anyway, so the bypass reads as configured and does nothing), and a non-empty set matching no route at all — the prefix mistake above. A superset is fine and expected: DEFAULT_HEALTH_PATHS names ten paths and most apps serve three. In cookie mode, check_authn_cookie_paths fails the boot when the refresh cookie's path does not cover the logout route, or when anonymous_paths leaves out the login, refresh or logout route. Under a root path, list those paths relative to it: behind a proxy that strips the prefix the middleware never sees it, so a full-path entry is refused, and so is a root_path declared with a trailing slash. The checks know only the app's own root_path. They find the middlewares by the fields they declare, so one wrapped in your own middleware or factory is not checked.

runtime_lifespan runs all three checks through run_startup_checks(app). An app that supplies its own lifespan calls that function there; none of the checks runs on its own:

from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

from forze_fastapi import run_startup_checks


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    run_startup_checks(app)

    async with build_runtime(...).scope():
        yield

Give the lifespan to the outermost app. Starlette never sends lifespan events to a mounted application, so a mounted app's own lifespan never runs: neither its runtime nor its checks would start. Run from the outermost app, the checks walk every Starlette or FastAPI app mounted beneath it, and hold each one's middlewares against the routes they reach, at the path they see. A bypass on the outer app that reaches a generated route of a mounted one fails the boot too.

Routing takes the first match in declaration order, and a mount matches every path under its prefix. The checks treat a route declared after a mount that matches its path as unreachable, so an entry naming only that route fails the boot.

The checks cannot see into any other mounted ASGI app, such as a Prometheus make_asgi_app(). A bypass or websocket allowlist entry that could admit a request into one fails the boot, even when a route declared before that app would serve it. A mount at / or a Host route is reached by every entry, and a mount with path parameters (/api/{tenant}) by every path under its static prefix. A StaticFiles mount is the exception: it serves files and no governed operation, and closes every websocket, so a single-page app mounted at / with StaticFiles(html=True) keeps its /livez bypass. Mount it after the probe routes. For any other app, two layouts pass:

  • serve the probe or scrape endpoint as a route of the gated app (attach_metrics_route for Prometheus), and bypass that route;
  • mount the other app on an outer app beside the gated one, outside its middlewares:
root = FastAPI(lifespan=runtime_lifespan(runtime))
root.mount("/metrics", make_asgi_app())  # no gate in front of it
root.mount("/api", api)  # api carries the middlewares and their bypass_paths

A mounted FastAPI app must not declare its own root_path. FastAPI writes it over the one the mount passes down, so its routes are matched against another prefix and the checks cannot tell what its middlewares see. The checks refuse such a mount unless the value equals the mount's own prefix.

When an upstream Forze service forwards its remaining time budget as X-Forze-Deadline-Budget, opt in to honoring it with InvocationMetadataMiddleware(..., bind_deadline_from_header=True) — binding is tighten-only, so a forged value can only shorten the sender's own request.

Both middlewares refuse raw websocket scopes (the upgrade handshake is closed with a policy violation): identity, tenancy, and the envelope are resolved for HTTP only, so a raw @app.websocket route would otherwise run with none of them — silently. Framework-attached websocket routes (attach_realtime_ws_route) are allowlisted by exact path (router prefixes included; on a mounted application, the full path or the path relative to the mount) with allowed_websocket_paths={"/realtime/ws"} — they resolve identity at connect themselves, and check_websocket_allowlist (run by run_startup_checks) fails the boot if an allowlisted path doesn't serve exactly one governed route. Only if you deliberately self-manage your own websocket routes, opt out app-wide with allow_raw_websockets=True; you then own identity, tenancy, and error shaping on every websocket route yourself. For governed duplex realtime, use the Socket.IO integration or the WebSocket route below; for server-push, the SSE route below.

A browser front end on another origin needs CORS, and it reads forze's own response headers — the X-Error-Code, the request and correlation ids, a download's filename, validator and range headers, a throttled error's Retry-After — only once they are exposed. AllowlistCORSMiddleware is Starlette's CORSMiddleware answering the origins an allowlist names (a port range or * on a loopback host, for a dev server) and exposing EXPOSED_RESPONSE_HEADERS:

from forze_fastapi.middlewares import AllowlistCORSMiddleware

app.add_middleware(
    AllowlistCORSMiddleware,
    allowed_origins=["https://app.example.com", "http://localhost:5173-5199"],
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
)

Add it last, so it is outermost: a refusal from the security middleware then carries the CORS headers too, and the browser can read its error code. An app that renames the invocation headers, or sets its own, passes expose_headers=(*EXPOSED_RESPONSE_HEADERS, "X-Mine").

items.title: Map errors to HTTP
items.text:
register_exception_handlers turns a CoreException into a response — the kind decides the status, the code rides both the body and the X-Error-Code header, and details are exposed only when the kind's egress policy allows:

from forze_fastapi.exceptions import register_exception_handlers

register_exception_handlers(app)
# raise exc.not_found("...") in a handler → 404 {"detail": "...", "code": "core.not_found",
#                                                "kind": "not_found"}

The body is {"detail", "code", "kind", "context"}, the shape the Socket.IO and WebSocket error frames carry; context appears only when the policy exposes details. Branch on code, never on detail: a stale ?rev= on an update answers 400 {"code": "revision_mismatch", ...}, which no other 400 shares. A server-side error keeps its code and gets a generic detail; an exception that is not a CoreException answers core.internal.

A throttled or unavailable error withholds its details, but it can still tell the client when to come back: the response carries a Retry-After header read from two details keys.

Key Value Retry-After retry_after non-negative seconds, int or float the seconds, rounded up retry_at an aware datetime that instant, rounded up to the second, as an HTTP-date

A usable retry_after wins when both are set; an unusable one — a negative or non-finite number, a string — falls through to retry_at. When neither is usable (a naive datetime is not, nor one whose zone raises), no header is sent, never an error. The retry layers read the same keys the same way, through retry_hint. retry_after is also what the HTTP client puts on an upstream 429, so a throttle passed through keeps its hint — but the client caps it at 3600 seconds, so a longer upstream wait arrives as 3600.

items.title: Readiness probe
items.text:
attach_readiness_route(router, runtime) adds a GET /readyz that reflects the runtime's scope state: 200 once lifecycle startup finished, 503 draining from the moment a drain is announced or shutdown closes the gate, 503 unavailable before that. Point your load balancer's readiness check at it so routing stops before any work is refused.

That answers whether the process is willing to take traffic. Pass probes to also ask whether it can reach what it needs — see Readiness.

items.title: Graceful shutdown under uvicorn
items.text:
When the orchestrator sends SIGTERM, the replica should withdraw readiness and run its drain phases while it still serves, and stop accepting only after that. Uvicorn's own signal handling stops the server at once, so serve the app with serve_uvicorn instead:

import asyncio
from datetime import timedelta

import uvicorn
from forze.application.execution import build_runtime
from forze_fastapi import serve_uvicorn

runtime = build_runtime(
    ...,
    drain_timeout=timedelta(seconds=5),
    shutdown_step_timeout=timedelta(seconds=2),
)
config = uvicorn.Config(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)

asyncio.run(
    serve_uvicorn(
        config,
        runtime,
        drain_budget=timedelta(seconds=5),
        announce_delay=timedelta(seconds=3),
        graceful_timeout=timedelta(seconds=5),
    )
)

Once startup has finished, the worst case of that exit is 25 seconds plus 2 per lifecycle step — the sum serve_uvicorn logs at startup. A signal that lands during startup waits for it first, and startup hooks have no timeout. Past two steps it no longer fits Kubernetes' default 30-second grace period: set terminationGracePeriodSeconds from the logged figure, with headroom.

On the first SIGTERM or SIGINT it runs runtime.drain() — readiness fails at once, announce_delay passes, the drain phases run — and only then lets uvicorn exit: stop accepting, finish in-flight requests, run the lifespan shutdown where the runtime closes its gate and tears down. A drain that fails still lets the server exit. A SIGINT during the drain cancels it and exits without waiting for open connections; a repeated SIGTERM is logged and ignored, so a signal delivered twice — to the process group and again by a wrapper — cannot cut a deploy short.
