Minting an upload URL (or beginning a multipart session) grants write to a key, so these endpoints should sit behind authn/authz — treat them like the deactivate route. presign_upload and every multipart-session op are command ops, so you can bind AuthnRequired + authz hooks on them in your registry (they then show up protected under apply_openapi_security). The minted URL is a bearer credential: it appears in the response body the client needs but is never logged (the access-log middleware logs only request path/status/duration, never the response body) — prefer short expires_in windows.

A presign/multipart op on a client-side-encrypting route is refused by the adapter (the app never sees the bytes, so it cannot encrypt them) and the error propagates to a normal error status. Server-side (SSE/CMEK) encryption is transparent and does not refuse.

items.title: Stored-file downloads
items.text:
The stored-file kit ships no generated JSON routes. It has four read-only download operations, and each one loads the row first: a row the caller can't read (another tenant's, or a missing one) answers not-found, and a pending or failed file is refused before storage is touched. download is always registered. The other three are opt-in, because an operation runs only the guards bound on its own key: enable each with StoredFileKitSpec(stream_downloads=True, range_downloads=True, presign_downloads=True), then bind your authn and authz on it as you do on download. A StoredFileFacade method for an operation left off raises a configuration error.

Operation Input Result download StoredFileIdDTO StoredFileDownloadDTO: the whole object in memory, for small files and tests download_stream StoredFileIdDTO StoredFileStream: the row plus a bounded-memory StreamedDownload named after the stored filename download_range DownloadStoredFileRangeRequestDTO (id, inclusive start, end or None for the end) StoredFileRangeDTO: the row plus the window's bytes, content_range and total_size; a start past the end is a precondition error presign_download PresignStoredFileDownloadRequestDTO (id, expires_in up to 7 days) StoredFilePresignedDownloadDTO: the row plus a presigned GET URL

A hand-written route hands the stream to streamed_download_response, which builds the generated download route's 200: Content-Disposition, ETag, Last-Modified, and Content-Length when the size is known. It doesn't answer Range or conditional requests.

from uuid import UUID

from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends

from forze.application.execution.operations import run_operation
from forze_fastapi.routes import streamed_download_response
from forze_kits.aggregates.stored_file import StoredFileIdDTO

files_router = APIRouter(prefix="/files", tags=["files"])


@files_router.get("/{file_id}/content")
async def file_content(file_id: UUID, ctx=Depends(ctx_dep)):
    args = StoredFileIdDTO(id=file_id)
    result = await run_operation(registry, "files.download_stream", args, ctx)

    return streamed_download_response(result.stream)

attach_stored_file_download_route attaches the full download route instead. It runs download_stream and download_range, so it needs both enabled, and it answers like the storage kit's streaming download: 206 for a Range, each window capped at max_range_bytes (16 MiB by default), 416 past the end, 304 for a matching If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since, and the streamed 200 otherwise. Each request opens the stream first, which reads the object's head but not its body, so a 304 transfers nothing.

from forze_fastapi.routes import attach_stored_file_download_route

files_router = APIRouter(prefix="/files", tags=["files"])

# GET /files/{id}/content
attach_stored_file_download_route(
    files_router,
    registry=registry,
    ns=kit.document.default_namespace,
    ctx_dep=ctx_dep,
)

On a client-side-encrypting route the kit's upload seals each file as one AEAD payload, which a range can't slice. download_range refuses such a file with core.storage.range_whole_payload_unsupported, and the route answers a Range with the whole file and a 200.

The stream reads the object in parts while the response is sent. If the file is deleted mid-download, the next read fails with not_found. The status is already sent, so the response is cut short: the client gets fewer bytes than Content-Length, or a chunked body with no final chunk. A stored file's key is never reused, so a stream can't mix two files.

presign_download follows the storage kit's presign rules: the URL is a bearer credential and the storage key's tenant check applies. The URL signs in the stored filename as the response's Content-Disposition, so the download saves under that name rather than the object key's.

Because its result is a credential, presign_download is marked sensitive. MCP tools, agent tools, generated routes and forze ops refuse it, so serve it from a hand-written route like the one above. An MCP server over a registry that enables it needs an operations= allowlist that leaves it out, because the default exposes every read-only operation and the refusal covers the whole registration. download_stream is not marked sensitive: it returns the same bytes as download, not a credential.

download_stream returns a byte stream, and download and download_range return raw bytes, not JSON, so their descriptors set streams=True. JSON can't carry a binary file: its bytes aren't UTF-8, so encoding them fails. MCP tools and resource templates, agent tools, forze ops and attach_operation_routes can't carry these operations. The MCP and forze ops defaults leave them out, and naming one anywhere is refused. Serve them from a route that calls streamed_download_response, like the one above.

A client-side-encrypting storage route can't serve presign_download: the bytes would leave the store without passing through the app, which decrypts them. The kit resolves that operation's storage as StorageSpec(direct_transfer=True), and the route refuses such a spec with a configuration error (storage_direct_transfer_encrypted). So check_wiring reports the operation before anything runs, and without check_wiring its first call fails before the handler runs. The kit's other operations keep working on that route.

items.title: Stored-file direct uploads
items.text:
upload takes the whole file in the request body. For large files, StoredFileKitSpec(direct_uploads=True) registers three commands that keep the bytes out of the app: the client sends them straight to the bucket through presigned URLs. Bind authn and authz on each one, as you do on upload.

Operation Input Result initiate_upload InitiateStoredFileUploadRequestDTO (filename, exact size, content_type, multipart, and expires_in for a single PUT: 15 minutes by default, at most 1 hour) StoredFileUploadSessionDTO: the pending row plus a presigned PUT (presigned) or a multipart upload_id presign_upload_part PresignStoredFileUploadPartRequestDTO (id, upload_id, part_number, expires_in with the same bounds) PresignedUrlDTO for one part; it touches the row, bumping its revision, and parallel calls retry the touch complete_upload CompleteStoredFileUploadRequestDTO (id, plus upload_id and parts for a multipart upload) the ready row
  1. initiate_upload mints the storage key, {tenant}/{file_id}, and writes a pending row that holds it. The client never names a key. A declared size over max_bytes is refused before anything is minted.
  2. The client PUTs the bytes to presigned.url with every header in presigned.headers: the signed content type, and the create-only precondition (If-None-Match: * on S3, x-goog-if-generation-match: 0 on GCS). For a multipart upload it asks presign_upload_part for each part instead, and keeps each part's ETag. S3 needs the ETags, and every part but the last must be at least 5 MiB there.
  3. complete_upload checks a multipart upload before assembling it: the stored sizes of the named parts must fit max_bytes and the declared size, or the row is marked failed and the session aborted. It assembles create-only, then reads the object's head. The object's size must equal the declared size and stay within max_bytes, and its content type must equal the declared one. A match marks the row ready. A mismatch marks the row failed, then deletes the object, and raises upload_mismatch or upload_too_large. If nothing has been uploaded yet, it raises upload_incomplete and the row stays pending.

An uploaded object is create-only: the single PUT URL creates it once and can never replace it, for as long as the URL stays valid, and a multipart completion refuses to assemble over an existing object. So the bytes complete_upload checked are the bytes the file keeps. Two complete_upload calls that race are settled by the row's revision: the loser raises revision_mismatch, and a loser that refused the object marks nothing and deletes nothing.

initiate_upload and presign_upload_part return credentials: a bearer write URL, or a session id that lets its holder add parts. Both are marked sensitive, so generated surfaces refuse them; serve them from your own routes. bind_stored_file_writes runs initiate_upload in a transaction, as it does upload, and leaves complete_upload outside one, so the failed mark survives the refusal raised after it.

A client-side-encrypting route can't serve the three direct-upload commands: the app never sees the bytes, so it can't encrypt them. As with presign_download, the kit resolves their storage with direct_transfer=True, so check_wiring reports them and a call fails before any row is written.

items.title: Sweeping abandoned uploads
items.text:
A client that initiates and never completes leaves a pending row, and possibly an object or an unfinished multipart upload. A buffered upload whose process died between its commit and the after-commit stage leaves a pending row too. stored_file_pending_sweep_lifecycle_step cleans them up on an interval (10 minutes by default):

from forze_kits.aggregates.stored_file import stored_file_pending_sweep_lifecycle_step

lifecycle_steps.append(stored_file_pending_sweep_lifecycle_step(kit))

A row's age counts from its last update. initiate_upload creates the row, and each presign_upload_part touches it. Each sweep reads the pending rows not updated for older_than (24 hours by default), in id order and in batches. For each row, the sweep:

  1. Marks the row failed, with the revision check that complete_upload uses when it refuses an upload. If a complete_upload races the sweep, one of them wins cleanly: the sweep leaves a completed file alone, and a complete that lost raises revision_mismatch.
  2. Aborts every multipart upload still open at the row's key.
  3. Deletes the object at the key, if one landed.
  4. Clears the row's storage_key.

The sweep then repeats steps 2 to 4 for the failed rows not updated for older_than that still hold a key. Those are rows whose cleanup failed after the mark, and rows complete_upload refused, whose single PUT URL could still land an object after the refusal.

older_than must be longer than 1 hour, the longest a direct-upload URL lives. Every URL is signed before the update that records it: initiate_upload signs before it creates the row, and presign_upload_part signs, then touches the row, and hands the URL out only if the touch succeeds. So every URL handed out expires within 1 hour of the row's last update, and none still works once the row is past the cutoff. Concurrent sweeps can't fail a row twice, so run the step on every replica, unwrapped. Pass tenants= for tenant-aware document and storage routes. A missing route fails startup. Only a wiring error, such as tenant_global_required, stops the loop. Any other error, including a configuration error, is logged for its row or tenant, and the row is retried on a later sweep.

On S3, initiate_upload opens the multipart upload inside its transaction, so a rollback after that leaves an empty upload with no row for the sweep to find. Keep a bucket lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads (AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload). On GCS a rollback leaves nothing, because opening a session writes nothing.

items.title: Authn routes
items.text:
attach_authn_routes projects an authn registry (build_authn_registry) the same way. Authn flows are RPC-shaped with one natural surface each, so there is no style choice — fixed action paths: POST /login and POST /refresh (200, token response), POST /logout (204, no body), POST /change-password (204), POST /password-reset/request (202, uniform ack — never the token) and POST /password-reset/confirm (204), and, behind admin_guards only, POST /deactivate (204). Login, refresh, and the password-reset pair are meant to be reachable without a bearer token (the operations authenticate via their bodies, or deliberately not at all for the reset request); logout and change-password declare AuthnRequired (so they 401 without a bound identity and show up protected under apply_openapi_security). The operations that act on another principal, deactivate_principal and the admin API-key routes below, are registered only when build_authn_registry gets admin_guards, and run behind them. The full wiring (including how the reset token reaches the user via the outbox) is in the Authn, authz & tenancy recipe.

Unlike the other helpers, attach_authn_routes needs neither ns= nor resource=: without them it uses the one namespace in the registry that holds password_login or refresh_tokens under the default . separator, which is spec.default_namespace for build_authn_registry(spec). It never guesses — several such namespaces, or none, is a configuration error that asks for ns=.

items.title: Cookie mode
items.text:
Browser clients that must not hold a token in JavaScript pass an AuthnCookieCarrier to attach_authn_routes(cookies=…). Login and refresh then set and rotate two HttpOnly cookies instead of returning token strings; the body keeps the scheme and the *_expires_in lifetimes, so a cookie client still learns how long its credential is valid. Refresh reads the refresh cookie when the request has no body or an empty JSON object ({}, as fetch wrappers and generated clients send); a token in the body takes precedence. Logout revokes the session and expires both cookies idempotently.

from fastapi import APIRouter
from forze_fastapi.security import AuthnCookieCarrier

router = APIRouter(prefix="/api/auth")
cookies = AuthnCookieCarrier(
    access_path="/api",          # API calls carry the access cookie
    refresh_path="/api/auth",    # the long-lived one: every authn route, no other API call
)

attach_authn_routes(router, registry=registry, ctx_dep=ctx_dep, cookies=cookies)

Logout revokes what a logout by access token revokes (every session of the principal). With no identity bound, which is the case once the access cookie has expired, it runs logout_by_refresh_token with the refresh cookie instead. That operation has no route of its own. So scope refresh_path to cover both the refresh and the logout route, as above. No single cookie path covers only /refresh and /logout: with refresh_path="/api/auth" the browser sends the refresh cookie to every authn route under that prefix, and only refresh and logout read it. runtime_lifespan refuses to start an app whose cookie-mode logout route the refresh cookie's path does not cover (check_authn_cookie_paths, run by run_startup_checks on the app and every app mounted beneath it).

Every tab and window shares the refresh cookie, so two of them can refresh with the same token at once. With a reuse grace the losing refresh answers 401 refresh_superseded instead of revoking the session as reuse. The client refreshes again once the winner's response has set the new cookie: a retry sent before then gets refresh_superseded again, so wait for the other refresh or retry after a short delay.

Point the inbound CookieTokenAuthn's cookie_name at the same access_cookie, and list the login, refresh and logout paths in the security middleware's anonymous_paths — otherwise a stale access cookie 401s the very route that would replace it. A 401'd logout never runs, so the session stays live and the cookies stay set. check_authn_cookie_paths also refuses to start an app whose security middleware leaves one of the three cookie-mode routes out of anonymous_paths. Cookies are always HttpOnly and Secure by default, with samesite="lax" as the outbound browser-side default. Inbound, CookieTokenAuthn ships a server-side CSRF gate on by default (CookieCsrf): a request using either cookie on an unsafe method must prove a same-host origin via Origin (or Referer), so the defense holds even when a proxy strips SameSite or a samesite="none" deployment relies on it. The middleware applies it to the access cookie. Login, logout and refresh apply the same ingress's gate to every request, with or without a cookie (the default gate if no CookieTokenAuthn reads the carrier's access_cookie), so the settings below cover all three. A cross-origin frontend (a SPA on another host) lists itself in CookieCsrf(allowed_origins={...}) — a dev server that picks a free port may be named as a range on a loopback host (http://localhost:5173-5199, or http://localhost:*); non-browser cookie clients that send neither header opt in with allow_missing_origin=True or authenticate via a header ingress. csrf=None disables the gate — a declared decision to bring your own CSRF layer. When several CookieTokenAuthn read one cookie, every gate they declare applies to it, so it is ungated only when all of them opt out.

items.title: API-key management
items.text:
attach_authn_routes also generates self-service API-key management as a resource collection (all AuthnRequired): POST /api-keys issues a key for the caller — the raw secret is in the response once, optionally a user→agent delegation key (actor_principal_id: another principal authentication accepts, and a registered service principal when AuthnDepsModule(authz_route=...) is set; otherwise 422 delegate_invalid) with a human label — GET /api-keys lists the caller's keys as non-secret descriptors (a hint like ab12…wxyz, never the secret), and DELETE /api-keys/{id} revokes one (204, and 204 again for a key already revoked; a key the caller does not hold is a 404, as an unknown one is). This is the minting surface for the MCP API-key flow: the user issues a key here and pastes it into the agent host.

An administrator finds a principal's keys with GET /admin/principals/{id}/api-keys (list_principal_api_keys: the same non-secret descriptors, revoked keys included, and an empty list for a principal with none) and revokes one with DELETE /admin/api-keys/{id} (revoke_principal_api_key, 204, and 204 again for a key already revoked; an unknown key is a 404). They exist only when the registry is built with admin_guards, the steps that decide who may act on another principal; they run behind them, and so does deactivate_principal, which without them is not registered either. One guard set gates all three. At least one guard must declare the permission keys it enforces (permission_keys()), as AuthzBeforeAuthorize does, or the registry is refused when built (admin_guards_unauthorized): AuthnRequired, TenantRequired or a logging step let every signed-in principal through. A step of your own counts once it implements permission_keys(), and its keys then show in the catalog and in MCP tool descriptions; a functools.partial or __wrapped__ wrapper counts as what it wraps. If one of your guards authorizes without declaring it, pass trust_admin_guards=True and answer for it. If you bound your own guards on deactivate_principal, pass them as admin_guards instead: the same step bound twice fails at freeze() with Step ID … is not unique.

The guards also run on the list, which is a read: there they run read-only, so a guard that writes (an audit row, say) fails the list with Cannot use command (write) port. Write such a record from an after-hook or through the outbox instead.

The admin API-key routes are global, like deactivate_principal: API-key accounts are not tenant-scoped, so they find a principal's keys or a key by id in every tenant, and the revoke's 404 tells a caller whether an id exists anywhere. An app whose administrators are scoped to a tenant must not expose these routes, or must guard them with a policy only platform administrators pass.

A delegated caller (an agent acting for the user) may list the keys but not issue or revoke them, and may not log out or change the password: only the user manages their own account. Nor may it act as an administrator, to list or revoke anyone's keys or deactivate a principal: an agent acting for an administrator is not one. Those routes answer 403 (delegate_denied), and so do switching and leaving a tenant below.

Identity, invocation metadata, and error mapping stay with the middlewares and exception handlers from the integration setup — generated routes only validate the input DTO and run the operation through the normal pipeline.

items.title: Tenancy routes
items.text: attach_tenancy_routes projects the self-service tenant-selector registry — fixed paths, no style choice: GET /tenants (the caller's tenants), POST /tenants/{id}/activate (switch the active tenant), DELETE /tenants/{id} (204, leave). In cookie mode, pass the same carrier as cookies=: /activate then sets and rotates both cookies and strips the token strings from its body, behind the gate login applies. It authenticates from the access cookie, so leave it out of anonymous_paths. The access cookie's access_path must cover the tenancy routes' mount, or the switch answers 401. The refresh cookie's path need not cover it: the response sets that cookie at its own path, and the route never reads it. The gate follows the csrf of the CookieTokenAuthn reading the access cookie: csrf=None on every such ingress turns it off for the switch too, as for login. attach_tenancy_admin_routes projects the admin plane: POST /tenants (201, create), GET /tenants/{id}/members, POST /tenants/{id}/deactivate (204), POST /memberships (204, invite) and DELETE /memberships (204, remove). Admin operations ship without hooks bound — guard them with AuthnRequired + authz hooks in the registry.

items.title: Aggregate routes
items.text: attach_aggregate_routes(router, kit, *, ctx_dep, style="rest", tx_route="default", storage_prefix="/blobs") is the composite: given an AggregateKit it attaches the kit's document (+ soft-deletion), search, and — when the kit declares storage — blob routes (under storage_prefix) onto one router with a single call, each sub-surface exactly as its dedicated attacher would. tx_route must match the transaction route the deps module registers.

items.title: Your own operation routes
items.text:
An operation no attacher ships gets its route from a binding table, not a hand-written endpoint. attach_operation_routes takes the table keyed by operation suffix under a namespace; the schema, operation_id (the namespaced key, e.g. stock.add) and dispatch come from the catalog, as for the generated routes.

from forze.base.primitives import StrKeyNamespace
from forze_fastapi.routes import (
    RouteBinding,
    attach_operation_routes,
    body_endpoint,
    id_endpoint,
    query_endpoint,
)

attach_operation_routes(
    router,
    registry=registry,
    ns=StrKeyNamespace(prefix="stock"),
    ctx_dep=ctx_dep,
    bindings={
        "levels": RouteBinding(method="GET", path="/levels", build=query_endpoint),
        "add": RouteBinding(method="POST", path="/add", build=body_endpoint, status_code=201),
        "get": RouteBinding(
            method="GET",
            path="/{id}",
            build=id_endpoint,
            param_descriptions={"id": "The stock item's ID."},
        ),
    },
)

A binding whose operation is not registered is refused, so a typo fails at startup rather than answering 404; pass skip_unregistered=True to skip it instead.

Every routed operation's key lives under the namespace, as <prefix>.<suffix>. A key registered without one, such as a bare add, cannot be bound: register it as stock.add instead. The refusal names a bare key it finds, so the cause is not mistaken for a typo.

query_endpoint reads the whole input DTO from query parameters, one per field; a list field repeats (?tag=a&tag=b). A field a query string cannot carry, such as a nested model or bytes, is refused when the route is attached. The operation receives the DTO a body with the same keys would build: only the parameters sent count as set, so a patch built from it leaves the rest alone, and validators and extras behave as for a body. A parameter the DTO does not declare is ignored unless the DTO forbids or allows extra fields. A literal + in a value, such as a timezone offset, must be sent as %2B: a query string reads + as a space.

body_endpoint, id_endpoint, id_rev_endpoint and id_rev_body_endpoint are the builders the document routes use. The id builders take id and rev from the path where it has their placeholder and from the query otherwise, typed and defaulted as the input DTO declares them. Each shipped builder names the placeholders it fills, and a path with any other placeholder is refused. An EndpointBuilder of your own takes (runner, input_type, op); give it a path_params frozenset to have its paths checked the same way.

A binding's param_descriptions describe its endpoint's parameters by name. Each becomes FastAPI's own Path where the path has the placeholder and Query otherwise, so id reads the same in both route styles. Only a plain path or query parameter takes one. When the route is attached, an empty description is refused, and so is a name the endpoint does not take. A body, the request, or a parameter with its own Query, Depends, … is refused too: describe that one in its own metadata. A query_endpoint parameter takes its description from the DTO field.

The operation's output type is the route's response model. It need not be a bare model: an operation that may find nothing declares output_type=Model | None and answers 200 with null, and MCP returns it as {"result": null}. An operation without one, such as a federated search, still has a model result written as a typed route's is: fields that are None are left out unless the attacher passes exclude_none=False, and the OpenAPI schema documents an untyped body. Any other result, such as a dict or a list, is written as FastAPI writes a route without a response model. Either way an infinite or NaN float is written as null.

items.title: Infrastructure routes
items.text:
• attach_jwks_route(router, jwks_provider, *, path="/.well-known/jwks.json", cache_max_age=300) — the JWKS document for token verification; excluded from the OpenAPI schema.
  • attach_readiness_route(router, runtime, *, path="/readyz", probes=None, probe_timeout=timedelta(seconds=2)) — 200 while the runtime is active and not draining, 503 otherwise; excluded from the schema. runtime may also be a zero-argument callable returning the runtime or None, asked per request, for an app that builds its runtime in the lifespan. probes maps a name to the deps key of a client to ask health(), adding a checks breakdown and a degraded 503 when a dependency is unreachable — see Readiness.
  • attach_liveness_route(router, *, path="/livez") — 200 unconditionally; reaching the handler is the check. Deliberately blind to drain, so a draining pod reads as alive-but-not-ready instead of dead. Excluded from the schema.
  • attach_metrics_route(router, reader, *, path="/metrics") — a Prometheus pull endpoint over an already-registered PrometheusMetricReader (needs opentelemetry-exporter-prometheus; any other reader is refused). Renders off the event loop, since collection runs every observable callback in the process. Single-process deployments only — see The Grafana stack.

items.title: Document auth in OpenAPI
items.text:
SecurityContextMiddleware extracts identity; it doesn't tell the schema. By default the generated OpenAPI (and the Scalar/Swagger UI) shows every endpoint as open — no Authorize button. apply_openapi_security closes that gap from the same AuthnRequirement you handed the middleware, so the scheme is declared once:

from forze.application.contracts.authn import AuthnSpec
from forze_fastapi.security import (
    AuthnRequirement,
    HeaderTokenAuthn,
    apply_openapi_security,
)

# Your authn aggregate's spec — the same one your routes and the engine resolve.
API = AuthnSpec(name="api", enabled_methods=frozenset({"token"}))

requirement = AuthnRequirement(
    ingress=(HeaderTokenAuthn(authn_spec=API, header_name="Authorization"),),
)
# ...plus whatever else your middleware takes.
app.add_middleware(
    SecurityContextMiddleware,
    ctx_dep=runtime.get_context,
    authn=requirement,
)

# After every router is attached:
apply_openapi_security(app, requirement)

It registers one securityScheme per ingress (bearer for a token on Authorization; apiKey in header or cookie otherwise) and attaches a security requirement — the ingress methods as alternatives — to exactly the operations the catalog flagged as needing a bound principal. That flag (requires_authn) is derived at freeze from the plan's AuthnRequired or authz hooks, so protected routes advertise the scheme while token-minting routes (/login, /refresh) stay open. Use exclude={"orders.deactivate", ...} to leave a flagged operation open.

This documents auth; it doesn't enforce it. The middleware refuses a request no ingress authenticates outside its anonymous_paths (list the mounted /auth/login and /auth/refresh there), and per-operation enforcement stays in the engine's AuthnRequired/authz hooks.

items.title: Match OpenAPI to what the app serves
items.text:
FastAPI documents its own 422 body (HTTPValidationError) on every route that takes input, but the Forze exception handlers answer errors — a failed request parse included — with the Forze envelope. Descriptions come from docstrings, so reST such as :class:`~shop.Order` reaches the rendered docs as written. One call fixes both:

from forze_fastapi import apply_openapi_conventions

# After every router is attached, and after apply_openapi_security:
apply_openapi_conventions(app)

Each FastAPI 422 becomes the ForzeErrorResponse envelope (detail, code, kind, optional context), and every operation without its own default response gains one in the same shape. Only detail is listed as required: every error Forze raises carries code and kind, but an HTTPException from your code or a FastAPI dependency answers with detail alone. The X-Error-Code header accompanies the errors that carry a code, so it is documented as optional. FastAPI's validation schemas are dropped once nothing references them. A 422 your route declares with its own model is left alone. A different model of yours already named ForzeErrorResponse is not overwritten: the schema request fails with a configuration error, since routers can still be attached after the call. Responses a route sends with no body at all, such as a storage download's 304 and 416, are not envelopes; the default entry does not describe them.

Every description and summary then has its reST rendered as Markdown without losing prose: roles and ``literals`` become code spans, field lists (:param:, :returns:, …) are dropped, code-block and :: literal blocks become fenced blocks, and any other directive (note, deprecated, versionadded, …) becomes a labelled blockquote. Fenced blocks already in Markdown pass through as written. Call it last: text a later wrapper adds, such as a security scheme's description, stays as written.

A generated client types a response field optional when its schema does not list it required, and pydantic leaves every field with a default optional, though the app sends it every time. apply_openapi_conventions(app, require_sent_fields=True) lists what every route returning a schema sends. Where only routes that keep nulls (exclude_none=False) return it, every field is required. Where a route drops nulls, the default for the routes Forze attaches, the fields that cannot be null are required, and a nullable one, left out when it is null, is not, even without a default. A schema is one component shared by all the routes that return it, so where a route that keeps nulls and one that drops them return the same model, its nullable fields are optional for both. A schema a request also uses is left as it is, and so is one a route trims some other way (response_model_exclude_unset, include, exclude).

tag_groups groups the sidebar that Scalar and Redoc render, through the top-level x-tagGroups extension. Groups and their tags keep the order you give:

from forze_fastapi import apply_openapi_conventions

apply_openapi_conventions(
    app,
    tag_groups={"Content": ["notes", "files"], "Access": ["auth"]},
)

A group without a name, tags given as one string ("notes" for ["notes"]), or a tag listed twice is a configuration error raised by the call itself. A listed tag that no operation is tagged with, a typo or a renamed router, is left out of its group with a warning, and a group left with no tags is dropped. Neither renderer shows a tag that no group lists, nor the operations under it. The tags you leave out therefore join a group named Other, in the order operations first use them: last, or where you list Other yourself. An operation with no tags is in no group: Scalar still lists it, Redoc does not, so tag every route. A later call with tag_groups replaces the groups; one without leaves them as they are. register_scalar_docs needs no setting, since Scalar reads the groups from the schema.

register_scalar_docs points Scalar at the URL the app serves its document at (app.openapi_url, prefixed with the request's root_path), so a versioned FastAPI(openapi_url="/v1/openapi.json") needs nothing extra. Pass openapi_url= for a document another route serves; an app with openapi_url=None must pass one.

items.title: Glossary
items.text: Plain-language definitions for the terms used across the docs, grouped by area. Skim it, or search for a single word.

items.title: Core concepts
items.text:
Aggregate : A business entity with identity, versioning, and invariants. Subclass Document to create one; add the AggregateRoot mixin when you need domain events.

Adapter : A concrete implementation of a port for a specific backend — PostgresDocumentAdapter implements the document port for PostgreSQL.

Execution context : The runtime object that resolves ports to adapters on demand. Handlers receive it and request capabilities without knowing which adapter backs them.

Operation : A single business action — create a user, list orders, delete a document. Operations are registered in an operation registry and resolved at runtime.

Operation registry : The frozen catalog mapping operation names to their handlers and hooks. Built with build_document_registry() and locked with freeze().

Port : A contract describing a capability the application needs — storage, cache, search, messaging. Ports live in the application layer; adapters implement them in infrastructure.

Specification (Spec) : The logical name ("users") that binds a model to its operations and adapters — DocumentSpec, SearchSpec, CacheSpec, and so on.

items.title: Spec types
items.text:
DocumentSpec : Declares a document aggregate with CRUD operations. Binds domain model, create command, and read model to a logical name.

SearchSpec : Declares a search index for full-text or structured queries over documents.

EmbeddingsSpec : Declares an embeddings provider (resolved via ctx.embeddings.provider(spec)) that turns text into vectors, for similarity (vector) search.

CacheSpec : Declares a cache layer for read-through or write-through caching.

QueueSpec : Declares a message queue for async task dispatch.

StreamSpec : Declares an ordered, replayable stream (an append log read by offset or consumer group).

PubSubSpec : Declares a fire-and-forget pub/sub topic for fan-out to live subscribers.

GraphModuleSpec : Declares a graph data model — typed node and edge kinds — for relationship queries.

items.title: Model types
items.text:
Domain model : The business entity with behavior and invariants. Subclass Document for identity, revision, and timestamps.

Create command : The frozen input for POST operations. Use BaseDTO (the CreateDocumentCmd alias is deprecated).

Update command : Partial update payload for PATCH operations. Typically a BaseDTO with optional fields.

Read model : The frozen projection returned from GET operations. May include computed fields not stored in the domain model.

Domain event : A record of something that happened in the domain. Subclass DomainEvent for event_id, occurred_at, and payload.

items.title: Runtime and wiring
items.text:
DepsModule : A module that registers adapters for specs. Examples: PostgresDepsModule, RedisDepsModule, MockDepsModule.

DepsRegistry : The container holding all registered deps modules and their wiring.

ExecutionRuntime : The top-level runtime that manages lifecycle, builds contexts, and coordinates shutdown.

Lifecycle plan : The dependency graph that determines startup and shutdown order for adapters.

Route (wiring) : The mapping from a spec name to its adapter configuration. Not to be confused with HTTP routes.

Transaction route : A transactional boundary that groups operations. Configured per-request or per-saga step.

Isolation level : The transaction isolation an operation requires — READ_COMMITTED < SNAPSHOT < SERIALIZABLE. Declared with set_isolation(...) and enforced fail-closed against the route's transaction manager.

items.title: Identity and tenancy
items.text:
AuthnIdentity : The verified identity of a request — who is making the call.

AuthzScope : The tenant partition an authorization decision or grant lookup runs within. (The permissions themselves resolve as EffectiveGrants — roles plus permissions.)

TenantIdentity : The tenant context bound to a request. Determines data isolation strategy.

Tenant tier : The isolation level for a resource: none (not tenant-scoped), tagged (a tenant marker, such as a column or a tenant_aware key prefix), namespace (a per-tenant container a resolver picks, such as a schema, collection, bucket or namespace), or dedicated (separate instance).

items.title: Patterns
items.text:
CQRS : Command Query Responsibility Segregation. Forze's query/command port split follows this pattern — writes go through command ports, reads through query ports.

OCC : Optimistic Concurrency Control. Forze uses revision numbers to detect concurrent modifications.

Outbox : A transactional pattern where events are written to a local table in the same transaction as state changes, then relayed to external systems.

Inbox : The receiving side of outbox — deduplicated message processing with exactly-once semantics.

Saga : A sequence of operations across aggregates or services, with compensation logic for rollback.

items.title: Mapping & codecs
items.text: You send a create command and get back a read model; an event is staged as one type and decoded as another. Two small layers handle all of it — and both default to field-name matching, so the happy path needs no hand-written conversion.

items.title: The model types
items.text:
From forze.domain.models:

Type Role Provides Document the persisted domain model id (uuid7), rev, created_at, last_update_at — with defaults; carries update() + invariants AggregateRoot mix in for event-emitting aggregates a pending-events buffer + @event_emitter BaseDTO frozen input/output projection nothing — you declare the fields ReadDocument read-model base id, rev, created_at, last_update_at — required (filled from the row) DomainEvent frozen event base event_id (uuid7), occurred_at

A spec's write side is declared with DocumentWriteTypes (a TypedDict from forze.application.contracts.document): domain, create_cmd, and an optional update_cmd.

CreateDocumentCmd is deprecated

It's an empty alias of BaseDTO. Declare create payloads as plain BaseDTO; identity isn't carried in the payload — create(payload, id=…) / ensure(id, …) take it explicitly.

class Order(Document):          # domain: + id, rev, created_at, last_update_at
    customer_id: str
    total_cents: int

class CreateOrder(BaseDTO):     # create command — frozen, no id
    customer_id: str
    total_cents: int

class OrderRead(ReadDocument):  # read model — inherits the four metadata fields
    customer_id: str
    total_cents: int

items.title: Codecs
items.text:
A codec serializes a model to/from a mapping (and JSON bytes). Record models are Pydantic, so one codec ships:

from forze.base.serialization import PydanticModelCodec, default_model_codec

PydanticModelCodec(OrderPlaced)   # for a pydantic BaseModel
default_model_codec(OrderPlaced)  # the same, derived from the model type

default_model_codec(model_type) is what specs use when you don't pass one.

A codec is required wherever a payload crosses a wire and the framework can't infer the type from a domain model:

Where Field Outbox OutboxSpec(codec=PydanticModelCodec(Payload)) Queue / stream / pub-sub QueueSpec(codec=…) Idempotency the wrap's result_type (a pydantic model)

Document, search, and analytics specs derive their codecs from the model types automatically; override with DocumentSpec(codecs=…) only if you need to.

items.title: Which serialization library, where
items.text:
The framework uses one rule, by who owns the shape:

Shape Library Why Your record models — read models, commands, DTOs, events, query params Pydantic validators, computed/materialized fields, custom coercion — the rich, customizable layer Framework-owned value objects — specs, deps, message envelopes, cursors, storage upload/download/metadata attrs closed, framework-declared shapes with no validation needs; cheap frozen value objects

The codec layer is Pydantic only: read models, commands (create/update), idempotency results, and other record contracts must be BaseModel subclasses. There is no second model library to opt into.

items.title: How a write maps
items.text:
A create flows through two conversions:

  1. DTO → command (handler layer, forze_kits) — the public request DTO (DocumentDTOs.create) is mapped to the spec's create_cmd. The default is a field-name-matching mapper; override per-operation via DocumentMappers.
  2. command → domain → read (codec layer, in the port) — the command is transformed into the domain model (which stamps id/rev/timestamps), persisted, and the stored row is decoded back into the read model.
from forze_kits.aggregates.document import DocumentDTOs, build_document_registry

dtos = DocumentDTOs(read=OrderRead, create=CreateOrder, update=UpdateOrder)
registry = build_document_registry(order_spec, dtos)   # default mappers

Both layers use Pydantic transform (dump-then-validate), so conversion is by matching field names — never positional. Supply a DocumentMappers(create=…) hook only when the boundary DTO and the command genuinely differ in shape.

items.title: Metric catalog
items.text:
Every metric below is emitted through the global OpenTelemetry meter named forze, by an instrument_* call you make once at assembly. Nothing appears until you make that call — the instrumentation surface is opt-in per plane. Point an SDK at a collector with bootstrap_telemetry and see them in Grafana with the stack recipe.

Names are stable. This table is checked against the constants in src/ by a unit test, in both directions: a metric that exists but is not documented fails, and so does a documented metric that no longer exists.

Conventions that hold throughout:

  • Unit 1 means a plain count. ms is milliseconds, s seconds.
  • Observable instruments are sampled by the SDK at collection time from a live object (pool, keyring, cache, mailbox). They are cumulative per process, so a restart resets them — rate() handles that correctly only if each process carries a distinct service.instance.id, which is why bootstrap_telemetry mints one by default.
  • tenant_id is never a metric label, anywhere, by design. Per-tenant questions are answered from traces and logs, which both carry it. See the cardinality doctrine.

items.title: Operations
items.text:
instrument_operations(registry) — the outermost middleware on every operation.

Metric Instrument Unit Labels Notes forze.operations counter 1 forze.operation, forze.operation.kind, forze.outcome kind is command / query; outcome is success / failed / error forze.operation.duration histogram ms same as above ms-ladder buckets installed by bootstrap_telemetry

The distinction that matters: outcome="failed" is a client-class domain failure (validation, not-found, conflict, precondition — a 4xx the caller may well handle) and leaves the span clean. outcome="error" is a genuine fault. Alert on error, chart both.

items.title: Resilience
items.text:
instrument_resilience(executor) — independent of the tracing gate; a production process with tracing off still reports these.

Metric Instrument Unit Labels Notes forze.resilience.events counter 1 forze.event, forze.policy, forze.route retries, timeouts, rate-limit/bulkhead rejections, budget exhaustion, breaker transitions forze.resilience.breaker.state gauge 1 forze.policy, forze.route 0 closed, 1 half-open, 2 open. A breaker that never tripped reports nothing — closed by absence forze.resilience.bulkhead.queue_depth observable gauge 1 forze.policy, forze.route calls queued behind the semaphore forze.resilience.bulkhead.limit observable gauge 1 forze.policy, forze.route current AIMD concurrency limit forze.resilience.hedge.delay observable gauge s forze.policy, forze.route effective adaptive hedge delay (windowed P² estimate)

breaker_open in the events counter covers both the open transition and every admission rejected while open, so its rate tracks shed load rather than flap count.

items.title: Tenant pools
items.text:
instrument_tenant_pools({"postgres": client, ...}) — one entry per routed client.

Metric Instrument Unit Labels Notes forze.tenancy.pool.size observable gauge 1 forze.client live tenant pools forze.tenancy.pool.capacity observable gauge 1 forze.client max_cached_tenants forze.tenancy.pool.created observable counter 1 forze.client cumulative pool creations forze.tenancy.pool.disposed observable counter 1 forze.client cumulative pool disposals forze.tenancy.pool.evicted_explicit observable counter 1 forze.client explicit evictions (rotation signals)

The alert that matters: a sustained created rate while size == capacity is LRU thrash — hot tenants' pools evicted by cold one-off traffic, each rebuild paying full connection establishment.

items.title: Crypto and KMS
items.text:
instrument_crypto({"default": keyring, ...}).

Metric Instrument Unit Labels Notes forze.crypto.data_keys.generated observable counter 1 forze.keyring KMS round-trips on the encrypt path forze.crypto.data_keys.unwrapped observable counter 1 forze.keyring KMS round-trips on the decrypt path forze.crypto.cache.hits observable counter 1 forze.keyring, forze.crypto.path path is encrypt / decrypt; data keys reused without a KMS call forze.crypto.cold_miss observable counter 1 forze.keyring synchronous crypt that hit a cold cache and raised cipher_not_warm

Hit ratio is hits / (hits + the matching generated|unwrapped) — composed at query time, never precomputed, so it aggregates correctly across processes.

The alert that matters: cold_miss should sit at ~0. A sustained rate means a read/write path is skipping warm / ensure_unwrapped.

items.title: Document L1 cache
items.text:
instrument_document_l1() — reads a process-wide registry of live L1 stores.

Metric Instrument Unit Labels Notes forze.cache.l1.size observable gauge 1 forze.document live entries forze.cache.l1.capacity observable gauge 1 forze.document configured capacity forze.cache.l1.hits observable counter 1 forze.document cumulative hits forze.cache.l1.misses observable counter 1 forze.document cumulative misses forze.cache.l1.evictions observable counter 1 forze.document includes rejected admissions

Sustained evictions while size == capacity is the scan-pollution signature that justifies W-TinyLFU (L1Spec(store_factory=tiny_lfu_l1_store)) or a bigger capacity.

items.title: Durable execution
items.text:
DurableTelemetry.create(), wired into the durable runner.

Metric Instrument Unit Labels Notes forze.durable.runs counter 1 forze.durable.name, forze.durable.outcome outcome is completed / failed / retrying / forward_incomplete / cancelled / timed_out / reclaimed / interrupted / unrecorded — alert on failed, not on the total: cancelled means somebody pressed Stop, and retrying is an attempt that failed and sent its run back for another under the runner's retry strategy. unrecorded describes the attempt, not the run: the body finished and its terminal write went unacknowledged, so the row is either already terminal (the write committed, the ack was lost) or still RUNNING for recovery — the worker cannot tell. A sustained rate of it means the run store is unreachable. interrupted is the neighbouring case where the body never finished at all (drain, shutdown) and no terminal state was written — expected during a deploy forze.durable.run.duration histogram ms forze.durable.name, forze.durable.outcome ms-ladder buckets installed by bootstrap_telemetry forze.durable.recovered counter 1 — runs a recovery sweep claimed: reclaimed from a process that died holding them, or simply due (enqueued, back for a retry, requeued) forze.durable.schedule.fires counter 1 forze.durable.name one per schedule fire

A recovered spike means runs are being reclaimed from processes that died holding them — normal in small numbers after a deploy, a signal when it is sustained. The counter cannot tell those from runs that were simply due, so enqueued runs, retries under a retry strategy and requeues set its baseline: alert above it.

items.title: Leadership
items.text:
instrument_leadership() — reads every leadership_lifecycle_step in the process.

Metric Instrument Unit Labels Notes forze.leadership.held observable gauge 1 forze.leadership.key 1 while this process holds the lease, through its term's grace and until the release forze.leadership.terms_ended observable counter 1 forze.leadership.key, forze.leadership.reason reason is lost / expiring / stopped / yielded / returned / raised / unclaimed

Summed across processes, held should be 1 per key. A sustained rate of lost or expiring means the lock backend is slow or unreachable from the leader; raised is the body's own failure.

items.title: Job progress
items.text:
instrument_job_staleness(monitor) — see Operation progress.

Metric Instrument Unit Labels Notes forze.jobs.stalled observable gauge 1 forze.job.kind started, unfinished, silent past the window forze.jobs.stalled.oldest_silence observable gauge s forze.job.kind seconds since the quietest stuck job reported; computed at scrape forze.jobs.staleness.scan_age observable gauge s — seconds since the last successful sweep; -1 before the first

Undeclared kinds land in the __other__ bucket rather than vanishing, so a kind added later is still counted.

Alarm on scan_age too, not only on stalled. The counts are a cache: if the sweep loop dies they freeze at their last value — almost always zero — and a rule watching only the count goes green at the exact moment it stops knowing anything.

items.title: Realtime gateway
items.text:
instrument_realtime_gateway(stats) — the live-emit path. All labelled forze.realtime.channel.

Metric Instrument Unit Notes forze.realtime.gateway.emitted observable counter 1 frames delivered to Socket.IO forze.realtime.gateway.emit_failed observable counter 1 sio.emit raised, including emit-timeout expiries forze.realtime.gateway.presence_skipped observable counter 1 empty principal room; recoverable via the mailbox forze.realtime.gateway.dedup_skipped observable counter 1 durable signals already seen forze.realtime.gateway.admission_rejected observable counter 1 rejected at the catalog admission gate forze.realtime.gateway.untenanted_dropped observable counter 1 no tenant resolved on a require_tenant gateway forze.realtime.gateway.mailboxed observable counter 1 stored for offline replay forze.realtime.gateway.bridge_failed observable counter 1 redelivered if durable, dropped if ephemeral forze.realtime.gateway.poisoned observable counter 1 dropped at the delivery ceiling — bounded loss

The two to alarm on: poisoned (every increment is a dropped durable delivery) and emit_failed climbing while emitted is flat (Socket.IO, or its Redis backplane, stopped taking frames).

items.title: Realtime backplane
items.text:
instrument_realtime_backplane(health), fed by the heartbeat lifecycle step. Labelled forze.realtime.channel.

Metric Instrument Unit Notes forze.realtime.backplane.seconds_since_ok observable gauge s seconds since the backplane last accepted a probe; -1 means never forze.realtime.backplane.consecutive_failures observable gauge 1 failed probes since the last success

A dead AsyncRedisManager listener silently stops every cross-node emit and nothing in python-socketio surfaces it. Alarm on seconds_since_ok exceeding a few heartbeat intervals; -1 is a wiring problem, not an outage.

items.title: Realtime connections
items.text:
instrument_realtime_connections(stats), with the same RealtimeConnectionStats handed to attach_realtime_connection and connection_drain_lifecycle_step. Labelled forze.realtime.channel.

Metric Instrument Unit Labels Notes forze.realtime.connections observable up-down counter 1 forze.realtime.namespace connections open on this node forze.realtime.connect_refused observable counter 1 forze.realtime.namespace, forze.realtime.reason protocol, auth, draining, admission, internal; a draining connect is turned away by closing its transport forze.realtime.drain_closed observable counter 1 forze.realtime.outcome closes the drain started: closed, failed, timed_out

What to watch: connect_refused{reason="draining"} that keeps climbing long after a deploy means a balancer still routes to a replica it should have dropped, and any drain_closed{outcome="timed_out"} means the drain's tail is too short for this node's closes.

items.title: Realtime mailbox
items.text:
instrument_realtime_mailbox(mailbox, cursors). Labelled forze.realtime.channel.

Metric Instrument Unit Notes forze.realtime.mailbox.stored observable counter 1 durable principal signals stored for replay forze.realtime.mailbox.replayed observable counter 1 entries fetched on connect-time replay forze.realtime.mailbox.trimmed observable counter 1 dropped by retention/ack trimming forze.realtime.mailbox.acked observable counter 1 per-device cursor advances forze.realtime.mailbox.overflowed observable counter 1 replays that lost their oldest backlog to the cap

The alert that matters: every overflowed increment is a device that fell more than cap entries behind and lost signals it will never see.

items.title: Access-token signing
items.text:
instrument_signing({"default": service, ...}) — the identity plane. Labelled forze.signer, forze.signer.algorithm, and forze.signer.kid when set.

Metric Instrument Unit Notes forze.authn.tokens.signed observable counter 1 access tokens issued; for a KMS-held key this tracks sign round-trips forze.authn.tokens.verified observable counter 1 verified successfully forze.authn.tokens.verify_failed observable counter 1 rejected as expired/invalid

A rising verify_failed rate is the signal that matters: key-rotation gaps, clock skew, or forgeries.

items.title: Revocation states
items.text:
instrument_revocation_states({"default": revocation_states}) — the identity plane's fast path for sessions and API keys. Labelled forze.revocation_states and forze.credential (session or api_key).

Metric Instrument Unit Notes forze.authn.revocation_states.hits observable counter 1 verifications answered from Redis alone, refusals included forze.authn.revocation_states.misses observable counter 1 verifications that read the database for a state Redis lacked or could not trust forze.authn.revocation_states.fallbacks observable counter 1 verifications whose Redis read failed, timed out or met an open breaker forze.authn.revocation_states.write_failures observable counter 1 revocations whose write-through failed every attempt forze.authn.revocation_states.clock_skew observable counter 1 API-key states refused because the application's clock runs two ttl or more ahead of Redis's

The alert that matters: every write_failures increment is a revoked credential that stays admitted for up to the states' ttl. See Authentication for every cause of that window.

items.title: Operations CLI
items.text: The how-to is Operations CLI; this page is the contract scripts rely on. The exit codes, the error object and the stdout shape are stable across releases.

items.title: Commands
items.text:
forze ops list      [--app REF] [--json]
forze ops describe  [--app REF] OP [--json]
forze ops call      [--app REF] OP
                    [--input JSON|@PATH|- | --FIELD VALUE ... | --batch @PATH|-]
                    [--tenant UUID] [--idempotency-key KEY]
                    [--timeout SECONDS] [--grace SECONDS]
                    [--correlation-id UUID] [--causation-id UUID]
                    [--api-key-file PATH] [--pretty]

OP is the operation key, dots included: orders.get. --app names the OpsApp as module:attribute, or a zero-argument callable returning one, and falls back to FORZE_OPS_APP. A group from build_ops_cli(app) has the declaration bound and no --app.

OP completes in the shell after describe and call once completion is installed with forze --install-completion. Completion loads the declaration from --app or FORZE_OPS_APP as list does, never builds the runtime, and offers nothing when the declaration cannot load. A group from build_ops_cli completes from its own declaration, installed by your root CLI's --install-completion. Every TAB imports the application module, so its import side effects run in the operator's shell.

list and describe never build the runtime. They write text, or JSON with --json. describe shows the title and description, the kind, the declared authn requirement and permissions, idempotency support, the deadline, the typed flags, the query surface, and the input and output JSON Schemas.

items.title: call options
items.text:
Option Effect Refused when --input JSON / @PATH / - the input object, inline, from a file, or from stdin; validated into the operation's input DTO, unknown keys refused the operation takes no input; the JSON does not parse (NaN and Infinity included) or is not an object; the file cannot be read; the input is inline and the DTO declares a SecretStr or SecretBytes field --batch @PATH / - one call per line of a JSONL file or of stdin, in one runtime; see Batches the value is neither @PATH nor -; combined with --input, typed flags, --idempotency-key or --pretty --tenant UUID a requested tenant, validated against the principal's membership, or matching the key's own tenant the identity is not an API key; nothing can validate it --idempotency-key KEY binds the key: a repeat with the same input replays the stored result the operation does not support one --timeout SECONDS bounds the operation; only ever tightens its declared deadline not a positive, finite number --grace SECONDS how long a first SIGINT or SIGTERM waits for the call to finish; default 10 negative, or not finite --correlation-id UUID, --causation-id UUID carried into the invocation metadata malformed --api-key-file PATH reads the API key from a file instead of the environment the identity is not an API key; the file cannot be read --pretty indents the result

A malformed --timeout, --grace, --tenant, --batch or id is a parse error: Click's usage text on stderr, exit 2, nothing on stdout. Every other refusal is an error object, an option call does not have included: it is read as a typed flag.

items.title: Typed flags
items.text:
An operation whose input is flat scalars also takes that input as flags after OP, instead of --input:

$ forze ops call notes.create --title "Quarterly report"
Field type Flag str, int, float, Decimal, UUID, date, datetime, an Enum of strings, an IntEnum, a Literal of strings; optional or constrained ones too --field-name VALUE, or --field-name=VALUE bool --field-name sets it, --no-field-name clears it
  • Spelling. A field's flag is its name with - for _. An alias never is.
  • Validation. The flags build the object --input would carry, and it is validated the same way: each value is the string you typed, coerced by the DTO; an omitted flag takes the field's default; a missing required field or a bad value exits 4 and is never echoed.
  • A value that looks like a flag. --title --pretty gives --pretty to call, and --title --draft is refused: the token after a flag that needs a value cannot start with --. Write --title=--pretty.
  • On argv. Every value is on the command line, where ps and shell history show it. A secret field is refused; pass any other sensitive value with --input @PATH.
  • All or none. An input takes no flags when one of its fields is anything else (a list, a model, a union), when it declares a SecretStr or SecretBytes field, or when a flag would be spelled like a call option (--timeout, --input, …) or like another field's. A call option means the same for every operation. describe lists the flags, or says why there are none.
  • Exclusive. Typed flags and --input cannot be combined.

items.title: Batches
items.text:
--batch @PATH or --batch - calls the operation once per line of a JSONL file, or of stdin, inside one runtime: one startup and one shutdown for the whole batch. Each line is an input object, as --input would carry; blank lines are skipped.

$ forze ops call notes.create --batch @notes.jsonl
{"line": 1, "result": {"id": "…", "title": "a", …}, "execution_id": "…", "correlation_id": "…"}
{"line": 2, "result": {"id": "…", "title": "b", …}, "execution_id": "…", "correlation_id": "…"}
  • Validated first. Every line is read and validated before the runtime is built. A line that does not parse or validate is the only line written, and nothing runs. The whole input is held in memory, so split a file too large for that.
  • One line out per call. Stdout holds one JSON document per line that ran, in order, each written as its call finishes: {"line": N, "result": …} or the error object with "line": N. Each carries its own execution_id; all share one correlation_id, the --correlation-id given or one minted for the batch. Each line is a governed call: its identity is verified and its tenant resolved again.
  • Stops at the first failure. The failed line is the last one written, and its exit code, by the table below, is the batch's. Exit 0 means every line succeeded.
  • No idempotency key. One key would claim every line, so --idempotency-key is refused. A retryable failure therefore exits 75 from a query and 69 from a command.
  • Signals. A signal stops the batch: the line in flight gets --grace as a single call does, and no line starts after it. When lines remained, the batch exits 130 or 143.
  • The batch as a whole. A refusal before any line runs (a conflicting option, an unreadable file, a runtime that does not start) is one error object without line.

items.title: Output
items.text:
After the declaration loads, call writes exactly one JSON document to stdout, followed by a newline. For the duration of the call, file descriptor 1 points at stderr, so whatever the application logs or prints lands there.

The result is encoded with the operation's declared output type. An operation that returns nothing writes null.

The error object is the masked error envelope: a server-side error carries the generic detail, and a denial about a resource type a non-disclosing posture covers reads as not found.

{"error": {"code": "core.authentication", "kind": "authentication", "detail": "Invalid API key",
           "retryable": false, "context": {}},
 "execution_id": "…", "correlation_id": "…"}

execution_id and correlation_id are always present, whatever failed: they are minted before the first step that can fail.

An interrupt before any commit started writes the one kind the CLI adds: "code": "interrupted", "kind": "interrupted", a detail naming the signal, and "retryable": false, since an operation may have side effects outside its transaction.

Two failures write nothing to stdout:

When Output Exit Parsing the arguments Click's usage text on stderr 2 Loading the declaration: no --app, an import error, a declaration that refuses itself, an object that is not an OpsApp a message, or the traceback without locals, on stderr 2 when none is named, else 78

items.title: Exit codes
items.text:
The code is derived from the error envelope's kind, after the denial posture applies. Retryability is read from the kind's egress policy first.

Exit Meaning From 0 success 1 internal error internal, including commit_ambiguous; any unhandled exception 2 usage a parse error; an unknown or unexposed operation; an input or option the operation cannot take 3 not found not_found, including a collapsed denial 4 rejected validation, domain, precondition, conflict 5 denied authentication, authorization 6 timed out timeout 69 temporary failure; a write may have landed a retryable kind, from a command called without an idempotency key 75 temporary failure; safe to retry as is a retryable kind, from a query or from a command called with an idempotency key 78 configuration configuration; the declaration or the runtime refused before the operation ran, a runtime that is not SERVERLESS included 130 / 143 interrupted SIGINT / SIGTERM, cancelled before any commit started

69, 75 and 78 are EX_UNAVAILABLE, EX_TEMPFAIL and EX_CONFIG from sysexits.h. The retryable kinds are concurrency, throttled, infrastructure and unavailable.

items.title: Error codes the CLI adds
items.text: Code Kind Exit Raised when cli_unknown_operation validation 2 the operation is unknown, or not exposed cli_input_not_accepted validation 2 --input, typed flags or --batch given to an operation that takes none cli_option_conflict validation 2 typed flags given with --input; --batch given with --input, typed flags, --idempotency-key or --pretty cli_flags_unsupported validation 2 typed flags given to an operation whose input takes none; the detail says why cli_malformed_flags validation 2 the typed flags do not parse: an unknown flag, a missing value or one spelled like a flag, a value to a switch, a field given twice, or an argument that is not a flag cli_input_unreadable validation 2 the @PATH file of --input or --batch cannot be read cli_malformed_input validation 2 the input, or a batch line, is not JSON, or not an object cli_inline_secret validation 2 the input declares a secret and was given inline or as typed flags cli_idempotency_unsupported validation 2 --idempotency-key on an operation that does not support one cli_tenant_unverifiable validation 2 --tenant with an anonymous or static identity tenant_request_unverifiable precondition 2 --tenant that neither a resolver nor the key's own tenant can validate cli_api_key_file_unused validation 2 --api-key-file without an API-key identity cli_api_key_unreadable validation 2 the --api-key-file file cannot be read cli_invalid_input validation 4 the input does not validate, or names an unknown key cli_api_key_missing authentication 5 the key's environment variable is unset or blank, and no file is given cli_runtime_not_serverless configuration 78 the runtime factory returned a runtime that is not SERVERLESS cli_unverified_identity_unacknowledged configuration — a StaticIdentity built without acknowledge_unverified_identity=True; raised while the module imports

items.title: Environment
items.text: Variable Read by Default FORZE_OPS_APP --app none FORZE_API_KEY ApiKeyIdentity(env=…) the variable an API-key identity reads

items.title: Outbox table schema
items.text: The outbox table is application-owned: you create and migrate it. This is the schema the relay claims from and the columns it reads. The wiring that stages and relays events is in the Transactional outbox recipe.

items.title: Postgres
items.text:
For Postgres (PostgresOutboxConfig(relation=("app", "outbox"))):

CREATE TABLE app.outbox (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    outbox_route TEXT NOT NULL,
    event_id UUID NOT NULL,
    event_type TEXT NOT NULL,
    tenant_id UUID,
    execution_id UUID,
    correlation_id UUID,
    causation_id UUID,
    occurred_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    payload JSONB NOT NULL,
    status TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    published_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
    processing_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
    last_error TEXT,
    attempts INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    available_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
    ordering_key TEXT,
    UNIQUE (outbox_route, event_id)
);

-- covers the claim predicate (route + pending + ripe, oldest first)
CREATE INDEX outbox_claim_idx
    ON app.outbox (outbox_route, status, available_at, created_at);

attempts is the durable retry counter; available_at schedules the next retry (NULL = claimable now); ordering_key is the optional delivery partition key (NULL = no partitioning, key falls back to the event id). Existing tables migrate with:

ALTER TABLE app.outbox
    ADD COLUMN attempts INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    ADD COLUMN available_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
    ADD COLUMN ordering_key TEXT;

items.title: Trace propagation (optional column)
items.text:
PostgresOutboxConfig(propagate_trace=True) persists each event's W3C traceparent so the relay forwards it as the traceparent header and the consume side links its span to the publish span. Opt in after adding the nullable column (legacy / NULL rows simply carry no parent); independent of hlc_ordering:

ALTER TABLE app.outbox ADD COLUMN traceparent TEXT;

items.title: Causal ordering (Hybrid Logical Clock)
items.text:
By default claims are ordered by created_at — assigned per flush batch, so rows staged together share a timestamp and tie arbitrarily, and clocks on different replicas can disagree. Set PostgresOutboxConfig(hlc_ordering=True) to claim in causal order instead: every event carries a Hybrid Logical Clock stamp that stays close to wall time yet always exceeds any timestamp the process has observed (including one merged from a consumed event's forze_hlc header), so a reaction sorts after its cause across replicas, and the time-ordered id breaks any remaining tie. Add the column first, then opt in (legacy NULL-hlc rows fall back to created_at):

ALTER TABLE app.outbox ADD COLUMN hlc BIGINT;

-- claim order becomes (hlc NULLS LAST, created_at, id); index to match
CREATE INDEX outbox_claim_hlc_idx
    ON app.outbox (outbox_route, status, available_at, hlc, created_at, id);

items.title: Restart monotonicity (clock high-water mark)
items.text:
The hlc column keeps causal order within a run, but a runtime's clock lives in memory: a restart resets it to (0, 0), after which it can re-issue a stamp at or below one it already relayed whenever wall time had regressed or a peer merge had carried the clock ahead. Persist the clock's high-water mark so a restart resumes above its prior emissions. The table is optional and node-global — one clock per runtime, spanning every tenant, so it is not tenant-partitioned:

CREATE TABLE app.hlc_checkpoint (
    node_key TEXT   NOT NULL,
    hlc      BIGINT NOT NULL,   -- packed HlcTimestamp: physical_ms << 16 | logical
    PRIMARY KEY (node_key)
);

Wire it with PostgresDepsModule(hlc_checkpoint=PostgresHlcCheckpointConfig(relation=("app", "hlc_checkpoint"))) and add hlc_checkpoint_recovery_lifecycle_step() to the runtime's lifecycle. For an outbox route that flushes inside a transaction (OutboxSpec(require_transaction=True)), the flush then advances the mark (the max HLC among the rows it stamps) inside that transaction — so a committed stamp is never durable without a mark covering it, and a rolled-back flush never advances it — while the lifecycle step loads the mark at startup and resumes the clock. A route that flushes standalone keeps resuming from (0, 0): its mark could not advance atomically with its rows, so no checkpoint is wired for it. Unwired entirely, every route resumes from (0, 0) as before. A single shared node_key (the default) records one deployment-wide mark; distinct per-replica keys avoid write contention on one row, and recovery reads the max across all keys either way.

items.title: Consume storage
items.text:
PostgresOutboxConfig(storage="consume") keeps only the rows still to relay. Each relay pass runs in one transaction, and the table holds pending and failed rows only:

Step retain (default) consume claim UPDATE to processing SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED: a row lock, no write published UPDATE to published DELETE retried UPDATE attempts, available_at, back to pending the same, the row stays pending parked UPDATE to failed the same

A row that publishes first time is written twice, inserted and deleted, and never updated, so nothing published is left for a retention job to prune. Postgres only: Mongo keeps retain.

  • The indexes stay three: the primary key, UNIQUE (outbox_route, event_id), which staging deduplicates on, and the claim index. A retry changes available_at, which the claim index above includes, so a retry is not a HOT update under it. Retries are rare, and a row that publishes first time never updates.
  • The dedup window narrows. Staging an event id again is deduplicated only while its row is still in the table, pending or parked as failed. Once the row is relayed and deleted, the same event id publishes again.
  • A failed pass republishes its batch. When a mark statement fails, a statement times out or the session is cut off, the whole pass rolls back. Every row it claimed is pending again, including the ones it already published: up to max_claim_rows (100) duplicates, where retain republishes at most one mark chunk of 32. Lower max_claim_rows for a smaller window.
  • A failing route backs off on its own. The background relay step ends the failed pass and skips that route until it has waited: one interval after the first failure, doubling with each consecutive one up to the larger of retry_max_backoff and interval, and a pass that commits resets it. On a step with tenants=, only the failing tenant waits; the others keep the step's cadence. A wake does not cut the wait short.
  • A pass is bounded. It stops publishing at pass_deadline (default 5 s) and commits what it did; the rows it did not reach stay pending, untouched. A publish still running at the deadline is cancelled and counted as a failed attempt, though it may already have reached the broker, so that event can arrive twice. A destination that swallows the cancellation and returns normally counts as published instead: it reached the broker, and counting it failed would publish it again. Each statement in the pass, the reclaim and the claim included, and each lock wait, is limited to pass_statement_timeout (default 1 s): on a large table without the claim index above, the claim times out and every pass fails. The server cuts the session off once it sits idle in the pass for longer than the two durations together. The pass sets these for its own transaction only, and only when it opens that transaction. A stricter limit the session already has, from the role or the connection's options, stays in force.
  • A shutdown drain keeps time to commit. It stops publishing a fifth of the budget it has left before its end, so its last pass commits instead of being cut and rolled back. That fifth has to cover the pass's closing statements, each allowed up to pass_statement_timeout, so keep shutdown_drain_timeout at least five times pass_statement_timeout; the defaults, 5 s and 1 s, just meet it. A closing statement that waits on a lock past the drain's end is cut with it, and that pass rolls back.
  • A pass inside your transaction sets nothing. Run a relay in a transaction of your own, for example to check a lease before committing, and the pass becomes a savepoint in it: your transaction's timeouts apply, and its rollback returns every row.
  • Staging can wait for a pass. Staging an event id whose row a pass has deleted but not yet committed waits for that pass to end.
  • A destination on the same Postgres client joins the pass. Its statements run in the pass's transaction, under pass_statement_timeout, and an SQL error there fails the whole pass.
  • A retry policy on the outbox route cannot save a pass. A statement that fails aborts the pass's transaction, so every retry of it fails too; the pass fails and the step backs off.
  • Behind pgbouncer, use session or transaction pooling. The timeouts are set with set_config(..., true), which ends with the transaction, so transaction pooling is safe. Statement pooling cannot hold a transaction across statements, so it cannot run a pass.

processing_at and published_at are never written. To move a live table over:

  1. Deploy the relays with storage="consume", keeping reclaim_stale_after set. Their claims take pending rows, and reclaim still returns the processing rows retain left behind for the next pass to relay.
  2. Leave the published rows to your existing retention job.
  3. Once no processing row is left, set reclaim_stale_after=None. Once the retention job has removed every published row, retire it. Only then drop the two columns, and any index that exists only for them:
ALTER TABLE app.outbox DROP COLUMN processing_at, DROP COLUMN published_at;

Reclaim reads processing_at, so dropping it while reclaim is on fails every pass, and the retention job reads published_at. Relays in both modes on one route stay at-least-once: a row a retain relay claimed is processing, which a consume claim never matches, until it is marked or reclaimed.

items.title: Delivery log
items.text:
With published rows deleted, the outbox no longer says what went out. delivery_log names a table the store appends each published row to, in the statement that deletes it:

PostgresOutboxConfig(
    relation=("app", "outbox"),
    storage="consume",
    delivery_log=("app", "outbox_delivered"),
)

It takes what relation takes, a (schema, table) pair or a per-tenant resolver, and resolves for the same tenant, at the claim, so a resolver that fails does so before the pass publishes anything. A single log table holds every tenant's records, so a per-tenant outbox beside one is only as isolated as the log's tenant_id filtering: a module that declares required_tenant_isolation="namespace" refuses it, and needs a per-tenant resolver for the log too. storage="retain" refuses the log.

The table is yours: forze only inserts into it, and never creates, drops or prunes its partitions. Dropping a day's partition is its whole retention. Nothing updates or deletes a committed row; the only dead rows are the inserts of passes that rolled back after a mark, which vacuum clears as usual. Partition it by day on published_at:

CREATE TABLE app.outbox_delivered (
    id UUID NOT NULL,              -- the outbox row's id
    outbox_route TEXT NOT NULL,
    event_id UUID NOT NULL,
    tenant_id UUID,
    published_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
) PARTITION BY RANGE (published_at);

-- no unique key: an event staged again after delivery is delivered again
CREATE INDEX outbox_delivered_event_idx ON app.outbox_delivered (event_id);

-- the net for a day nobody added
CREATE TABLE app.outbox_delivered_default PARTITION OF app.outbox_delivered DEFAULT;

-- a partition per day, added days ahead: built apart, then attached
CREATE TABLE app.outbox_delivered_20261018 (LIKE app.outbox_delivered);
ALTER TABLE app.outbox_delivered ATTACH PARTITION app.outbox_delivered_20261018
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-10-18 00:00+00') TO ('2026-10-19 00:00+00');
