A lifecycle step registers its phase at startup, on the ctx its hook receives:

from datetime import timedelta

from forze.application.execution import ExecutionContext


async def startup(ctx: ExecutionContext) -> None:
    async def hand_over(allowed: timedelta) -> None:
        ...  # hand the routes back, within `allowed`

    ctx.drain_phases.register(
        "hand-over",
        hand_over,
        order=10,
        max_duration=timedelta(seconds=5),
    )

Phases run in ascending order and share one budget:

  • Each phase may take min(max_duration, budget left), and is called with that figure so it can shrink its own window to fit.
  • A phase without max_duration may take everything that is left. Give the early phases a cap, or one slow phase leaves the later ones nothing.
  • A phase that overruns is cancelled. One that ignores the cancellation is abandoned a second later. A phase left less than 100 ms is skipped, and a phase that fails does not stop the next. Each of these is logged.

So drain() returns within announce_delay + budget, plus a second when a phase ignores its cancellation.

Phases are not the background loops registered in ctx.drainables — relays, consumers, pollers. Those stop after the gate has closed, between units of work. A phase runs before that, while the replica still serves, which is the point of it.

Two phases ship with forze, both closing realtime connections spread over a window so their clients reconnect elsewhere a few at a time: connection_drain_lifecycle_step for Socket.IO, and realtime_sse_drain_lifecycle_step for the FastAPI SSE and WebSocket tails. spread_drain_lifecycle_step in forze.application.execution.background is the same phase for connections of your own.

items.title: What a step can read
items.text:
A step cannot hold the runtime that runs it: the runtime is built around its lifecycle plan, so it does not exist yet when its steps are built. A step reads the scope's state from the ctx its hooks receive instead:

Attribute True once ctx.lifecycle.started every lifecycle startup hook has returned ctx.lifecycle.announced a drain was announced — readiness is withdrawn ctx.drain_gate.draining the gate closed — new operations are refused

items.title: Fit the budget to the grace period
items.text:
The orchestrator kills the process when its grace period runs out — on Kubernetes, terminationGracePeriodSeconds, 30 seconds by default. The worst case of an orderly exit has to fit inside it:

announce_delay
+ drain budget                  (drain_budget when shutdown() drains)
+ 1 s                           (a phase that ignores its cancellation)
+ the HTTP graceful timeout     (uvicorn's timeout_graceful_shutdown)
+ drain_timeout                 (in-flight operations)
+ shutdown_step_timeout × 3     (cancelling what drain_timeout left running,
                                 stopping background loops, closing background work)
+ shutdown_step_timeout × steps (lifecycle shutdown, one per step)

With every default and no HTTP server that is already 51 seconds before the first lifecycle step: 10 for the drain, 1, 10 for drain_timeout and 3 × 10. Most exits take a fraction of it, but the grace period has to cover the one that does not. A budget that does not fit gets the process killed in the middle of a phase or of teardown — exactly the exit this ordering exists to avoid. Shrink the timeouts, raise the grace period, or both, with headroom. serve_uvicorn logs this sum, figure by figure, when the server starts, and so does runtime_lifespan with a drain_budget, in each worker.

items.title: Declare the fleet posture
items.text:
Some startup work is safe in one process and a stampede in twenty — N replicas all running CREATE INDEX or a data migration at the same moment. Declaring the posture makes that a composition-time error instead of a 3 a.m. incident:

from forze.application.execution import DeploymentProfile

runtime = build_runtime(..., deployment=DeploymentProfile.FLEET)

Under FLEET, building the runtime fails for any lifecycle step marked mutates_shared_state=True that is not also singleton_guarded. The markers are declared by the step author — mutation can't be detected structurally, so the validation is honest-by-declaration: mark the steps that touch shared backends, and the profile enforces that each one is guarded.

items.title: Singleton lifecycle steps
items.text:
The guard itself ships in forze_kits: wrap a step in a distributed lock so one replica runs it and the rest skip —

from forze.application.contracts.dlock import DistributedLockSpec
from forze_kits.lifecycle import singleton_lifecycle_step

step = singleton_lifecycle_step(
    ensure_indexes_step,
    spec=DistributedLockSpec(name="ensure-indexes"),  # resolved from the scope
    owner=instance_id,
)

You pass the lock spec, not a live port: the guard resolves the command port from the execution context (ctx.dlock.command(spec)) at startup, so it slots into a lifecycle plan that's assembled before any scope exists.

Startup runs with no tenant bound, so the lock's route must be tenant-global: not tenant_aware, and not on a client routed per tenant that has no tenant to route by. Either one fails startup with a configuration error coded tenant_global_required, here and in leadership_lifecycle_step below. Under a declared tenant-isolation floor, mark the route RedisDistributedLockConfig(tenant_global=True) so the floor leaves it out.

The first replica to acquire the lock runs the startup and releases it; replicas that find the lock held skip — the holder is doing the work. Shutdown later runs only on the replica whose startup actually executed. The step must be idempotent ("ensure"-style): a replica that starts after the holder released will acquire and run it again. Size the lock's TTL to comfortably exceed the step's duration — no heartbeat extends it here.

Migrations are deploy steps

singleton_lifecycle_step is for ensure-style work: indexes, queue declarations, seed data. One-shot work like a schema migration wants run-exactly-once semantics, which a skip-if-held lock does not give — run it as a deploy step in your pipeline, not as a runtime step.

items.title: Run one replica's worth of work
items.text:
The singleton guard holds its lock only while startup runs, so it cannot keep one replica doing something for the life of the process. A replica that starts later finds the lock free and starts the work again, and when the replica that started it dies, nobody takes over. For work that must run on one replica at a time — a publisher, a single sequencer, a coordinator — use leadership_lifecycle_step. Every replica campaigns for a renewing lease, and the one that holds it runs your body until the lease is gone.

Work that tolerates running everywhere needs neither. The framework's outbox relay, durable recovery and scheduler pollers and realtime sweeps are safe on every replica, so run them unwrapped.

from forze.application.contracts.dlock import DistributedLockSpec
from forze_kits.lifecycle import LeadershipSpec, leadership_lifecycle_step

publisher = LeadershipSpec(
    lock=DistributedLockSpec(name="lobby-publisher", requires_fencing_token=True),
    key="lobby-publisher",
)


async def claim(ctx, term):
    # ... SET fence = :token WHERE fence < :token — no row: another holder has this token
    return await claim_lobby_fence(ctx, term.token)


async def publish(ctx, term):
    while term.live():  # one unit at a time, so the body stops between units
        # ... WHERE fence <= :token — no row: a newer holder has written, so stop
        if not await publish_lobby_snapshot(ctx, fence=term.token):
            return


step = leadership_lifecycle_step(publisher, owner=instance_id, lead=publish, claim=claim)

The step's startup only starts the campaign, on every replica, so it is marked requires_long_running and nothing else: FLEET accepts it without a singleton guard, and SERVERLESS refuses it.

items.title: How a term ends
items.text:
The leader renews the lease every renew_every (a third of the lock's TTL by default) and tells the body that its term is ending through term.ended, early enough that the body's yield_grace — and, if it overruns, the release_timeout it gets to unwind once cancelled — finishes before the lease could lapse. Both deadlines are measured from when the latest successful renewal was sent, so a slow answer shortens the term rather than lengthening it. The spec refuses timings that do not fit: renew_every + yield_grace + release_timeout + margin must be shorter than the TTL, and release_timeout no longer than yield_grace.

term.reason When What happens to the body lost a renewal answers that the lease is gone cancelled at once expiring renewals failed until yield_grace before the lease could lapse; the body's own term.live() check can see it first, as on resuming after a pause cancelled release_timeout before the lease could lapse stopped the process is shutting down cancelled after yield_grace, or earlier if renewals are failing yielded another replica asked for the unit (see below) as for stopped returned / raised the body ended on its own — unclaimed the claim hook found its token already claimed lead never runs

The lease is released only once the body is done, and the next replica then leads within one campaign_every. A release that fails or overruns release_timeout leaves the lease to lapse at its TTL instead, and the next replica leads within one campaign_every after that. A body that does not finish within release_timeout of being cancelled keeps the lease until its TTL runs out, so no successor starts before then; one that starts after it may run beside that body, which is what fencing is for. Write the body to stop at unit boundaries: cancellation at an arbitrary await is what the grace exists to avoid.

items.title: What fencing is for
items.text:
A responsive leader whose body finishes within release_timeout of being cancelled runs only while it holds the lease. A body that checks term.live() between units also stops at its first check after a paused process or a blocked event loop resumes past the term's soft deadline: the check compares that deadline with the clock, so it refuses before the step's own timer has run. Nothing in the lease can stop the rest: the unit a pause interrupted, a body that ignores its term or its cancellation, or a lock backend that lost its data while the leader cannot yet know. Fencing covers those. Set requires_fencing_token on the lock, pass term.token with every write the body makes, and have the store refuse a token lower than the highest it has seen.

A token can repeat after the lock backend loses its data, so the first write of a term claims the token and later writes accept an equal one:

-- claim, before the body's first write: the stored fence must be strictly lower
UPDATE digests SET fence = :token WHERE name = :name AND fence < :token;
-- every later write of the term
UPDATE digests SET body = :body, fence = :token WHERE name = :name AND fence <= :token;

Pass the claim as claim=; the step runs it before lead, and a claim that matches no row ends the term as unclaimed and campaigns again. A later write that matches no row means a newer holder has written: end the term by returning from lead.

After the lock backend loses its data, its fencing counter starts again from one while the store keeps the highest fence it saw. Every term's claim is then refused, and the fleet climbs one token per campaign interval until the counter passes the store's fence — leadership stalls for as many campaigns as the store's fence is high. fence_floor is the fix: give the step a read of the store's highest fence, and set requires_fence_advance on the lock spec.

publisher = LeadershipSpec(
    lock=DistributedLockSpec(name="lobby-publisher", requires_fence_advance=True),
    key="lobby-publisher",
)


async def lobby_fence(ctx):
    return await read_lobby_fence(ctx)  # SELECT fence FROM lobby WHERE id = 1


step = leadership_lifecycle_step(
    publisher, owner=instance_id, lead=publish, claim=claim, fence_floor=lobby_fence
)

A replica that finds the lease free reads the floor and moves the lock's counter past it before acquiring, so the first term after a loss draws a token above the store's fence and its claim goes through at once. With the counter intact the advance changes nothing. A lock backend that cannot advance its counter fails the step at startup. A floor that cannot be read in time is skipped and the replica acquires anyway: a token below the store's fence is refused by the claim, and the next campaign reads the floor again. A floor the lock can never advance past, such as None, stops the campaign for good. The Redis page covers the capability itself. The one-replica publisher recipe runs the whole pattern.

items.title: The clock behind margin
items.text: Redis keeps a lease's expiry on its own clock. If that clock steps forward — an NTP correction, a failover to a replica whose clock runs ahead — the lease ends early, while the leader still counts on its own monotonic clock. margin (one second by default) is the allowance for that: the leader treats its lease as gone margin before the TTL. Size it for your deployment's clock discipline, and keep the TTL at least ten times the backend's renewal latency, or terms flap.

items.title: Handoff on request
items.text: With handoff="on_request", a replica whose prefer(ctx) returns true asks for the unit by holding a second lock, {key}:want (so no lease key may end in :want), and renewing it every campaign interval. The holder yields at its next renewal, unless it prefers the unit itself or the asker has not renewed its request within two campaign intervals — a dead asker's want-lock outlives it by a TTL, and yielding to it would only leave the unit unled. Other replicas stand aside while someone asks, until they have seen the lease free for three campaign intervals, so a fleet whose asker cannot take the lease is unled for about four at most. An asker gives the want-lock up after three failed acquires in a row, or at once when one is not answered in time, and does not ask again for one TTL, so holders yield to an asker that cannot take the unit at most once a TTL. A failing prefer or want-lock read does not count: that replica just campaigns without handoff. A replica that may_campaign refuses never asks.

items.title: Operating it
items.text:
• Stopping. The step stops within yield_grace + 3 × release_timeout plus a second: the grace, then the body's unwind, the release, and a want-lock's or a late acquire's release. Keep that under the runtime's shutdown_step_timeout (ten seconds by default), or the loop is cancelled before it releases and the next leader waits out the TTL.
  • Campaign calls. may_campaign, prefer, fence_floor and the campaign's reads of the lock are each cut off after campaign_every. Handoff and the fence floor are best-effort: when prefer, the want-lock or the floor fails or overruns, the replica campaigns as if they were off — acquiring without the advance at worst draws a token the claim refuses. may_campaign is the app's own gate, so a failure there sits that campaign out. A configuration error from any of them stops campaigning for good, as below. An acquire is never cancelled: one that lands after the step stopped waiting, or whose answer is lost after it landed, is released.
  • A body that raises is released and restarted after the supervisor's backoff. A configuration error, from the body or from any campaign call, stops campaigning for good, with a critical log, while the process stays up — wiring does not fix itself by retrying. So do the two fencing refusals no retry can clear: a counter at its ceiling (dlock.fence_exhausted) and a fence_floor the lock cannot advance past (dlock.fence_out_of_range, such as None for a store with no row yet).
  • Metrics. instrument_leadership() exports forze.leadership.held and forze.leadership.terms_ended; see the metric catalog. A sustained rate of lost or expiring means the lock backend is slow or unreachable from the leader.

items.title: What's shared, what's per-process
items.text:
Most coordination state already lives in your backends (idempotency records, distributed locks, the outbox). The resilience layer's state is process-local by default, and each piece has a deliberate fleet answer:

State Default In a fleet Circuit breaker per-process share via redis_circuit_breaker_store — one replica's open circuit protects them all Rate limits per-process (fleet rate = permits × replicas) share via redis_rate_limit_store — the declared rate becomes the fleet's rate Bulkheads per-process stays local by design — fleet capacity is max_concurrency × replicas, and adaptive bulkheads converge across uncoordinated replicas

Wiring for the shared stores is on the resilience page. The framework's periodic loops — the outbox relay tick, consumer crash-restart backoff — are jittered out of the box, so N replicas don't synchronize into a thundering herd against the same claim query.

Knowing a fleet drains cleanly — or spots one thundering against a claim query — is something you confirm by watching it; that's Observability.

items.title: Concurrency & isolation
items.text: A concurrency test that relies on real timing is flaky: the race you want to provoke fires once in a hundred runs, never in CI, and never the same way twice. The fix is to stop racing and start scheduling — drive the concurrent transactions through an exact interleaving you choose, so the outcome is the same every run. forze.testing ships the driver for that, and it's the basis for verifying an adapter is as honest as it claims.

items.title: Force an interleaving
items.text:
Write each participant as a coroutine that calls await gate.checkpoint() at every point where a context switch is allowed. The Conductor's schedule is the global step order — list a participant once per checkpoint it should pass — and only one participant ever runs at a time:

from forze.testing import Conductor, Gate

async def worker(gate: Gate, name: str):
    log.append(f"{name}:start")    # before the first checkpoint — setup
    await gate.checkpoint()
    log.append(f"{name}:work")
    await gate.checkpoint()
    log.append(f"{name}:commit")   # after the last checkpoint — runs to completion

await Conductor(schedule=("A", "A", "B", "B")).run({
    "A": lambda g: worker(g, "A"),
    "B": lambda g: worker(g, "B"),
})

The schedule is the interleaving: ("A","A","B","B") runs A to completion then B; ("A","B","A","B") steps them in lock-step. Same code, different schedule, deterministic outcome each time — the determinism a real race can't give. It's a general primitive (just asyncio), independent of the rest of the framework.

items.title: Verify an adapter's isolation
items.text:
The mock and a real database both claim SNAPSHOT / SERIALIZABLE, and your app's correctness rests on them agreeing. A forced interleaving lets you check it — drive a textbook anomaly and assert the adapter behaves as its declared level requires. Write skew is the canonical one: two transactions each read the same rows, decide it's safe to drop one, and write a different row, so optimistic-concurrency checks never conflict — only true serializable catches it.

from forze.application.contracts.transaction import IsolationLevel

async def session(gate: Gate, ctx, mine):
    async with ctx.tx_ctx.scope("mock", isolation=IsolationLevel.SERIALIZABLE):
        d1 = await ctx.document.query(SPEC).get(id1)
        d2 = await ctx.document.query(SPEC).get(id2)
        await gate.checkpoint()                       # both read before either writes
        if d1.on_call and d2.on_call:
            await ctx.document.command(SPEC).update(mine, ..., OffCall())
        await gate.checkpoint()
    # commit on scope exit — serializable raises on the read-write conflict

Two concurrent transactions are two coroutines, each with its own context over one shared MockState; the schedule forces both reads before either write, then one commit then the other. At SNAPSHOT both commit (write skew permitted) and the invariant breaks; at SERIALIZABLE one aborts and it holds. Run the same scenario against a real adapter (via testcontainers) and assert it reaches the same verdict, and you've turned "trust the mock" into "verified the mock."

This is one anomaly at one pair of levels, driven by hand. For exhaustive, seed-driven exploration of concurrency, faults, and crashes across your whole app — with a minimized, replayable counterexample when something breaks — reach past this to Deterministic simulation.

items.title: Testing
items.text: Forze's port-based architecture makes testing straightforward: handlers see only ports, so tests swap real adapters for in-memory fakes. No Docker, no database setup, no external services.

items.title: Unit testing with MockDepsModule
items.text:
MockDepsModule provides in-memory adapters for every contract. To run a handler against it, build a context with context_from_modules (shipped in forze.testing) — no runtime, no transport, just the context your ports resolve from:

from forze.testing import context_from_modules
from forze_mock import MockDepsModule

async def test_create_user():
    ctx = context_from_modules(MockDepsModule())

    user = await ctx.document.command(user_spec).create(CreateUser(name="Ada"))

    assert user.name == "Ada"
    assert user.id is not None

Every port — documents, search, cache, queues, streams, storage — works against shared in-memory state. Write a user in one test, query it in the same test, and the data is there. (command(...) is the write side — create / update; query(...) is the read side — get / find.)

A command(...) port is handed out guarded, so a write inside a read-only operation is refused wherever the port came from. isinstance and attribute assignment on the guard itself do not work. To ask whether it implements a protocol, use implements(port, SomeAware) from forze.application.contracts.deps, which also sees through port spans and port logging, as in production. To patch one of its methods, reach the real one with forze.testing.unguarded(port).

One thing to know before you rely on that: the mock stores what was written and reads it back through the read model, so an aggregate whose read model requires a field no write produces cannot round-trip through it. That is the ordinary shape of a read model assembled by a SQL view — a joined reference, an aggregate total, a computed flag.

Declare those fields on the spec (derived_read_fields={"supplier": None}) and supply their values with the seed:

SpecSeed(
    spec=ORDERS,  # needs a `write` spec: seeding goes through its create command
    count=20,
    derived={"supplier": {"id": ..., "rev": 1, "name": "Acme", "number_id": 7}},
)

The values are fixture data — nothing recomputes them when a source row changes, because the mock does not implement the view. What the test then exercises is your handler around the read, which is what a unit test is for; the derivation itself is the database's, and belongs in an integration test against the real view. A required field declared derived and left unsupplied is refused by name, rather than surfacing as a pydantic error about a missing key.

A seed cannot reach a row your code creates, though — and under deterministic simulation the workload creates every row there is. Register what the relation would have produced instead, and the mock consults it per row:

MockDepsModule(
    derived_values=MockDerivedRegistry().on(
        "orders",
        lambda row: {"supplier": {"id": row["supplier_id"], "rev": 1, "name": "Acme"}},
    ),
)

Keep it a function of the row: a source that reads a clock or a counter makes two runs of one seed disagree, and a simulation you cannot replay is one you cannot minimize. A seeded or persisted value still wins, so a test that wrote a specific row keeps it. Registering nothing keeps the refusal above, which is the posture that makes a missing value discoverable.

A view that aggregates child rows, such as released_quantity = SUM(child.quantity) WHERE child.parent_id = id, needs the other rows as well. A source with two required positional parameters receives, as its second argument, the view an analytics resolver gets:

MockDepsModule(
    derived_values=MockDerivedRegistry().on(
        "batches",
        lambda row, view: {
            "released_quantity": sum(
                r["quantity"] for r in view.rows(RELEASES) if r["batch_id"] == row["id"]
            ),
        },
    ),
)

view.rows(spec) returns stored rows as the reading transaction sees them, so a handler that writes a child and then reads the parent in the same transaction counts that child, as the real view does. The rows are stored rows, so a child's own derived fields are not on them: aggregate over stored fields, as an analytics resolver does. A rolled-back child drops out again. A tenant-aware child route is read in the bound tenant's partition, as for a resolver. A tenant-aware parent route also narrows the rows to the bound tenant, leaving out rows another tenant owns or no tenant owns. So children kept on a route that is not tenant-aware, which carry no tenant_id, are never counted for a tenant-aware parent, even where the real view would count them. The source runs on every read of every row, so the value follows the children without anything recomputing it. That is fine for fixtures; on a large seed, pin the field instead.

on() reads the source's signature once. A source that accepts one positional argument stays row-only, as before, even if it could also take two (def f(row, scale=2), *args). A signature that accepts neither (row) nor (row, view) is refused with mock.derived.source_shape.

Where the value is one row reached by one key — a joined column, or an expanded reference like warehouse: {id, name} — declare the join instead (DerivedReadField(source=..., via=..., fields=("id", "name")), see reading data) and the mock resolves it with no callback at all.

items.title: Checking derived fields against the real view
items.text:
A declared join or a registered callback is the mock's copy of your view, and it can drift from the real one while every mock-backed test stays green. run_derived_fidelity checks one spec against a real backend: it loads one seed into both stores, reads the same ids through both, and compares only the derived fields:

from forze.testing import context_from_modules
from forze_dst.conformance import run_derived_fidelity
from forze_mock import MockDepsModule
from forze_mock.seeding import apply_seed


async def test_orders_match_the_view(postgres_ctx, plan) -> None:
    report = await run_derived_fidelity(
        spec=ORDERS,
        seed=lambda ctx: apply_seed(ctx, plan),  # one SeedPlan, loaded into both stores
        real=postgres_ctx,  # reads ORDERS from the view
        mock=context_from_modules(MockDepsModule()),  # plus derived_values=... for marked fields
    )

    assert report.agrees, report.render_markdown()
    assert all(tally.compared for tally in report.tallies), report.render_markdown()

Each disagreement is one DerivedMismatch for one field on one row, holding both values. A read that raises on one side is recorded as a ReadRefused value, so one bad row does not hide the rest. A value that JSON serialization refuses is recorded as Unserializable, which never agrees with anything. A derived field the read model excludes from serialization is refused up front, since it could only ever agree as None.

agrees means only that nothing mismatched. A field that is None on both sides, or a row both sides refused, agrees without testing the join. So also check the per-field tallies: each one counts the rows actually compared, the rows null_on_both and the rows refused_on_both, and render_markdown() prints them.

Keep the plan's instant pinned (the default), so both stores create the same ids. Leave SpecSeed.derived out of the plan: the real store has no column to write those values to, and the point is to test the join or callback your tests use, not a value you supplied. For a tenant-aware spec, pass tenant=TenantIdentity(...); it is bound on both contexts for the seed and the reads.

items.title: Analytics answered from current state
items.text:
By default the mock answers an analytics query from rows you seed into MockState.analytics_query_hits. Those rows never change. A handler that reads a query to decide what to do sees the same numbers after every write, so under simulation it never takes the branch the real numbers would send it down.

Register a resolver instead, and the mock computes the query on each call from the documents it holds:

from forze_mock import MockAnalyticsRegistry, MockDepsModule


def totals_by_customer(view, params):
    sums = defaultdict(int)
    for row in view.rows(ORDERS):
        sums[row["customer"]] += row["amount"]
    return [{"customer": c, "total": t} for c, t in sums.items() if t >= params.min_total]


MockDepsModule(
    analytics=MockAnalyticsRegistry().on(TOTALS, "by_customer", totals_by_customer),
)

view.rows(spec) returns a document spec's stored rows in storage form: the columns a SQL query over the table would see. You get the rows the calling transaction sees. Inside a transaction, its own uncommitted writes are included and a concurrent transaction's are not. Outside one, you get the committed rows. A field the document spec seals arrives encrypted, exactly as SQL sees the column. Analytics cannot decrypt it today, even if the analytics spec declares the field encrypted. The document codec binds the ciphertext to the document spec's name and the analytics codec to forze.field, so the read fails authentication. Keep sealed fields out of a resolver's rows.

On a tenant-aware analytics route, a call with no tenant bound is refused with tenant_required. Otherwise view.rows returns only rows whose tenant_id names the bound tenant, even when the document route keeps every tenant in one namespace. A tenant-aware document route narrows view.rows the way a document read does, whatever the analytics route declares: the bound tenant's partition, without rows another tenant owns or rows with no owner.

The resolver receives the call's validated params. Its rows then go through the same max_rows cap and read-model decoding as seeded rows. A query with no resolver keeps its seeded rows. on() refuses a query key the spec does not declare, and a second resolver for the same query.

A resolver is a second implementation of the query, and only a test keeps it in step with the SQL. forze_dst.conformance.compare_analytics_query is that test. It loads one seed into the mock and into the real engine, runs the query on both, and diffs the rows:

from forze_dst.conformance import compare_analytics_query
from forze_mock.seeding import apply_seed

comparison = await compare_analytics_query(
    TOTALS,
    "by_customer",
    MinTotal(min_total=10),
    mock=mock_ctx,
    real=postgres_ctx,
    seed=lambda ctx: apply_seed(ctx, plan),
)
assert comparison.agrees, comparison.render()

Rows are compared as a multiset after the read model, so a Decimal from the engine and an int from the resolver agree when the read model types the field. In an untyped field, 1 and 1.0 agree and true never matches 1, in either mode. Pass ordered=True only for a query with an ORDER BY. render() prints one line for each row that only one side returned, or, in ordered mode, for each position that differs. Two empty answers do not agree: a seed that produced no rows the query selects would pass any resolver. Pass allow_empty=True only for a query whose correct answer is empty. To use the same query as a simulation invariant, see query_invariant.

items.title: Transaction rollback in tests
items.text:
Mock transactions are faithful by default: a write inside a transaction that rolls back is undone, so a "forgot to run it in the same transaction" bug fails in your unit test exactly as it would in production. No flag needed.

  • Rolls back — documents, outbox rows, inbox marks, and document-backed identity stores. A handler that stages an outbox event and then fails leaves no rows behind.
  • Survives rollback — queues, streams, storage blobs, caches, counters, idempotency keys, locks, search and analytics state (these aren't transactional in production either).

The default journal mode is atomic without serializing, so concurrent transactions still interleave. Two modes are opt-in — MockDepsModule(transactions="strict") (a serializing global-snapshot manager) and transactions="none" (the legacy no-op). See Transactions for the full picture, and Deterministic simulation for exploring concurrency and isolation under the faithful default.

items.title: Testing with identity context
items.text: A handler reads ctx.authn / ctx.tenancy from the identity plane, resolved during operation execution — not from a value you set by hand. To test such a handler, wire the mock's identity stubs and drive the authn flow (seed an account, authenticate) rather than constructing an identity directly. See Identity and the authn, authz & tenancy recipe for the wiring.

items.title: What the mock can't model
items.text:
The mock is faithful at the port boundary, but logic that lives below a port is not in it. If your app leans on database triggers, generated columns, CHECK constraints, or LISTEN/NOTIFY — efficient, native, but invisible to the app — a mock-based test can't run it, and an invariant a trigger maintains will even false-pass or false-fail because the mock writes the rows but never fires the trigger. That logic belongs in an integration test against the real database (below). Keeping invariant logic above the port is what keeps it portable across adapters and testable without one. A foreign key's ON DELETE (cascade, restrict, set null) is the exception once the child spec declares it as a Reference: the mock applies it on kill, and Postgres startup checks the key exists.

The mock search stands in for both an external index and an in-place search over a document table, so its query side accepts a spec's sealed_by; only its write side (search command and management) refuses it, as Meilisearch does. A sealed_by that doesn't match how the rows were written — by a document port, or by a search upsert — therefore fails at read time with core.crypto.aead_auth_failed, not at wiring.

items.title: Integration testing with testcontainers
items.text:
For tests that need real infrastructure — or to exercise database-level logic the mock can't model — use testcontainers to spin up ephemeral databases:

import pytest
from testcontainers.postgres import PostgresContainer
from forze.application.execution import build_runtime
from forze_postgres import PostgresClient, PostgresDepsModule, PostgresLifecycleModule

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def postgres_dsn():
    with PostgresContainer("postgres:18", driver=None) as pg:
        yield pg.get_connection_url()

async def test_postgres_integration(postgres_dsn):
    client = PostgresClient()
    runtime = build_runtime(
        PostgresDepsModule(client=client, rw_documents={"users": users_pg}),
        lifecycle_modules=[PostgresLifecycleModule(client=client, dsn=postgres_dsn)],
    )

    async with runtime.scope():          # starts the pool, runs lifecycle
        ctx = runtime.get_context()
        await ctx.document.command(user_spec).create(CreateUser(name="Ada"))

Integration tests are slower and require Docker, but they catch issues that mock adapters miss — schema migrations, constraint violations, connection handling.

items.title: Hybrid contexts: one real backend, mock for the rest
items.text:
Most integration tests only need one plane to be real. Pass MockDepsModule alongside the real modules and you get exactly that — real Postgres for documents and transactions, the mock for the queue the relay publishes into, the cache, the locks, everything else:

runtime = ExecutionRuntime(
    deps=DepsRegistry.from_modules(
        PostgresDepsModule(client=pg, tx={"default"}, outboxes={"events": events_pg}),
        MockDepsModule(state=shared_state),
    ).freeze(),
)

Everything MockDepsModule registers is marked a fallback: a background environment rather than a claim on a key. Where a real module registers the same contract, the real one wins; where none does, the mock answers. Module order does not matter — provenance decides, not position. Two real modules registering the same route still raise at build time, exactly as before, and so do two mock modules in one context.

You can mark your own registrations the same way — Deps.plain(deps, fallback=True) / Deps.routed(routes, fallback=True) — if you ship an environment module of your own. Real backend modules never set it.

A route the real module never registered reaches the mock

In a context that includes a fallback, an unregistered route does not fail — it falls back to the plain catch-all. A typo in a spec name therefore resolves to the mock instead of raising, and the mock is the capability superset, so it may accept a call the real backend would refuse.

Freeze names that hazard set at INFO (Hybrid deps wiring: … catch-all behind real routes: document_query, …) — the keys your real module routes and the mock still backs; the full fallback-served list is at DEBUG. The same report is check_wiring(...).fallbacks, and report.fallbacks.catch_all is the set to look at. To prove a test really hit the real adapter, assert your route is registered rather than inferred:

assert "orders" in ctx.deps.store.routed_deps[DocumentQueryDepKey]

Production is unaffected: it has no fallback module, so every overlap is still fail-loud.

items.title: Testing operations directly
items.text:
To exercise a registered operation — with its stage hooks and transaction plan, not just a raw port — run it with run_operation against a mock context. No HTTP, no transport:

import pytest
from forze.application.execution.operations import run_operation
from forze.base.exceptions import CoreException
from forze.testing import context_from_modules
from forze_mock import MockDepsModule

async def test_pay_order():
    ctx = context_from_modules(MockDepsModule())
    order_id = await run_operation(registry, "create_order", None, ctx)

    await run_operation(registry, "pay_order", PayCmd(order_id=order_id), ctx)

    order = await ctx.document.query(order_spec).get(order_id)
    assert order.paid

    # a domain failure surfaces as a CoreException (with a `.code`), the same as in production
    with pytest.raises(CoreException):
        await run_operation(registry, "pay_order", PayCmd(order_id=order_id), ctx)  # already paid

This tests domain logic and the operation's hooks without touching FastAPI or HTTP serialization.

items.title: Testing sagas and events
items.text:
A handler that emits a domain event stages it to the outbox inside the same transaction, and a saga reacts to it. To test that arc, wire the event handlers into the mock — MockDepsModule(domain_events=...) — run the operation, then inspect what was staged:

events = await ctx.outbox.query(order_events_spec).claim_pending()
assert len(events) == 1

See Events & sagas for the full model and the runnable order-fulfillment walkthrough that drives the whole aggregate → event → saga → outbox → relay → inbox flow in-process.

items.title: Reflection gates: test a property, not a case
items.text:
Some guarantees are about a whole surface — every import in a module tree, every port signature, every operation id — and a per-case test can't keep up with a surface that grows. forze.testing ships three gates for that; each discovers its set by reflection, checks the property over everything found, and refuses an empty discovery, so a rename can't turn the gate into a test that quietly checks nothing:

from uuid import UUID
from forze.testing import (
    assert_operation_namespaces,
    assert_pure_module,
    assert_scope_first,
)

def test_engine_is_pure():
    # allowlist catches the module nobody thought to name; the forbidden list is a
    # named refusal that widening the allowlist can never step over
    assert_pure_module(
        "app.core.engine",
        allowed=["math", "decimal", "attrs"],
        forbidden=["time", "random", "uuid", "os"],
    )

def test_ports_take_the_tenant_first():
    # positional-only is the mechanism: a keyword parameter can be omitted and
    # filled by a default — a caller must be physically unable to leave the key out
    assert_scope_first("app.ports.documents", name="tenant_id", annotation=UUID)

def test_edges_stay_disjoint():
    assert_operation_namespaces({
        "product": product_registry.operation_ids(),
        "operator": operator_registry.operation_ids(),
    })

Failures list every violation at once with its location. assert_scope_first takes exclude=["Port.method"] for deliberate exceptions — and an exclusion that matches nothing fails, so the list can only shrink.

items.title: Test organization
items.text:
A typical test structure for a Forze application:

tests/
├── unit/
│   ├── test_users.py      # domain logic, MockDepsModule
│   ├── test_orders.py
│   └── test_sagas.py
├── integration/
│   ├── test_postgres.py   # real DB, testcontainers
│   └── test_redis.py
└── conftest.py            # shared fixtures

Keep unit tests fast and parallelizable; run integration tests in CI or before deploy.

items.title: See also
items.text:
• Concurrency & isolation — force a deterministic interleaving; verify an adapter's isolation
  • Deterministic simulation — seed-driven exploration of concurrency, faults, and crashes
  • Contracts — ports and adapters overview
  • Transactions — strict mode details

items.title: Aggregate decisions
items.text: A state transition has a rule: which states it is legal from, and what it changes. Left in the handler, that rule scatters — the guard in one place, the write in another, sometimes duplicated and easy to forget. A decider puts it back on the aggregate: a pure method that validates the transition and returns the merge-patch to persist.

items.title: A decision on the aggregate
items.text:
A decider is an ordinary method on the aggregate. It reads the current state, raises if the transition is illegal, and returns the update DTO — no I/O, no ports:

class Order(Document, AggregateRoot):
    status: str = "pending"

    def confirm(self) -> "OrderUpdate":
        """Decide the ``pending`` -> ``confirmed`` transition (illegal from any other status).

        A pure decision method on the aggregate: it guards the transition and returns the merge-patch
        the repository persists under the order's revision. The rule lives here once — the saga step
        and the ``_on_confirm`` emitter both key on it instead of re-encoding it.
        """

        if self.status != "pending":
            raise exc.domain(f"cannot confirm an order in status {self.status!r}")

        return OrderUpdate(status="confirmed")

    @event_emitter(fields={"status"})
    def _on_confirm(before, after: Self, diff: JsonDict) -> DomainEvent | None:  # type: ignore[no-untyped-def]
        if after.status == "confirmed" and before.status != "confirmed":
            return OrderConfirmed(aggregate_id=after.id)

        return None

confirm() is the single home for the pending → confirmed rule. The @event_emitter beside it still fires OrderConfirmed when the status actually changes — the decider owns when the transition is allowed, the emitter owns what event it produces.

items.title: Load, decide, apply
items.text:
A handler runs the decision through AggregateRepository (forze_kits.aggregates): load the aggregate (so its behavior can run), decide by calling the method, apply the patch under the aggregate's revision:

async def _confirm(ctx: ExecutionContext, s: CheckoutCtx) -> CheckoutCtx:
    # Pivot. A pre-commit failure (e.g. payment declined) compensates `reserve`.
    if s.simulate_failure:
        log.error("payment declined — failing the pivot step")
        raise exc.domain("payment declined")

    # Load the aggregate, let it decide the transition, persist the patch under its rev (OCC).
    # confirm() single-sources the pending->confirmed rule (+ guards it); the resulting status
    # change fires @event_emitter -> OrderConfirmed, dispatched in THIS step's transaction (the
    # command flow), which the outbox bridge stages.
    orders = aggregate_repository(ctx, ORDER_SPEC)
    order = await orders.load(s.order_id)
    await orders.apply(order, order.confirm())
    # Transactional outbox: flush the staged event within the same transaction.
    await ctx.outbox.command(OUTBOX_SPEC).flush()

    log.info(
        "order confirmed — OrderConfirmed staged to outbox", order_id=str(s.order_id)
    )
    return s

apply() persists the merge-patch as update(id, rev, patch), so a concurrent write that moved the revision is rejected — the same optimistic-concurrency guard as any other write (concurrency conflicts). The re-applied patch fires the aggregate's emitters, and the resulting domain events dispatch in the same transaction; the repository never dispatches them itself.

items.title: Why move it down
items.text:
The hand-written alternative — command.update(id, rev, OrderUpdate(status="confirmed")) straight in the handler — works, but the rule lives nowhere: nothing guards that the order was pending, and the transition is re-encoded at every site that needs it (the step that writes it, the emitter that reacts to it). The decider:

  • single-sources the rule — one confirm(), called from every site, instead of a literal patch repeated per call;
  • guards the transition — an illegal confirm() raises exc.domain instead of silently writing a bad state;
  • stays visible to the correctness brand — the guard runs on the operation path, so a simulation that drives an illegal transition observes the rejection (unlike a pure @invariant, which the mock enforces before the write even lands).

Reach for a decider when a write is a transition with a rule; a plain command.update is still right for a field edit that carries no domain rule. When the rule spans more than one record, its cross-record counterpart is a system invariant.

items.title: Capability execution
items.text: Core Concepts introduced an operation as "a handler plus its plan." This chapter is that plan: the stages that wrap a handler, what each one may touch, and how Forze orders them — the mechanism every transaction, event, and authorization check rides on.

items.title: An operation is a pipeline
items.text:
The handler computes the result; everything around it is a stage. Stages run in a fixed order — some outside any transaction, some inside it, some only after it commits.

Stage When it runs Typical use before before the handler auth, input checks, rate limiting wrap around everything below before metrics, retries, idempotency prepare (two-phase) outside the transaction, before it opens external calls / compute that feed the write tx_before inside the transaction, before the handler locks, preconditions on_success (tx) inside the transaction, after the handler writes that must commit together after_commit after the root transaction commits best-effort follow-up on_success (outer) after everything succeeded out-of-transaction follow-up on_failure / finally_ on the outcome cleanup, error hooks

You author these on the registry's scope binders — bind_outer() for the outer scope, bind_tx().set_route(...) for the transactional one — then freeze().

A wrap may pass narrowed arguments on, as a document-scope authorization wrap does. Everything inside it then sees what it passes on: prepare, the transactional stages and the handler. Stages outside it see the arguments the operation was called with.

items.title: The handler owns the result
items.text:
One principle keeps the pipeline honest: the handler defines the result; stages never replace it. They observe, guard, and react — they don't substitute their own return value.

  • before sees only the args.
  • on_success and after_commit see the args and the result.
  • on_failure sees the exception; finally_ sees the outcome.

A stage may raise to abort the operation, but it can't quietly swap the answer. That's exactly why you can bolt on an audit log or a permission check without risk of corrupting what the handler returns.

items.title: Ordering within a stage
items.text:
When several hooks share a stage and one depends on another — authentication before authorization, a lock before a write — you don't hand-sort them. Each step declares capabilities: what it provides and what it requires.

from forze.application.contracts.execution import BeforeStep

registry = (
    registry
    .bind("orders.create")
    .bind_outer()
    .before(
        BeforeStep(id="authn", factory=authn_factory, provides=("authn.principal",)),
        BeforeStep(id="authz", factory=authz_factory, requires=("authn.principal",)),
    )
    .finish(deep=True)
    .freeze()
)

Forze orders the stage from those edges (topologically, then by priority, then declaration order). Use depends_on=(...) to order by explicit step id when there's no capability to name. For a single linear guard, a higher priority is enough — reach for capabilities only when hooks genuinely share prerequisites.

items.title: Cross-cutting patches
items.text:
bind(...) plans named operations. To apply a default across many — a tx route, a deadline, an audit hook — use patch(selector), which carries the same binder chain but targets every operation a selector matches:

from datetime import timedelta

from forze.base.primitives import str_key_selector

registry = (
    registry
    .patch(str_key_selector.all_keys())
    .with_deadline(timedelta(seconds=10))
    .finish(deep=True)
)

Patches are late-bound — selectors resolve at freeze() against the full set of operations — so a top-level patch(all_keys()) applied after assembling the registry covers everything in it. That reach is fail-closed across OperationRegistry.merge(...): a broad patch authored inside one sub-registry that would reach a sibling's operations makes merge raise, naming the offending selectors (a patch matching only its own part, or one added after the merge, is never flagged). Resolve a flagged reach by scoping the patch to a namespace (patch(selector, namespace=ns) — "everything I contribute"), settling it into concrete per-operation plans (materialize_patches()), or allowing it explicitly (merge(..., cross_registry=True)) when the patch is meant to govern downstream-contributed operations.

items.title: Validated at freeze, not at request
items.text:
freeze() is where the plan is checked and locked. Capability graphs must resolve — no missing or duplicate providers, no cycles — dispatch targets must exist, and any transactional stage must declare a route. A misconfigured pipeline fails when you build the registry, at startup, rather than on a user's first request.

That freeze-time check covers the transactional stages too — when those stages open a transaction, and what happens when one rolls back, is the subject of Transactions.

items.title: Concurrency & conflicts
items.text: Two requests that read the same document and write it back shouldn't silently clobber each other. Forze uses optimistic concurrency keyed on a revision number, with a history-based merge that lets non-overlapping edits through and rejects genuine collisions.

items.title: The revision
items.text:
Every Document carries a rev — an integer that starts at 1, is frozen on the model, and is bumped by the store on each write. You read at a revision, then write back the one you read:

order = await ctx.document.query(order_spec).get(order_id)
await ctx.document.command(order_spec).update(
    order.id, order.rev, OrderUpdate(status="paid"),
)

The rev you pass is the revision you expect to be current.

items.title: What happens on a concurrent write
items.text:
The store compares your expected rev to the stored one:

  • Match — apply the change and bump rev.
  • Differ — load the history snapshot at your revision and run a three-way merge. Edits that touch disjoint fields merge through (last-writer-wins per field); edits that touch the same fields raise exc.conflict (historical_consistency_violation). A field your write resends with the value it had at your revision touches nothing and is not written, so a concurrent change to it is kept.
  • A future revision raises exc.precondition (revision_mismatch); a revision whose history snapshot is missing raises exc.precondition (history_not_found_retry). Neither is retried for you: re-read the document and resubmit with its current rev.

So a stale write doesn't blindly overwrite: it either merges cleanly or surfaces a conflict for the caller to resolve.

History powers the merge

The three-way merge needs document history enabled. Without it, any revision mismatch is a precondition error rather than a merge attempt.

items.title: Refusing any change since you read
items.text:
The merge is right for ordinary edits and wrong for an action that approves one version: confirming an order as reviewed, signing off a document, accepting a quote. Any change since the reviewer read it should send them back. Pass merge=False to refuse every revision but the stored one, history or not:

await ctx.document.command(order_spec).update(
    order.id, order.rev, OrderUpdate(status="confirmed"), merge=False,
)

To record the sign-off without changing any field, touch it at the revision you read:

await ctx.document.command(order_spec).touch(order.id, rev=order.rev)

A stale rev raises exc.precondition (revision_mismatch), even for an update that changes nothing. The check is atomic: the write matches the revision you passed, so a writer committing between the store's read and its write makes it fail too. merge=False with no revision to check is refused as configuration.

An update that changes nothing writes nothing. Postgres checks its revision under a row lock, and Firestore in its transaction's read; both keep the row until commit. Mongo checks the revision it read and keeps nothing, since it locks a document only by writing it. Inside a Mongo transaction that read is the transaction's snapshot, so a writer can still commit before yours. Touch at the revision when the check must last until commit there.

update_many(..., merge=False) applies the check to every row, and touch_many(pks, revs=...) takes one revision per id. Every row is checked before any is written. A row a concurrent writer moves after that check is refused at its own write, and only a transaction undoes the rows written before it. Postgres opens one of its own; Mongo, Firestore and the in-memory store do not. Run a strict bulk write in a transaction when it must be all or nothing. The in-memory store keeps no history, so it is always this strict.

items.title: Related write helpers
items.text:
• Document.validate_historical_consistency(old, patch) is the check behind the merge — True when the concurrent change and yours touch disjoint fields.
  • Document.historical_update(old, patch) is what the merge writes: the part of patch that changes old, or None on a conflict.
  • command.touch(pk) bumps last_update_at and rev without other changes; touch(pk, rev=rev) bumps only a document still at rev.

Retrying a conflict safely is only half the story — a retried write must also not apply twice. That guarantee is Idempotency.

items.title: Errors & failures
items.text: In Forze a failure is a typed value with a kind. A handler (or a stage) raises a CoreException; its kind says what went wrong; the operation aborts and its transaction rolls back; and the edge turns it into a response. One model, end to end.

items.title: The failure taxonomy
items.text:
Raise a failure through the exc factory — the kind is the method:

from forze.base.exceptions import exc

raise exc.domain("A shipped order is final.")
raise exc.conflict("Email already registered.", code="email_taken")

Every CoreException carries a kind, a human summary, a machine code (defaults to core.<kind>), and optional details. The kinds:

Kind Use it for validation malformed input domain a business rule was violated precondition a required state wasn't met (e.g. a stale revision) conflict the change collides with current state concurrency a transient, retryable contention failure not_found the target doesn't exist authentication / authorization who they are / what they may do configuration the app is wired wrong (a startup-time mistake) infrastructure a backing system failed (transient) throttled a rate limit rejected the call (transient — capacity refills) timeout the invocation's time budget ran out (final — the budget is spent) unavailable it works, but is switched off right now — a feature flag, a maintenance window (transient) internal an unexpected bug

items.title: Raising aborts the operation
items.text: A raised CoreException propagates straight out: the operation stops, the transaction rolls back (no partial writes), and deferred after-commit work never runs. Stage hooks observe the failure — finally_ and on_failure get to clean up — but they don't swallow it; the kind reaches the caller intact.

items.title: Outcomes, when you need them
items.text: Handlers return their result or raise. When code needs the outcome rather than a raise — a finally_ hook, say — it receives an Outcome: Success(value) or Failure(exc).

items.title: Two flags every kind carries
items.text:
Beyond its meaning, each kind has an egress policy with two booleans:

  • expose_details — are the details safe to show a caller? (internal, authentication, authorization, configuration, infrastructure, throttled, timeout, and unavailable say no.) An error an integration translated from its backend's never shows its details, whatever its kind: they describe the failed call, and stay on the exception for your code and your logs.
  • retryable — is this transient? Only concurrency, infrastructure, throttled, and unavailable are. This flag is what the resilience retry policies key on — you can only retry a kind that declares itself retryable. (timeout is deliberately not retryable: within one invocation the budget is spent; a fresh invocation carries a fresh deadline.)

items.title: At the edge
items.text: Core stays transport-neutral — it never picks an HTTP status. The FastAPI integration turns a CoreException into a response, exposing details only when the kind's policy allows and logging the rest server-side. Raise unavailable rather than infrastructure for something an operator switched off: it answers 503, but its summary reaches the client and it is not logged as a server error, since nothing is broken.

items.title: Idempotency
items.text: Client retries and at-least-once delivery mean the same operation can arrive twice. Idempotency makes the duplicate a no-op that returns the first attempt's result — the handler and its writes run exactly once.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
When a request carries an idempotency key, the engine wraps the operation as the outermost wrap of its pipeline. On each call it:

  1. fingerprints the arguments (a stable payload hash);
  2. claims (operation, key, payload hash);
  3. if that claim already completed, returns the stored result — decoded back into the operation's typed result — and skips the handler and its transaction entirely;
  4. otherwise runs the handler and stores the encoded result.

The before hooks run ahead of the wrap chain, so authentication and authorization still run first — a replayed result is never an unauthorized one. What a duplicate skips is everything inside the wrap: the inner wraps, the transaction, and the handler.

items.title: Keys and payloads
items.text:
• The key comes from the caller. Over HTTP it's the Idempotency-Key header, bound to the context by the FastAPI middleware. No key → no dedup; the operation just runs.
  • The same key with a different payload is a conflict — a key can't be reused for a different request.
  • A key belongs to the caller. A claim is scoped to the tenant and the authenticated principal — on a delegated call, the subject together with its whole actor chain — so two callers who pick the same key never meet: each runs its own operation and replays its own result, and neither is told the other used it. An agent retrying its own request for a user replays; the user, or another agent, reusing that key runs its own operation under its own authorization. Calls with no authenticated principal share one anonymous space of their own. A tenant-aware store keeps each tenant's claims apart, whichever caller took them.

Upgrading to chain-scoped claims

A delegated call's claim taken before this scope was stored under the subject's own key, so until its window lapses the subject acting directly replays a record an agent produced. A tenant-aware Postgres store now carries the tenant in its keys, so a claim taken there before the upgrade is not replayed after it, once, within its window.

Two identities ride on a claim, and they answer different questions:

Question Effect Principal whose key is it? another caller's key behaves as unused Owner (the invocation) who may finish it? a claim reclaimed by a duplicate cannot be completed by the one that lost it

Keys stored before claims were scoped to a principal have a different shape, so a key claimed before that upgrade does not replay after it: a retry that spans the deploy runs again. Drain the dedup window across the deploy if that matters. Every shipped store scopes its claims; a store of your own should inherit ClaimPrincipalMixin and wire principal_provider, and one that does not is named in a warning when an operation resolves it.

items.title: Wiring
items.text: Declare an IdempotencySpec (it carries a TTL for how long a result is remembered) and register an idempotency adapter — commonly Redis — under that name. The operation's result type must be a Pydantic model, since the stored result is encoded and decoded. Wired end to end in the Add idempotency recipe.

items.title: When an operation outlives its window
items.text:
The TTL is a dedup window, so an operation slow enough to outlive it can find its key already reclaimed by a duplicate. The claim records which invocation took it, and a store refuses to complete or release a claim that now belongs to someone else — otherwise the slow operation would overwrite the live one's claim, and a third duplicate would replay a result for work that never finished.

On Postgres this needs one column on your table:

ALTER TABLE <your idempotency table> ADD COLUMN owner uuid;

It is nullable and additive, so nothing breaks before you run it and existing rows need no backfill, and you can apply it to a running deployment — the store notices the column within a minute and starts fencing, no restart required. Until you run it, that table works exactly as before but without the refusal above, and the store logs the relation once so the state is visible rather than assumed. Redis, Mongo and the mock need no migration.

Size the TTL for your redelivery horizon and this stays a corner case; the column is what makes the corner safe rather than silent.

items.title: Idempotency vs the inbox
items.text: Both dedupe, at different layers: idempotency dedupes inbound operations by caller-supplied key; the inbox dedupes consumed events by event id. Same principle — exactly-once effects over an at-least-once world.

items.title: Preview binding
items.text:
Idempotency answers "did I already send this?" Preview binding answers "is this still what I saw?" — the question every "confirm this" flow has: a quote, a filing, a consent form, an invoice. Between preview and submit the facts can move — another user edits a row, a scheduled job lands — and the caller then confirms something they never saw.

A preview returns its projection with a fingerprint. The confirming command carries the fingerprint back, the projection is computed again inside the command's transaction, and a mismatch refuses — never merges, never overwrites.

items.title: Declaring a flow
items.text:
One declaration, read by both sides, so the two can never fingerprint different things:

from pydantic import BaseModel

from forze.application.execution import ExecutionContext
from forze.domain.models import BaseDTO
from forze_kits.domain.preview import PreviewBinding, ReviewedCommand


class QuoteArgs(BaseDTO):
    quote_id: str


class ConfirmQuote(QuoteArgs, ReviewedCommand):  # the preview's arguments, plus `fingerprint`
    pass


class QuoteShown(BaseModel):
    lines: list[str]
    total: int
    rendered_at: str


async def show_quote(ctx: ExecutionContext, args: QuoteArgs) -> QuoteShown: ...


QUOTE = PreviewBinding(name="quote", projector=show_quote, exclude={"rendered_at"})
  • The preview returns await QUOTE.reviewed(ctx, args) — a Reviewed[QuoteShown] carrying data and fingerprint.
  • The confirmation is bound with QUOTE.bind(registry.bind("quote.confirm").bind_tx().set_route("pg").finish()), and its command is a ReviewedCommand.
  • exclude names fields the fingerprint ignores: a rendering hint, a generated_at stamp. Exclude rendering details, never the data being confirmed — a fingerprint over nothing confirms anything. A name the projection does not declare is refused.

items.title: What the confirmation does
items.text:
Inside its transaction, before the handler runs, the binding computes the projection again and compares fingerprints. On a mismatch the operation fails with precondition, code preview_changed, naming the flow. It says the preview is stale and not what changed — the caller may no longer be allowed to see the new value. The remedy is to show the preview again and confirm what it shows now.

The confirmation runs at snapshot isolation (isolation= raises it to serializable; read committed is refused). Below snapshot, a write landing between the check and the handler's own reads would reach the handler, which would then act on a state nobody was shown. Snapshot can refuse a concurrent write with a concurrency error, which is retryable. An operation that already declares serializable passes isolation=IsolationLevel.SERIALIZABLE to bind — two different levels on one operation are refused when the registry freezes.

Detection, not a lock

Nothing is held between preview and confirmation. Two callers can both preview, and the second one's confirmation refuses — correct, and not what "binding" might suggest. Keeping concurrent writers apart is SerializedBy's job.

The fingerprint is sha256-c1:<hex> over a canonical form of its own — sets sorted, dates in ISO 8601, UUIDs and decimals as strings — identical in every process and unmoved by dependency upgrades. A future form takes a new prefix, so a fingerprint from an old one refuses rather than matching. It is not signed: a tampered fingerprint only makes its own confirmation fail.

items.title: System invariants
items.text: An @invariant keeps a single entity correct: it sees one record and decides whether that record is valid. But some rules span records, and no single entity owns them — a ledger's entries must sum to zero, an order may have at most one captured payment, a tenant's seats in use must not exceed its plan. A check on one row cannot see the others. A SystemInvariant declares such a law, and Forze enforces it at the right isolation and proves it under simulation.

items.title: A law over a read-set
items.text:
A system invariant is a predicate over an aggregate of a scoped set of records. You declare three things: the records it ranges over (a ReadSet), how to collapse them to one number (SumOf or CountAll), and what that number must satisfy (holds):

from forze.application.contracts.invariants import SystemInvariant, ReadSet, CountAll

one_capture_per_order = SystemInvariant(
    name="single-capture-per-order",
    read_set=ReadSet(
        spec=PAYMENT,
        scope_keys=("order_id",),
        where={"$values": {"status": "captured"}},
    ),
    aggregate=CountAll(),
    holds=lambda n: n <= 1,
)

The law holds per distinct scope value — once per order here, because scope_keys=("order_id",). Empty scope_keys declares a global law (one check over the whole where-filtered collection); reuse tenant_aware in where for a per-tenant scope. holds is a pure function of the aggregate, and must be deterministic and side-effect-free, because the same predicate runs in production and inside the simulation. It receives a CountAll's cardinality as an int, and a SumOf's total as an exact Decimal when the read model declares the field Decimal, else as a float. The type follows the declaration, not the backend, so a law sees the same value on the mock, Postgres and Mongo: lines of 0.1 and 0.2 total exactly Decimal("0.3"), never 0.30000000000000004. A sum the read model does not declare (a path into a dict) is passed as a float, with a warning when the law is declared.

A Decimal total does not mix with float arithmetic

Comparing a Decimal with an int or a float works, but arithmetic does not: total * 1.1 raises TypeError. Write the factor as a Decimal (total * Decimal("1.1")). Violation messages print the value as it is, so a count reads 3, not 3.0.

items.title: Compare two read-sets
items.text:
Some laws bound one aggregate by another: an order's lines never exceed the order's quantity, refunds never exceed sales. Declare the second side with against, a Measure scoped by the same values, and holds takes both aggregates:

from forze.application.contracts.invariants import Measure

lines_within_order = SystemInvariant(
    name="lines-within-order",
    read_set=ReadSet(spec=ORDER_LINE, scope_keys=("order_id",)),
    aggregate=SumOf("qty"),
    against=Measure(
        read_set=ReadSet(spec=ORDER, scope_keys=("id",)),
        aggregate=SumOf("qty"),  # the order's own field: a sum over its one row
    ),
    holds=lambda lines, order: lines <= order,
)

The two sides' scope_keys pair by position: here each order's lines (order_id) meet the order whose id matches. Every evaluator matches a UUID by its string and a plain Enum member by its value, so a str field can refer to a UUID id or to a string-valued Enum. A pairing no evaluator would match, such as an int against a str or a UUID, or a date against a datetime, is refused when the law is declared, as is a holds that does not take two arguments. Runtime enforcement takes the law's own scope params ({"order_id": ...}) and binds the other side from them.

The two sides are separate reads, and a detective check runs outside any transaction, so a write can commit between them. Runtime evaluation therefore reads the law's own side again after the other, and uses the pair only if that side did not change. If it changes on each of three reads, evaluation raises exc.concurrency with the code system_invariant_unstable_read rather than judge values no committed state held.

Every scope with rows on either side is checked, and the side with no rows there counts as 0. A scope with rows on neither side does not exist, so no evaluator calls holds for it. That is what makes a minimum checkable. A one-sided law only ever sees scopes that have rows, so CountAll with n >= 1 cannot notice an order whose last line was removed. Put the orders on the other side and every order becomes a scope:

order_has_a_line = SystemInvariant(
    name="order-has-a-line",
    read_set=ReadSet(spec=ORDER_LINE, scope_keys=("order_id",)),
    aggregate=CountAll(),
    against=Measure(read_set=ReadSet(spec=ORDER, scope_keys=("id",)), aggregate=CountAll()),
    holds=lambda lines, orders: orders == 0 or lines >= 1,
)

Keep the side you enforce from as read_set: an aggregate kit reads the law's own scope_keys off the row it wrote, so a kit over order lines needs order_id there, not id.

items.title: Enforce it: detective or preventive
items.text:
Two enforcement modes, from forze_kits.invariants, trade timing against cost:

  • enforce(law, ctx, params) — detective. It schedules the check for after the writing transaction commits (via run_or_defer), so it observes committed state, and raises exc.domain if the law broke. The offending write is already durable — this reports the breach, it does not undo it. Cheap, and right when you can compensate after the fact.
  • enforce_preventive(law, ctx, params) — preventive. It evaluates the law inside the writing transaction, before commit, so a violation rolls the write back — the bad state never lands. Call it after the writes, inside the scope:
async with ctx.tx_ctx.scope(route, isolation=law.required_isolation):
    ...  # your writes
    await enforce_preventive(law, ctx, params)

Prevention is only sound at or above the law's required_isolation (default SERIALIZABLE): a weaker level lets a write-skew interleaving slip two concurrent writes past the check, each blind to the other. So enforce_preventive fails closed — it raises exc.configuration if the active transaction is weaker than required (or absent) rather than hand back enforcement a race would defeat. Opening the scope at the required level already pays the backend half of the gate, since scope(isolation=…) fail-closes against the manager's TxCapabilities.

items.title: Ask before you write: propose
items.text:
For an agent or a UI that wants to know "would this write be accepted?" before committing to it, propose dry-runs the write:

from forze_kits.invariants import propose

verdict = await propose(ctx, do_the_write, [(law, params)], route=route)
if not verdict.holds:
    handle(verdict.failed)   # the laws that would break

propose opens its own root transaction, applies the write through the governed ports (so tenancy, encryption, and domain guards all run), evaluates each law against the result, then rolls everything back — nothing persists. The ProposalVerdict is holds=True only if the write applied cleanly and every law held; failed names the laws that wouldn't, and error carries the rejection if the write itself was refused.

propose is a filter, not a proof

holds=True means "the write applied cleanly and the laws held against the state the dry-run saw". Under concurrency the answer can change between the dry-run and the real write (TOCTOU), and it is only as sound as the backend's rollback — so use it to filter and explain a proposed write, never to certify it safe. It also fails closed (exc.precondition) if called inside a transaction: a nested scope is only a savepoint, whose rollback isn't guaranteed across backends, so the dry-run's writes could ride the enclosing commit. The proof is the oracle below.

items.title: Prove it under simulation
items.text:
Because a law is declared as data — scope fields, not an opaque filter-builder — DST can compile it into an oracle that checks every scope the run produced, not a hand-listed few:

from forze_dst import Simulation
from forze_dst.oracle import compile_oracle

oracle = compile_oracle(one_capture_per_order)
simulation = Simulation(
    operations=registry,
    deps=lambda: MockDepsModule(),
    observe=oracle.observe,
    invariants=[*oracle.invariants],
)

By default the oracle checks the law over final state, with one grouped aggregate per side. A one-sided law checks only the scopes that have rows; a paired law checks every scope with rows on either side. compile_oracle(law, per_commit=True) upgrades to a per-commit trace fold: it checks the law after every committed transaction, catching a violation that a later transaction heals — the transient a final-state check misses. Per-commit mode reads the value trace, so it needs SimulationConfig(capture_values=True).

This is the guarantee propose can't give. Where propose filters one write against the state it saw, the oracle drives the law through thousands of hostile interleavings and proves it holds across all of them — and because the same holds predicate runs in production enforcement, in the dry-run, and in the oracle, what you simulate is exactly what you ship.

items.title: Transactions
items.text: When several writes must succeed or fail as a unit, wrap them in a transaction scope. Forze owns the boundary — begin on entry, commit on a clean exit, roll back on an exception — while the adapter does the real database work.

items.title: A transaction scope
items.text:
Open a scope by route, the same logical name the deps wiring registered under tx={...}. Everything inside commits together:

async with ctx.tx_ctx.scope("orders"):
    order = await ctx.document.command(order_spec).create(cmd)
    await ctx.document.command(line_spec).create(line_cmd)
# committed here; an exception inside would have rolled it all back

Both writes land on a transactional backend, so both roll back together. Not everything you can call inside a scope does — see What commits together.

The route must be registered for transactions when you wire the module — PostgresDepsModule(client=pg, ..., tx={"orders"}) — otherwise the scope can't resolve a transaction manager.

A scope holds a connection only from the first query

With lazy_transaction enabled (the default) on the Postgres, Mongo, and Firestore clients, opening a scope acquires no pooled connection until the first query inside it — so parsing or calling an external service before you touch the database doesn't park a connection idle-in-transaction, and a scope that runs no query holds and commits nothing.

items.title: What commits together
items.text:
A scope has a scope key — the kind of transaction, such as a database versus a cache. A port joins the active transaction only if its scope key matches; a port of a different kind runs outside it.

Atomicity is bounded to one manager

A transaction coordinates only the operations that share its scope key and client. Two Postgres writes against the same connection commit atomically; a Postgres write and a Redis write do not. When you need consistency across systems, you don't reach for a bigger transaction — you stage the cross-system effect and apply it after commit (see below and Events & sagas).

Queues, streams, object storage, caches, locks, and search/analytics writes are not transactional in production, so they never roll back with the scope.

Counters are the case worth calling out, because they look like an ordinary Postgres write and are not one: a counter allocation runs on its own connection, outside the caller's transaction, on every backend — Redis, Postgres, Mongo and Firestore alike. A rolled-back transaction does not give the number back. That is deliberate: a sequence you could roll back would reissue an invoice number already handed out. Treat an allocated number as spent and let gaps happen.

items.title: Two-phase handlers: work before the write
items.text:
Lazy acquisition keeps the transaction off the connection until your first query — but only for work that runs before that query. When an external call has to sit between a read and a write, split the handler into two phases instead:

class QuoteAndCreate(TwoPhaseDocumentHandler[QuoteRequest, int, WidgetRead, WidgetCreate]):
    enrich: PricingService

    async def prepare(self, args):                 # outside the transaction
        return await self.enrich.quote(args.sku)   # external call — no tx held

    async def apply(self, args, price):            # inside the transaction
        return await self.writer.create(WidgetCreate(price=price))

Register it with .two_phase():

registry.bind("quote").two_phase().bind_tx().set_route("orders").finish()

The engine runs prepare in the outer scope — before the transaction opens — and threads its return value into apply, which runs inside the transaction.
