So the transaction wraps only the writes, never the external call. Worked end to end in the two-phase handler recipe; for CPU-heavy prepare work, offload it off the event loop.

What prepare can and can't do

prepare runs under the read-only flag, so it cannot write: a write port refuses there, the handler's own self.writer included (use self.reader for reads, self.writer only in apply). Its reads run outside apply's transaction, so there's no read/write atomicity between the phases — validate on write in apply (an optimistic-concurrency rev check). prepare runs exactly once per invocation: if a retry or hedge wrap re-runs the operation, only apply repeats — with the payload prepare already produced.

items.title: Nesting
items.text:
Scopes nest naturally. A nested scope of the same kind joins the outer transaction rather than starting a new one — with a savepoint where the backend supports it, so an inner failure can roll back without losing the outer work:

async with ctx.tx_ctx.scope("orders"):
    await ctx.document.command(order_spec).create(cmd)

    async with ctx.tx_ctx.scope("orders"):   # joins the same transaction
        await ctx.document.command(line_spec).create(line_cmd)

A nested scope whose kind doesn't match the active transaction is a programming error and is rejected immediately — you can't open a cache transaction inside a database one and expect them to commit together.

items.title: Read-only transactions
items.text:
QUERY operations open their scope read_only=True, so the backend begins a read-only transaction where it supports one (Postgres BEGIN … READ ONLY) and rejects accidental writes. You rarely set this by hand — the operation kind does it for you.

A manager whose store refused every write in the transaction it opened says so through ReadOnlyAware.read_only_enforced(). Postgres and the mock's journal and strict managers do, but not for a scope nested in a transaction opened outside forze, which becomes a savepoint. A nested scope on another route resolves another manager and opens a transaction of its own, so the read-only root counts only while it is the only route a finished scope entered. After-commit work queued with run_or_defer may write, so it gives up the skip too. A query interrupted after such a read is safe to re-run rather than commit_ambiguous.

items.title: Isolation
items.text:
Most operations are fine at the backend's default isolation. When one needs a stronger guarantee — no lost update, no write skew — declare it on the operation and the kernel holds the backend to it:

plan = (
    OperationPlan()
    .bind_tx()
    .set_route("orders")
    .set_isolation(IsolationLevel.SERIALIZABLE)
    .finish()
)

The level is fail-closed. When the root scope is first entered, the kernel checks that the route's transaction manager actually supports it (a manager opts in by reporting its TxCapabilities); if it can't — or reports nothing — the operation raises exc.configuration (code="tx_isolation_unsupported") rather than silently running weaker isolation. Declaring isolation without a transaction route is rejected at registry freeze for the same reason: there is no transaction to carry it.

IsolationLevel is intent-named and ordered — READ_COMMITTED < SNAPSHOT < SERIALIZABLE — and each adapter maps it to its backend's spelling. The mock honors all three through an in-memory MVCC overlay (it rejects the write-write, write-skew, and phantom conflicts the level forbids), so an isolation-dependent bug is catchable in a unit test or under simulation.

items.title: Serializing an operation
items.text:
Some operations must not run twice at once for the same input. A recompute of an order's totals reads every line and writes the sum. Two of them in parallel can each read a different set of lines, and the second to commit wins with a stale sum. Optimistic concurrency does not help when the conflict is between two reads of rows that neither write touches.

SerializeOperation makes invocations that share a key take turns. The lock is taken inside the operation's transaction and held until the root transaction commits or rolls back:

from forze.application.hooks.locking import SerializeOperation

registry = (
    registry.bind("orders.recompute")
    .bind_tx()
    .set_route("orders")
    .before(SerializeOperation(key=lambda args: args.order_id).to_step())
    .finish(deep=True)
)

A second orders.recompute for the same order waits at that step until the first one's transaction ends. Different orders, and different tenants, never wait on each other. The lock is keyed by the operation's registered name, the bound tenant and the key, so another operation never shares it unless both name a group. Under a two-phase handler it covers apply only: prepare runs before the transaction opens.

The key function returns one value or a tuple of values. Each must be a str, an int, a UUID or a timezone-aware datetime. A datetime locks on its instant, so two offsets of one moment take the same lock. Any other type (None, an enum member, a bool, a float) is refused as configuration (operation_lock_key_unsupported); pass an enum's .value. A naive datetime is refused as validation (operation_lock_key_naive_datetime). What the key function returns is known only when the operation runs, so these refuse that call, and the error names the operation.

An operation that runs nested in another one's transaction takes the lock in a savepoint. If the nested operation succeeds, its lock stays until the root transaction ends, as its writes do. If it fails, Postgres rolls the savepoint back and releases the lock with the writes it guarded, while the outer transaction carries on. The mock keeps the lock until the root ends either way, which is stricter.

Wiring problems surface before the first request:

  • Placed in the outer scope, which runs before the transaction opens, it is refused at registry freeze (tx_lock_outside_transaction_scope).
  • An operation with no transaction route is refused there too (tx_lock_without_route), as is a group spread over several routes (tx_lock_group_spans_routes).
  • A route whose backend has no transaction-scoped lock is refused when the operation is resolved, on its first call or under check_wiring (tx_lock_unsupported). Postgres has one; Mongo and Firestore do not. The lock comes from the route's transaction manager, so it is always the lock of the store that transaction runs on, whatever else is wired. It never falls back to a Redis lease.

On Postgres the lock is pg_advisory_xact_lock on the transaction's own connection. Nothing expires mid-transaction and nothing needs a fencing token, because only a commit or a rollback releases it. A wait counts against the operation's deadline. The mock takes the same per-owner write locks a SerializedBy write takes, under the journal and strict managers. transactions="none" opens no transaction, so it binds no lock and the operation is refused at resolve.

To take a lock by hand inside a scope, call the port the step uses:

async with ctx.tx_ctx.scope("orders"):
    await ctx.tx_locks("orders").hold(key)  # key: a 64-bit int, e.g. advisory_lock_key(...)

Outside a transaction it is refused (tx_lock_outside_transaction), since the lock would end with its own statement. One hold call takes its keys in sorted order. Two calls, or two transactions taking keys in opposite orders, can deadlock; one side is refused as a retryable concurrency, on Postgres and the mock alike.

Which lock to reach for

The SerializedBy guarantee and command.hold(...) lock a document owner: every write for that owner takes the lock, whoever wrote the code. SerializeOperation locks an operation input: only invocations of that operation, or of its group, take it, and the key need not be any document's field. A distributed lock is a lease for work outside any transaction; its release is not tied to a commit.

items.title: Sharing one lock between operations
items.text:
Two different operations sometimes must exclude each other: a job that recomputes a derived table, and another operation that reads it and writes into it. Give both the same group, and the group takes the operation's place in the lock key:

serialize = SerializeOperation(key=lambda args: (), group="requirements")

registry = (
    registry.bind("requirements.recompute")
    .bind_tx()
    .set_route("orders")
    .before(serialize.to_step())
    .finish(deep=True)
    .bind("requirements.extend")
    .bind_tx()
    .set_route("orders")
    .before(serialize.to_step())
    .finish(deep=True)
)

Every operation naming the group waits on every other one with the same key, as invocations of one operation do. The tenant stays in the key, so different tenants still never wait on each other. A group keys in its own namespace, so a group named orders.recompute never shares the lock of the operation of that name. The name must be a non-empty string without surrounding whitespace, or the constructor refuses it as configuration (operation_lock_group_invalid); a StrEnum member keys as its plain value.

Setting, changing or dropping an operation's group changes its lock key. During a rolling deployment, old and new nodes would then hold different locks and not wait on each other, so drain the operation's writers before rolling the change out.

The lock lives in the backend of the route's transaction manager, so two routes would hold two unrelated locks. Freeze refuses a group whose operations run on different transaction routes (tx_lock_group_spans_routes), even when both routes reach one database. It compares the operations of the registry it freezes, so merge registries before freezing to check a group across them.

items.title: After the commit
items.text:
Some work must happen only if the transaction commits — publishing an event, sending a notification, enqueuing a job. Doing it inside the scope risks acting on a change that later rolls back. Defer it instead:

await ctx.tx_ctx.run_or_defer(send_confirmation)

Inside a transaction, the callback is queued and runs after the root scope commits successfully. Outside any transaction, it runs immediately. This single mechanism is the foundation of the transactional outbox — covered next.

Deferred work is also cancellation-protected: a client disconnect or a deadline expiring between the commit and the deferred callbacks can't skip them — they run to completion, then the cancellation re-raises. A committed transaction is never left half-announced.

A deferred callback that fails never takes the committed result down with it: the failure is logged and the operation still returns normally. To surface those failures for alerting instead of relying on logs, install a handler when building the runtime — build_runtime(..., after_commit_error_handler=...) — and it is notified out-of-band with an AfterCommitError describing each failed callback. The handler must not raise.

items.title: Transactions under the mock
items.text:
The mock transaction manager is faithful by default (transactions="journal"): an aborted transaction undoes only its own writes, so a "forgot to run it in the same transaction" bug fails in tests exactly as it would in production, and concurrent transactions still interleave — the basis simulation needs. It rolls back what a database would — documents, outbox rows, inbox marks, the document-backed identity stores — and deliberately not the non-transactional backends (queues, streams, storage, caches, counters, locks, search/analytics): rolling those back would hide the cross-system gaps the outbox exists to close. Nested scopes act as savepoints, a QUERY root enforces read_only (a participating write raises code="read_only_tx"), and the manager honors the declared isolation level through its MVCC overlay.

Two other modes are opt-in when wiring MockDepsModule: transactions="strict" restores a global snapshot on rollback, so concurrent root transactions serialize; transactions="none" is the legacy no-op (writes persist through a rollback) kept only for comparison.

Row locks — a for_update read, and the lock a write takes on the row it changes — are claims by default: nobody waits, and of two transactions over a locked row the one that commits second is aborted with a conflict. That is safe, but it cannot tell a correct lock order from a deadlock-prone one, since both abort under contention. MockDepsModule(row_locks="block") makes the contender wait instead, as Postgres does: it parks until the holder commits or rolls back, then carries on against the committed row. At SNAPSHOT or SERIALIZABLE isolation, a row changed since the transaction's snapshot fails with exc.concurrency(code="serialization_failure") instead, as Postgres refuses it. A wait that would close a cycle — two transactions taking the same rows in opposite orders — aborts the waiter with exc.concurrency (code="deadlock_detected", the rows in its details), and a simulation reports it as a no_lock_order_deadlock violation. The mock only blocks on the simulation loop, which reports a wait that never ends instead of hanging; on any other loop it falls back to claims. It needs the default transactions="journal".

"nowait" and "skip_locked" are a mock divergence in either mode. On Postgres, NOWAIT raises instead of waiting and SKIP LOCKED passes over a held row; the mock gives both plain for_update behaviour, as the RowLockMode contract allows for backends without them, so in blocking mode they wait. The mechanism divergences on Fidelity list skip-locked-degrades-to-for-update.

A transaction rolls back when an operation raises; what those failures are, and how a raised error becomes a response, is Errors.

items.title: Wiring
items.text: Core Concepts showed that an ExecutionRuntime takes a frozen dependency registry and a frozen lifecycle plan. A real service builds both from several integration packages at once. This chapter is how you get from forze[postgres,redis] to a running runtime.

items.title: Integration modules
items.text:
Every integration package ships a deps module — a small object that registers its adapters, keyed by specification name. You never construct adapters yourself; you hand the module its client and the routes it should serve.

Module Registers (examples) PostgresDepsModule document query/command, search, transactions RedisDepsModule cache, counters, idempotency S3DepsModule object storage MockDepsModule in-memory adapters for every contract

items.title: Build the dependency registry
items.text:
DepsRegistry.from_modules(...) merges every module into one registry. The same logical name — "orders" — appears in the spec, in each module's route map, and nowhere does a handler learn which backend answered.

from forze.application.execution import DepsRegistry
from forze_postgres import PostgresClient, PostgresDepsModule
from forze_redis import RedisClient, RedisDepsModule

pg = PostgresClient()
redis = RedisClient()

deps = DepsRegistry.from_modules(
    PostgresDepsModule(client=pg, rw_documents={"orders": orders_pg}, tx={"orders"}),
    RedisDepsModule(client=redis, caches={"orders": orders_cache}),
)

One name, everywhere

A module route key (rw_documents={"orders": ...}) must match the DocumentSpec.name it serves. Merging two modules that register the same contract under the same route raises a CoreException at build time — a misconfiguration caught before the app starts, not at the first request.

Build incrementally with registry.with_modules(...) when modules come from different parts of your codebase.

One registration kind is exempt from that conflict: a fallback module (Deps.plain(..., fallback=True), which is how MockDepsModule registers everything) yields to a real module instead of colliding with it. That is what lets a test or a partially-migrated app say "real Postgres, mock everything else" in one deps list — see hybrid contexts. Production wiring marks nothing, so every overlap there stays fail-loud.

items.title: The lifecycle plan
items.text:
Deps describe what to build; the lifecycle plan decides when clients connect and disconnect. They're kept separate on purpose — registration is pure and cheap, while opening a pool is an ordered, fallible startup step.

from forze.application.execution import LifecyclePlan
from forze_postgres import PostgresConfig, PostgresLifecycleModule
from forze_redis import redis_lifecycle_step

lifecycle = (
    LifecyclePlan.from_modules(
        PostgresLifecycleModule(
            client=pg,
            dsn="postgresql://forze:forze@localhost:5432/forze",
            config=PostgresConfig(min_size=1, max_size=10),
        ),
    )
    .with_steps(redis_lifecycle_step(dsn="redis://localhost:6379/0"))
)

Each step declares what it requires and provides, so the plan orders startup by dependency (and runs shutdown in reverse). If a startup step fails, the steps that already ran are torn down before the error propagates.

items.title: Freeze and construct
items.text:
The runtime takes frozen inputs and does not coerce them — freezing is what validates the plan and makes it safe to share across every request.

from forze.application.execution import ExecutionRuntime

runtime = ExecutionRuntime(
    deps=deps.freeze(),
    lifecycle=lifecycle.freeze(),
)

From here, async with runtime.scope(): opens the pools and serves requests, as covered in Runtime.

Freezing validates the plan's shape — not that every operation can actually resolve its ports from these deps. A rarely-hit operation asking for a port nobody registered would otherwise fail on its first call. To close that gap, dry-run the frozen operation registry with check_wiring (exported from forze.application.execution): it eagerly resolves every operation — handler, hooks, transactional stages, saga dispatch targets — through the same code path a real call takes, and collects every failure instead of stopping at the first:

from forze.application.execution import ExecutionContext, check_wiring

report = check_wiring(operations, lambda: ExecutionContext(deps=runtime.deps.resolve()))
report.raise_if_failed()

Run it as a startup gate in dev and staging, or as a test against your mock wiring, and a missing dependency surfaces before traffic does.

items.title: Routed clients
items.text:
When the current tenant decides which database or cache to talk to, swap the plain client for a routed one — RoutedPostgresClient, RoutedRedisClient — and use that integration's routed lifecycle step. The deps and specs don't change; only the client and its lifecycle step do.

from forze_postgres import RoutedPostgresClient

# resolves a per-tenant DSN from secrets — see Multi-tenancy for the resolver wiring
pg = RoutedPostgresClient(...)
# PostgresDepsModule(client=pg, ..., introspector_cache_partition_key=current_tenant)

How routing resolves a tenant to a connection — and the schema-per-tenant alternative — is the subject of Multi-tenancy.
